# Technical Specification

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 Executive Summary

### 1.1.1 Project Overview

This repository contains **`Hello`**, a deliberately minimal single-class Java console application, together with the operational guide and licence that surround it. The entire executable system is one file: `Hello.java`, 20 lines and 1,073 bytes, declaring `public class Hello` in the default package with a single member — the JVM entry point `public static void main(String[] args)`. That method performs exactly one action, `System.out.println("Hello from Java!")`, and then returns normally.

`README.md` states the character of the system in its own words: `Hello` "is a minimal single-class Java console application. It writes one fixed greeting to standard output and then terminates; it reads no input, opens no resource and keeps no state" (`README.md`, line 12). The source itself carries the same contract in its class Javadoc, which describes a "Minimal, stateless console application" that has no field, creates no instance, and "imports nothing outside `java.lang`, so a JDK alone builds and runs it" (`Hello.java`, lines 1–5).

The complete tracked inventory of the repository is five files, of which exactly one is source code:

| Tracked Artifact | Size | Role in the System |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Hello.java` | 20 lines / 1,073 bytes | The entire executable system: class `Hello` and its `main` entry point |
| `README.md` | 77 lines / 4,053 bytes | Operational guide: overview, requirements, build, run, output contract, layout, licence |
| `LICENSE` | 674 lines / 35,149 bytes | Complete GNU General Public License, Version 3 (29 June 2007) |
| `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` | 476 lines / 45,009 bytes | Project-status report, validation record, and development guide |
| `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` | 8,321 lines / 839,724 bytes | Prior generation of this technical specification |

The proportions are themselves a defining property of the project: the two generated Markdown artifacts under `blitzy/documentation/` account for 884,733 of the repository's 925,008 tracked bytes, while the program they document is 1,073 bytes. The system has no build manifest, no dependency declaration, no test suite, no continuous-integration descriptor, no container definition, and no configuration file of any kind — verified by direct existence checks at the repository root for `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts`, `settings.gradle`, `build.xml`, `Makefile`, `.gitignore`, `.gitattributes`, `.java-version`, `.sdkmanrc`, `module-info.java`, `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.editorconfig`, `Jenkinsfile`, `.travis.yml`, `.github/`, `.circleci/`, `requirements.txt`, and `package.json`, all absent. The only directory in the entire working tree is `blitzy/documentation/`; there is no `src/` and no `test/`.

### 1.1.2 Core Business Problem

The program does not solve a domain problem — it solves a **toolchain-and-comprehension problem**. Concretely, the repository addresses three needs that its own artifacts make explicit:

1. **Proving that a Java toolchain works end to end with nothing else in the way.** Because `Hello.java` declares no package, imports nothing outside `java.lang`, and requires no resolved dependency, a successful compile-and-run exercises the JDK and JVM alone. `README.md` (line 18) states the requirement precisely: "A JDK is all that is required," and confirms the repository "pins no Java version" and "has no dependency manifest, so nothing has to be resolved or downloaded before building." Any failure observed while running this program is therefore attributable to the environment, not to the program.

2. **Removing ambiguity about how to build and launch the program.** The three earliest commits (`c537a19` "Initial commit", `f1847fa` "Add files via upload", `0726b1d` "Add initial README file with basic information") left a repository whose README was a placeholder. Commits `3c3af75` "Document Hello.java: one comment per written functionality", `dabe2c9` "Replace README placeholder with project guide", `14ed6db`, and `ce8e85c` replaced that placeholder with the eight-section operational guide now in `README.md` and added four explanatory comments to the source. `README.md` records this change itself, dated 2026-09-16 (lines 5–8).

3. **Making a trivially small codebase legible without reading it as a puzzle.** Non-obvious properties that a reader would otherwise have to infer are now written down at the point of use: why the class launches by the bare name `Hello` (default package), why `args` exists but is never consulted, that the single `println` is the only write to any sink, and that termination is by normal return rather than `System.exit` (`Hello.java`, lines 1–5, 7–14, 16, 18; `README.md`, lines 46–51, 63).

### 1.1.3 Key Stakeholders and Users

Stakeholders are identified from repository evidence — commit authorship, the audience each document addresses, and the licence terms — not from any stakeholder register, which the repository does not contain.

| Stakeholder | Evidence in the Repository | Interest in the System |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repository owner / original author | Commits `c537a19`, `f1847fa`, `0726b1d` authored by `rjhonsi` | Owns the program, the GPLv3 licensing choice, and the outstanding hygiene decisions |
| Operators and learners running the program | `README.md` Requirements, Build, Run, Expected Output sections (lines 16–63) | Need a dependency-free, reproducible build-and-run path and a stated output contract |
| Maintainers editing the source | `Hello.java` class and `main` Javadoc; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9 Development Guide | Need the design intent (statelessness, ignored `args`, normal return) preserved across edits |
| Automated documentation agents | 10 commits authored by "Blitzy Agent" plus merge `2a78292` by `blitzy-qa[bot]` | Produce and maintain `blitzy/documentation/` and this specification |
| Downstream recipients under GPLv3 | `LICENSE` (complete GPL v3 text, 29 June 2007); `README.md` line 77 | Hold the rights to run, study, modify, and redistribute the covered work |

There are no authenticated end users, no roles, and no permissions: the program exposes no user interface, no port, no network surface, and no authentication or authorisation surface. Its only interaction channel is the standard-output stream of the process that launches it.

### 1.1.4 Expected Business Impact and Value Proposition

The value this repository delivers is **certainty at negligible cost** — a runnable artifact whose behaviour is fully specified in advance, so that it can be used as a fixed reference point.

| Value Dimension | Observed Basis | Resulting Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zero setup cost | No dependency manifest; "A JDK is all that is required" (`README.md`, line 18) | Nothing to resolve, download, or configure before the first build |
| Deterministic, verifiable output | One `println`; `args` never dereferenced; no `System.exit` (`Hello.java`, lines 11–18) | Identical stdout on every run regardless of arguments; empty stderr; exit status 0 |
| Unambiguous operating instructions | Two documented launch paths with a stated JDK-11 floor for the single-file path (`README.md`, lines 20–44) | An operator can build and run correctly on first attempt, on old or current JDKs |
| Clean-working-tree discipline | Recommended `mktemp -d` compile destination and "Do not commit the class file either way" (`README.md`, line 30) | Compiler output is kept out of the checkout, which has no `.gitignore` |
| Unrestricted reuse | Complete GPLv3 text in `LICENSE` | Copyleft rights to run, modify, and redistribute are explicit, not assumed |

The impact is intentionally narrow. The repository contains no revenue model, no service-level agreement, no user-volume target, and no operational metric of any kind, and this specification does not assert any. Where the repository does record quantified project outcomes, those figures are its own: `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` reports the work "84.2% complete — 32.0 of 38.0 hours" (line 15) and "49 checks executed, 49 passed, 0 failed" comprising 37 acceptance assertions plus 12 direct toolchain checks observed on JDK 25.0.3 (line 107), while stating that "the repository carries no committed test suite, and adding one is outside this change's scope."

### 1.1.5 Basis of the Findings in This Specification

Two evidentiary boundaries apply throughout this Introduction and are stated once here.

No Java toolchain is installed in the environment from which this specification was produced: `java` and `javac` are both absent from `PATH`, `JAVA_HOME` is unset, and `/usr/lib/jvm` does not exist. Every behavioural statement is therefore derived **statically**, by reading `Hello.java`, or is **attributed** to the repository's own committed records — principally `README.md` and `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md`, the latter reporting execution first-hand on a Linux host with OpenJDK 25.0.3 (lines 245, 255–256). No compilation or execution was performed while writing this section.

One committed statement is known to be out of date. `README.md` line 67 asserts, "The repository is flat: three tracked files at the root, and no subdirectories." The current tracked inventory is five files, and the subdirectory `blitzy/documentation/` exists holding two of them. The narrower claims in that same section — the purpose of `Hello.java`, `README.md`, and `LICENSE` — remain accurate; only the count and the flatness claim do not.


## 1.2 System Overview

### 1.2.1 Project Context

#### 1.2.1.1 Business Context and Positioning

`Hello` occupies the position of a **canonical reference program**: the smallest artifact that still proves a Java toolchain can compile a source file, launch a JVM, and write to standard output. Every property of the repository reinforces that positioning rather than a product positioning.

| Positioning Signal | Repository Evidence | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No published artifact | No `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, or `settings.gradle`; no group/artifact coordinates anywhere | The program is consumed as source from the checkout, never as a distributed binary |
| No releases | `git tag` returns zero tags across 14 commits | There is no versioned release line and no upgrade path to manage |
| No version pinning | `README.md` line 18: the repository "pins no Java version"; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` Appendix D: Java language level "None declared" | Portability across JDKs is preferred over a reproducible pinned build |
| Copyleft licensing | Complete GPL v3 text in `LICENSE`; `README.md` line 77 | The work is positioned for open study and redistribution, not proprietary embedding |
| Documentation-dominant | 884,733 of 925,008 tracked bytes are the two `blitzy/documentation/` Markdown files | Explaining the program is the larger part of the project's output |

There is no market, competitive, or commercial framing anywhere in the repository, and none is asserted here.

#### 1.2.1.2 Current State and Its Limitations

This is not a replacement of a prior system; it is the **documentation upgrade of an existing program whose executable behaviour was deliberately left untouched**. The commit history divides cleanly into three eras:

| History Era | Commits | What Changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Origin (author `rjhonsi`) | `c537a19`, `f1847fa`, `0726b1d` | The program and licence were added; the README was a placeholder line |
| Documentation upgrade | `3c3af75`, `dabe2c9`, `14ed6db`, `ce8e85c` | Four comments added to `Hello.java`; the README placeholder replaced by the eight-section guide |
| Generated specification rounds | `1b99a4b`…`b4a1188`, merged by `2a78292` | `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` and `Technical Specifications.md` added |

The limitations of the system as it now stands are structural rather than defects in the code. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §1.4 states plainly that "No defect is open in the delivered code" while recording that **11 items remain open**. The limitations that bear on this specification are:

- **No automated gate.** The repository carries no build descriptor, test suite, or CI workflow, so as `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §1.4 puts it, "Nothing re-runs the documentation checks on future changes." Its Appendix F identifies `javac -Xlint:all -Werror` as "the project's static-analysis surface, as no linter is configured."
- **No hygiene controls.** There is no `.gitignore`, so an in-place `javac Hello.java` leaves an untracked `Hello.class` in the checkout (`README.md` line 30); and no `.gitattributes`, while `Hello.java` is stored with CRLF endings on all 20 of its 20 lines and `README.md`, `LICENSE`, and the generated guide are LF-only.
- **An unverified version floor.** `README.md` line 20 states that the `java Hello.java` single-file source launch "needs JDK 11 or later," and `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §2.2 still lists confirming that floor on an actual JDK 11 runtime as 1.0 hour of outstanding Medium-priority work.
- **Stale layout claims in two committed documents.** Both `README.md` line 67 and `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` Appendix C describe the repository as flat with three tracked files and no subdirectory. The tracked inventory is five files and `blitzy/documentation/` exists.
- **Unpublished work on the default branch.** `main` sits at `0726b1d` and `jr_java1` at `2a78292`; `git rev-list --left-right --count main...jr_java1` reports `0 11`, so `main` is an ancestor of the working branch and is 11 commits behind it. All documentation work is absent from the default branch.
- **No unit or integration coverage figure.** `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3 records that "The repository carries no committed test suite, and adding one is outside this change's scope," substituting a nine-group acceptance suite (V1–V9) plus direct toolchain checks.

#### 1.2.1.3 Integration with the Surrounding Landscape

The system integrates with exactly four things outside itself, and with nothing else. There is no enterprise landscape to integrate into: `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` Appendix B states, "Not applicable. The program binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call; there is no service, database, broker or cache in this project," and its §1.5 records that "no credential, key, network egress, environment variable or secret is used by anything in this project." Appendix E confirms `JAVA_HOME` is not required and that no other variable or secret is read by any tracked file.

| Integration Point | Interface | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JDK toolchain | `javac` compiles the single unit; `java` launches the class or the source file | `README.md` lines 27, 37, 43; `Project Guide.md` Appendix D (OpenJDK 25.0.3) |
| Operating-system process contract | stdout receives the greeting; stderr stays empty; exit status 0 | `Hello.java` lines 16–18; `README.md` line 63 |
| Git and its hosting platform | Clone, branch, and the merge of pull request #1 (`2a78292`) | `git log`; local branches `main`, `jr_java1`; six remote refs |
| GPL v3 obligations | Copyleft terms governing redistribution of the covered work | `LICENSE`; `README.md` line 77 |

The Java standard library is the only code dependency, and only its implicit portion: `Hello.java` has no `import` statement, so it draws solely on the automatically imported `java.lang` — which is why, as its class Javadoc records, "a JDK alone builds and runs it."

### 1.2.2 High-Level Description

#### 1.2.2.1 Primary System Capabilities

| Capability | Behaviour | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Emit one fixed greeting | Writes the literal `Hello from Java!` followed by the platform line separator to standard output | `Hello.java` line 17 |
| Terminate cleanly | `main` returns normally with no `System.exit`; the JVM then shuts down of its own accord, yielding exit status 0 | `Hello.java` lines 18–19; `README.md` line 63 |
| Behave identically under any arguments | `String[] args` is accepted for the entry-point signature and never dereferenced | `Hello.java` lines 11–13 |
| Build with no dependency resolution | One compilation unit, no imports beyond `java.lang`, no manifest to resolve | `Hello.java` lines 1–5; `README.md` line 18 |
| Offer two equivalent launch paths | `javac Hello.java` then `java Hello`; or `java Hello.java` directly (JDK 11+), with byte-identical output | `README.md` lines 27, 37, 43, 46 |
| Document its own operation | Eight-section operational guide plus in-source Javadoc on the class and entry point | `README.md`; `Hello.java` lines 1–14 |

The output payload is fixed and measurable: `Hello from Java!` is 16 ASCII characters, so standard output carries 17 bytes where the platform separator is LF and 18 where it is CRLF — consistent with `README.md` line 63, which notes that "the exact byte count varies between platforms; the literal and its single trailing separator do not."

#### 1.2.2.3 Core Technical Approach

Six deliberate choices define the approach, each visible in the source or stated in the committed documentation:

1. **One compilation unit in the default package.** No `package` declaration means the class is launched by the bare name `Hello`; the class Javadoc names this as the reason (`Hello.java` lines 1–5).
2. **Statelessness by construction.** No fields, no instance creation, no static mutable state — so there is nothing to initialise, synchronise, or reset between runs.
3. **A single output sink.** The line comment at `Hello.java` line 16 fixes this as a design property: "Sole output: one write to standard output … no other sink is written."
4. **Termination by normal return.** No `System.exit` anywhere; `README.md` line 63 characterises this as "a deliberate property of the program rather than an omission."
5. **Zero external dependencies, zero configuration.** Nothing to resolve or download before building (`README.md` line 18); no environment variable or secret is read by any tracked file (`Project Guide.md` Appendix E).
6. **Documentation as the delivery mechanism.** With the program fixed, the project's output is explanatory: in-source Javadoc on the class and `main`, two inline comments on the output and termination paths, and an eight-section README that states the contract an operator can verify.

Toolchain versions are recorded rather than enforced: `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` Appendix D reports OpenJDK 25.0.3 for `java`, `javac`, and `javadoc`, notes that "the compile-then-run path was exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21," and records that no `--release` or `--source` setting exists anywhere in the repository.

### 1.2.3 Success Criteria

#### 1.2.3.1 Measurable Objectives

Every objective below is stated as an observable, binary condition drawn from the committed documentation or the source.

| # | Objective | Observable Condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| O-1 | Compile cleanly | `javac Hello.java` exits 0 with no diagnostics (`README.md` line 30); `Project Guide.md` §3 records zero diagnostics even under `-Xlint:all -Werror` |
| O-2 | Produce the exact output | stdout is `Hello from Java!` plus one platform line separator (`README.md` lines 57–63) |
| O-3 | Keep stderr empty and exit 0 | No diagnostic output; termination via normal return (`README.md` line 63) |
| O-4 | Be argument-insensitive | Output identical with or without arguments; `args` never dereferenced (`Hello.java` lines 11–13) |
| O-5 | Keep both launch paths equivalent | `java Hello` and `java Hello.java` give byte-identical stdout (`README.md` line 46) |
| O-6 | Document every written functionality | Class Javadoc, `main` Javadoc with `@param args`, and comments on the output and termination paths (`Hello.java`; `README.md` line 7) |
| O-7 | Preserve behaviour across the documentation change | The documentation upgrade added comments only; runtime behaviour and stored byte format unchanged (`Project Guide.md` §4) |

#### 1.2.3.2 Critical Success Factors

- **Behaviour preservation under edit.** The value of the artifact lies in its predictability, so any change must keep the single `println`, the ignored `args`, and the `System.exit`-free termination intact.
- **Dependency-free buildability.** Introducing any manifest or third-party import would forfeit the "a JDK alone builds and runs it" property that makes the program a clean toolchain probe.
- **Documentation that matches the tree.** The two committed layout claims are already stale (`README.md` line 67; `Project Guide.md` Appendix C), which is the concrete failure mode this factor guards against.
- **Working-tree cleanliness without an ignore rule.** Because no `.gitignore` exists, the documented `mktemp -d` compile destination is the control that keeps `Hello.class` out of the checkout (`README.md` line 30).
- **Byte-format stability.** `Hello.java` is CRLF throughout with no `.gitattributes`; an editor or platform that normalises endings would rewrite all 20 lines.
- **Owner decisions on the open items.** Six of the eleven open items in `Project Guide.md` §1.4 are explicitly "Owner decision" — version pinning, licence notice, line-ending policy, ignore rule, release and signing infrastructure.

## 1.3 Scope

### 1.3.1 In-Scope

#### 1.3.1.1 Core Features and Functionalities

**Must-have capabilities.** The system's committed functionality is exhaustively enumerable, because it is one statement in one method in one file.

| ID | Must-Have Capability | Acceptance Condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C-1 | A single compilable Java source file requiring only a JDK | `javac Hello.java` succeeds with exit 0 and no diagnostics |
| C-2 | A launchable entry point reachable by the bare class name | `java Hello` runs the class from the default package |
| C-3 | Emission of the fixed greeting to standard output | stdout carries `Hello from Java!` plus one platform line separator |
| C-4 | Clean, silent termination | stderr empty, exit status 0, no `System.exit` call |
| C-5 | Argument insensitivity | `args` accepted but never dereferenced; output unchanged by any arguments |
| C-6 | Equivalence of both documented launch paths | `java Hello` and `java Hello.java` produce byte-identical stdout |
| C-7 | An operational guide covering build, run, and output | `README.md` supplies Requirements, Build, Run, and Expected Output sections |
| C-8 | Explicit licence terms | Verbatim GPL v3 text present in `LICENSE` and referenced from `README.md` |
| C-9 | Self-explaining source | Class Javadoc, `main` Javadoc with `@param args`, and comments on the output and termination paths |

**Primary user workflows.** All four are documented in `README.md` and require nothing beyond a JDK, a POSIX shell, and the repository root as the working directory.

| ID | Workflow | Commands / Steps | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| W-1 | Compile in place, then run | `javac Hello.java` → `java Hello` | `README.md` lines 27, 37 |
| W-2 | Compile to a fresh directory outside the checkout, then run | `B="$(mktemp -d)" && javac -d "$B" Hello.java` → `java -cp "$B" Hello` | `README.md` line 30 |
| W-3 | Launch the source file directly, leaving no class file | `java Hello.java` (requires JDK 11 or later) | `README.md` lines 40–44 |
| W-4 | Verify the output contract | Compare stdout to the literal, confirm stderr empty and exit status 0 | `README.md` lines 57–63 |

W-2 is the path the guide recommends: `mktemp -d` "returns a uniquely named one readable only by its owner, whereas a fixed, predictable destination can be pre-created, replaced or redirected through a symbolic link by another local process before the compiler writes into it," and either way the guide instructs, "Do not commit the class file."

**Essential integrations.** In scope are precisely the four interfaces in §1.2.1.3: the JDK toolchain (`javac`, `java`, and `javadoc` for the coverage check), the operating-system process contract (stdout, stderr, exit status), Git with its hosting platform, and the GPL v3 obligations attached to the covered work. Nothing else is integrated.

**Key technical requirements.**

| Requirement | Specified Value | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Toolchain | A JDK; no other software required | `README.md` line 18 |
| Version floor — compile-then-run | None stated; documented as working on "considerably older releases" | `README.md` line 20 |
| Version floor — single-file source launch | JDK 11 or later | `README.md` line 20 |
| Dependencies | None; no manifest, nothing to resolve or download | `README.md` line 18 |
| Configuration | None; no environment variable or secret read by any tracked file | `Project Guide.md` Appendix E |
| Static-analysis surface | `javac -Xlint:all -Werror`; no linter configured | `Project Guide.md` Appendix F |
| Comment-coverage tool | `javadoc -Xdoclint:all`; HTML output never committed | `Project Guide.md` Appendix F |
| Stored source format | `Hello.java` CRLF on all 20 lines, pure ASCII, no `.gitattributes` | Direct measurement |

#### 1.3.1.2 Implementation Boundaries

**System boundary.** The system is the JVM process launched from `Hello.java` and the tracked files that describe and license it. Inside the boundary: one compilation unit, one entry point, one output statement, the operational guide, the licence, and the two generated documents under `blitzy/documentation/`. Outside the boundary: the JDK itself (required but not vendored), the host operating system that supplies the line separator, Git and its hosting platform, and any `Hello.class` produced by a build — an untracked artifact the guide explicitly instructs must not be committed.

| Boundary Dimension | In Scope | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Executable surface | One process, one thread of control, one statement of work | `Hello.java` lines 15–19 |
| Input surface | None — no stdin read, no file read, no arguments consulted | `Hello.java` lines 11–13 |
| Output surface | Standard output only; stderr deliberately left empty | `Hello.java` line 16; `README.md` line 63 |
| Persistence surface | None — no state kept between or within runs | `README.md` line 12 |
| Network surface | None — no port bound, no listener, no network call | `Project Guide.md` Appendix B |
| Tracked footprint | 5 files, 925,008 bytes, one subdirectory (`blitzy/documentation/`) | `git ls-files`; direct measurement |

**User groups covered.** Operators and learners who build and run the program, maintainers who edit the source, the repository owner who holds the outstanding decisions, the automated documentation agents that author `blitzy/documentation/`, and downstream recipients exercising GPL v3 rights. The system defines no roles, accounts, or permissions of its own; it has no authentication or authorisation surface, so "user group" here means audience, not an access-control construct.

**Geographic and market coverage.** Not applicable in any deployment sense — there is no hosted service, no region, no tenancy model. The only host-dependent aspect of behaviour is the line separator: `README.md` line 63 records that the separator "is the one the host defines, so the exact byte count varies between platforms; the literal and its single trailing separator do not." No locale handling, resource bundle, or character-set configuration exists; the greeting is a hard-coded ASCII literal in `Hello.java` line 17, and `Hello.java`, `README.md`, and `LICENSE` contain no byte at or above `0x80`.

**Data domains included.** There is exactly one data element in the system — the compile-time string constant `Hello from Java!` — and one derived value, the platform line separator supplied by the runtime. There is no schema, no record, no file format, no serialisation, and no data at rest or in transit. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §6 states that the application has no input, resource, network, authentication, authorisation, dependency, or data-at-rest surface.

### 1.3.2 Out-of-Scope

#### 1.3.2.1 Explicitly Excluded Features and Capabilities

Each exclusion below was confirmed by direct inspection of the working tree, not inferred.

| Excluded Capability | Verification |

| Modularisation | No `module-info.java`; the class sits in the default package |
| Automated testing | No test suite and no test directory; `Project Guide.md` §3 declares adding one out of scope |
| Continuous integration / delivery | No `.github/`, `.circleci/`, `Jenkinsfile`, or `.travis.yml`; `Project Guide.md` §1.4: "Nothing re-runs the documentation checks on future changes" |
| Containerisation / orchestration / IaC | No `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, or any infrastructure descriptor |
| Persistence and data services | No database, broker, or cache (`Project Guide.md` Appendix B) |
| Network services, APIs, ports | No port bound, no listener, no network call (`Project Guide.md` Appendix B) |
| User interface of any kind | Console output only; no UI, hosted page, or port (`Project Guide.md` §4) |
| Authentication, authorisation, secrets | No credential, key, environment variable, or secret read by any tracked file (`Project Guide.md` §1.5) |
| Configuration management | No configuration file; no `.editorconfig`; nothing to tune |
| Logging, metrics, tracing, monitoring | No logging framework and no diagnostic output — stderr is deliberately empty |
| Input handling and validation | `args` never dereferenced; no stdin, file, or resource is read |
| Explicit error handling | No `try`/`catch`, no thrown exception, no error branch anywhere in `Hello.java` |
| Internationalisation / localisation | Hard-coded ASCII literal; no resource bundle or locale logic |
| Concurrency | Single-threaded `main`; no thread, executor, or synchronisation construct |
| Release engineering and versioning | Zero tags across 14 commits; no version pinned anywhere |
| Repository hygiene controls | No `.gitignore`, no `.gitattributes`, no per-file copyright header |
| Governance files | No `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md`, or `CODEOWNERS` |

`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §1.6 and §2.2 record the deferred work with its own priorities and estimates, totalling 6.0 hours. These are the repository's recorded intentions, not commitments made by this specification.

The guide classes four further items — verification-oracle, release, policy, and commit-signing infrastructure — as "Non-documentation items outside this scope," each marked "Owner decision" and "Deferred," and records confidence in the remaining estimates as medium "because four of the six items are decisions whose scope the owner sets rather than fixed units of work."

A seventh consideration arises from direct observation rather than the guide: the layout claims in `README.md` line 67 and `Project Guide.md` Appendix C — three tracked files, no subdirectory — no longer match the five-file tree containing `blitzy/documentation/`, and correcting them is not covered by any recorded item.

#### 1.3.2.3 Integration Points Not Covered

No integration exists beyond the four in §1.3.1.1. Specifically excluded are service registries and artifact repositories (no coordinates are declared, so the program is never published or consumed as a dependency); package managers (`Project Guide.md` §9 records that none is required); message brokers, caches, and databases (Appendix B); identity providers and secret stores (§1.5); external monitoring or log aggregation; and any HTTP, RPC, or file-based interface. `JAVA_HOME` is explicitly not an integration point: Appendix E records it as not required and "not used by anything in this project."

#### 1.3.2.4 Unsupported Use Cases

| Unsupported Use Case | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| Driving behaviour through command-line arguments | `args` is never dereferenced; output is identical whether or not arguments are supplied |
| Supplying input on stdin or reading any file | No input path exists in `Hello.java` |
| Reusing `Hello` as a library from packaged code | The class is declared in the default package, which code in a named package cannot import |
| Single-file source launch on a JDK earlier than 11 | `java Hello.java` requires JDK 11 or later (`README.md` line 20); the compile-then-run path must be used instead |
| Running without a JDK on the host | A JDK is the sole prerequisite and is not vendored in the repository |
| Relying on a fixed stdout byte count across platforms | The line separator is host-defined; only the literal and its single trailing separator are invariant |
| Treating a non-zero exit status or stderr content as a program state | The program has exactly one outcome: empty stderr and exit status 0 |
| Expecting a committed gate to validate a change | No build descriptor, test suite, or CI workflow is committed |
| Using the program as a performance, load, or soak benchmark | No measurement, instrumentation, or timing exists; no such target is recorded anywhere |
| Deploying it as a service | No listener, no port, no packaging, and no deployment descriptor exist |

# 2. Product Requirements

## 2.1 Feature Catalog

This section decomposes the `Hello` repository into discrete, individually testable features. The system is unusually small — the entire executable surface is five non-comment lines in `Hello.java` — so the catalog is exhaustive rather than representative: every feature below corresponds to an artifact or an observable behaviour that exists in the tree at `HEAD` (`2a78292`), and no feature is asserted that is not anchored in a file.

### 2.1.1 Catalog Scope, Closure and Provenance

**How this catalog was derived.** Each feature maps to one of the nine must-have capabilities enumerated in Section 1.3.1.1 (`C-1` … `C-9`) and is anchored to a verified artifact. The behavioural features (F-001 … F-003) were derived by static reading of `Hello.java`, whose complete executable content is five lines — the class declaration (line 6), the entry-point signature (line 15), the single `System.out.println("Hello from Java!")` (line 17) and the two closing braces (lines 19–20). The remaining features correspond to tracked artifacts: the toolchain contract implied by the absence of every build descriptor, the Git distribution channel, `LICENSE`, `README.md`, the in-source comment set, and `blitzy/documentation/`.

**Priority basis.** `Critical` marks a feature without which the program cannot be launched or cannot produce its documented output at all; `High` marks a feature whose loss would break a must-have capability or a licence obligation without preventing launch; `Medium` and `Low` mark features that support comprehension, distribution or project governance. No priority is inherited from a commercial or contractual source — the repository records none.

**Status basis.** Every feature is `Completed` in the sense that its artifact exists and is tracked at `HEAD`. Four features carry qualifiers because `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §1.4 records **11 open items** alongside the statement that "No defect is open in the delivered code": the unverified JDK 11 floor (F-004), the unpublished default branch (F-005), the absent per-file copyright notice (F-006), the partial citation coverage and the stale layout claim (F-007), and the accepted `javadoc` default-constructor warning (F-008). No feature is `Proposed`, `Approved` or `In Development`; the repository contains no backlog, roadmap or issue tracker in which such a status could be recorded.

**Relationship to the repository's own committed register.** The repository already contains a feature register: `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §2.1 catalogues seven features (F-001 … F-007) and 27 requirements, and its §2.6.3 anchors that register at **version 1.0, commit `0726b1d`**. ### 2.1.2 F-001 — JVM Entry-Point Contract

| Attribute | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Unique ID | F-001 |
| Feature Name | JVM Entry-Point Contract |
| Feature Category | Runtime Interface |
| Priority Level | Critical |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview.** `Hello.java` line 6 declares `public class Hello` with no `package` statement, and line 15 declares `public static void main(String[] args)` as its only member. This is the sole mechanism by which any code in the repository becomes executable: the JVM resolves the class by the bare name `Hello` and invokes `main`. The class declares no field, no explicit constructor and creates no instance — a grep for field and constructor declarations returns only the class and `main` signature lines.
- **Business value.** It is what makes the repository a runnable toolchain probe rather than an inert source listing. Because the class sits in the default package, the launch command is the shortest form the platform allows, with no directory layout, classpath root or module path to establish first.
- **User benefits.** An operator types `java Hello` and the program runs; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.8 records the matching failure mode and its resolution ("the class is in the default package, so the bare name is correct"). Arguments may be supplied freely: the `main` Javadoc at `Hello.java:11-13` states that `args` is "accepted only to satisfy the signature the JVM requires of an entry point and deliberately never read".
- **Technical context.** `args` occurs on exactly two lines of the file — line 11 (the Javadoc `@param` tag) and line 15 (the signature) — and on no executable line, so non-dereference is a static property of the source rather than a runtime observation. The file name matches the public class, which is the precondition for single-unit compilation; `Project Guide.md` §9.8 records the diagnostic produced when that correspondence is broken (`error: class Hello is public, should be declared in a file named Hello.java`).

| Dependency type | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Prerequisite features | None — F-001 is the root of the runtime dependency chain |
| System dependencies | A JVM supplied by the JDK (F-004); the class-loading and `main`-resolution contract of the platform |
| External dependencies | The implicitly imported `java.lang` package only; the file declares no `import` |
| Integration requirements | The operating-system process contract — the JVM is launched as a process and `main` is invoked once; no other integration surface exists |

### 2.1.3 F-002 — Fixed Console Message Emission

| Attribute | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Unique ID | F-002 |
| Feature Name | Fixed Console Message Emission |
| Feature Category | Output Behaviour |
| Priority Level | Critical |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview.** `Hello.java` line 17 performs `System.out.println("Hello from Java!")`. This is the entire work of the program: one write of a 16-character ASCII literal followed by one platform line separator. The preceding comment on line 16 fixes the property as deliberate — "Sole output: one write to standard output … no other sink is written."
- **Business value.** It supplies a fixed, byte-level oracle. `README.md` lines 57–63 publish the expected output as a fenced block, and `Project Guide.md` §4 records that "the fenced expected-output block compares byte-identical to real standard output", so the artifact can be used as a reference point whose correct behaviour is known in advance.
- **User benefits.** The result is reproducible without configuration: the same line appears on every run, on every launch path, with or without arguments. `Project Guide.md` §4 records runs "with no arguments, many arguments, and hostile arguments including shell and injection payloads" all producing identical output.
- **Technical context.** `System.` appears on only two lines of the file — line 17 (the call) and line 18 (a comment) — so standard output is demonstrably the only sink referenced anywhere in the source. `println` rather than `print` is what appends the separator, which is host-defined; `README.md` line 63 therefore states the contract as the literal plus one trailing separator rather than a fixed byte count, and `Project Guide.md` §4 records 17 bytes on a host whose separator is LF. There is no loop, branch or conditional in the file (`for`, `while`, `if` and `switch` statement forms all return zero matches), so the emission happens exactly once per process.

| Dependency type | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Prerequisite features | F-001 — the write executes only because `main` is invoked |
| System dependencies | The JVM's initialised `System.out` stream and the host-defined line separator |
| External dependencies | None beyond `java.lang`; no logging, formatting or i18n library is present |
| Integration requirements | The process stdout stream must be connected by the launching shell; `README.md` lines 57–63 define the contract an operator compares against |

### 2.1.4 F-003 — Deterministic Normal Termination

| Attribute | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Unique ID | F-003 |
| Feature Name | Deterministic Normal Termination |
| Feature Category | Process Lifecycle |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Description**

- **Overview.** After the single write, control returns from `main` at `Hello.java` line 19 and the JVM shuts down of its own accord. The comment on line 18 records the intent: "control returns from main with no System.exit call, so the JVM terminates normally once this method completes." A search for `System.exit(` in the file returns zero matches.
- **Business value.** It makes the program safe to embed in any shell pipeline or verification script: the exit status is a constant, so a wrapper can test it without special-casing. `README.md` line 63 calls the absence of `System.exit` "a deliberate property of the program rather than an omission".
- **User benefits.** Standard error stays empty and the exit status is 0, so a caller can distinguish a real environment failure from normal operation with no interpretation. `Project Guide.md` §9.7 shows the observed result directly: `java Hello; echo "exit=$?"` prints the greeting followed by `exit=0`.
- **Technical context.** The termination path is unconditional because there is no error path to take: the file contains no `try`, `catch`, `throw` or `new`, no `System.in` or `Scanner` reference, and no `Thread` or executor construct. `Project Guide.md` §6 states the consequence — the program "reads no input, dereferences no argument, opens no resource, binds no port, makes no network call", so there is no injection surface and no data-at-rest concern.

| Dependency type | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Prerequisite features | F-001 (invocation) and F-002 (the work that precedes the return) |
| System dependencies | The JVM shutdown sequence; the operating-system exit-status convention |
| External dependencies | None |
| Integration requirements | The launching shell observes the exit status and the empty error stream; no other consumer exists |

### 2.1.5 F-004 — Dependency-Free JDK-Only Build and Launch

| Attribute | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Unique ID | F-004 |
| Feature Name | Dependency-Free JDK-Only Build and Launch |
| Feature Category | Build & Toolchain |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed — the JDK 11 floor for the single-file launch path is not verified on a JDK 11 runtime |

**Description**

- **Overview.** The repository is built and launched with the JDK alone. `README.md` line 18 states it plainly — "A JDK is all that is required" — and records that the repository "pins no Java version" and "has no dependency manifest, so nothing has to be resolved or downloaded before building". Three launch forms are documented and recorded as verified in `Project Guide.md` §9.5: `java -cp "$B" Hello`, `java Hello`, and `java Hello.java`.
- **Business value.** Zero setup cost and zero supply-chain surface. `Project Guide.md` §9.3 answers dependency installation with a single word — "None." — and §1.5 records that "no credential, key, network egress, environment variable or secret is used by anything in this project".
- **User benefits.** Two interchangeable workflows suit different needs: compile-then-run works on "considerably older releases" (`README.md` line 20) and was exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21; single-file source launch needs JDK 11 or later and "leaves no class file behind" (`README.md` line 40). `README.md` line 46 records that "Both paths produce byte-identical standard output".
- **Technical context.** One compilation unit, zero `import` statements, no `module-info.java`, and no `--release` or `--source` setting anywhere in the repository (`Project Guide.md` Appendix D records the language level as "None declared"). `javac -Xlint:all -Werror` is the project's entire static-analysis surface, "as no linter is configured" (Appendix F), and it compiles clean. Because no `.gitignore` exists, an in-place compile leaves an untracked `Hello.class`; `README.md` line 30 supplies the out-of-tree alternative `B="$(mktemp -d)" && javac -d "$B" Hello.java` with the matching `java -cp "$B" Hello`, and explains the choice of a freshly generated owner-only directory over "a fixed, predictable destination [that] can be pre-created, replaced or redirected through a symbolic link by another local process".

| Dependency type | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Prerequisite features | F-001 (the unit to compile and the class to launch) |
| System dependencies | `javac` and `java` on `PATH`; a POSIX shell for the documented commands; `mktemp -d` for the recommended build destination |
| External dependencies | A JDK, not vendored in the repository. `Project Guide.md` Appendix D records OpenJDK 25.0.3 as the version used; `JAVA_HOME` is explicitly not required (Appendix E) |
| Integration requirements | The JDK toolchain interface only. No package manager, virtual environment, container, database, broker or bound port is involved (`Project Guide.md` §9.1) |

### 2.1.6 F-005 — Source-Only Distribution via Git Remote

| Attribute | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Unique ID | F-005 |
| Feature Name | Source-Only Distribution via Git Remote |
| Feature Category | Distribution |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed — the delivered documentation is not yet reachable on the default branch |

**Description**

- **Overview.** The program is consumed as source from a clone. `git ls-files` returns five tracked files — `Hello.java`, `LICENSE`, `README.md` and the two documents under `blitzy/documentation/` — with no compiled or packaged artifact among them, and `git tag` returns zero tags across the 14 commits.
- **Business value.** There is no release line, artifact repository or coordinate to maintain, so distribution costs nothing and cannot drift from the source. Nothing can be consumed as a stale binary because no binary is published.
- **User benefits.** A clone is sufficient to build, run, read and redistribute the work; the tracked tree is small enough to read in full (925,008 bytes, of which 1,073 are source).
- **Technical context.** Six remote refs exist (`origin/HEAD` → `origin/main`, `origin/main`, `origin/jr_java1`, `origin/jr_java2`, `origin/jr_java3` and `origin/blitzy-6d6c8680-f3ef-4055-9d11-0fc35e375843`), and `git rev-list --left-right --count main...HEAD` reports `0 11` — `main` is an ancestor of the working branch and 11 commits behind it, so the entire documentation delivery is absent from the default branch. `Project Guide.md` §1.6 lists "Push the branch and merge the two-file change" as a High-priority 0.5-hour item. Stored byte format is part of what is distributed: `Hello.java` carries CRLF on all 20 lines while `README.md` and `LICENSE` are LF-only, and no `.gitattributes` exists to normalise either; `Project Guide.md` §5.2 records that normalising would "rewrite all five code lines and change the file's content digest".

| Dependency type | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Prerequisite features | F-001, F-006, F-007, F-008, F-009 — the artifacts being distributed |
| System dependencies | `git` (Appendix D records 2.51.0) and the working tree; no build or packaging step participates |
| External dependencies | The Git hosting platform that holds the remote refs and merged pull request #1 (`2a78292`) |
| Integration requirements | Clone, branch and merge only. No artifact repository, package manager or registry is involved; no group or artifact coordinate is declared anywhere |

- **Overview.** `LICENSE` holds the verbatim GNU General Public License, Version 3, 29 June 2007 (674 lines / 35,149 bytes, opening "GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE / Version 3, 29 June 2007"), and `README.md` line 77 states the licence and links to it.
- **Business value.** Redistribution rights are explicit rather than assumed, which is what makes the repository usable as teaching and reference material without further negotiation.

- **Technical context.** The licence governs a covered work that was modified, so `README.md` line 5 carries the dated notice "*Modified 2026-09-16.*" and `Project Guide.md` §5.1 row 8 records it as satisfying the "dated modification notice for a modified GPLv3 work" requirement. `LICENSE` itself was not touched by the documentation upgrade — `Project Guide.md` §1.3 records "`LICENSE` untouched" and §2.1 credits a "scope and continuity discipline" task with confirming it byte-identical at base, commit and working tree; its blob is `f288702`. The one gap is intentional: no per-file copyright header exists in `Hello.java`, because, as §5.2 records, "that notice needs a named holder and year and no tracked file records either — commit metadata identifies an author, not a rights holder."

### 2.1.9 F-008 — In-Source Explanatory Documentation

| Attribute | Value |
| --- | --- |

| Feature Category | Documentation |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed — documentable-member coverage stands at 2 of 3 by design |

**Description**

- **Overview.** `Hello.java` carries four comments, one per written functionality: the class Javadoc at lines 1–5, the `main` Javadoc with its `@param args` tag at lines 7–14, the output-path line comment at line 16 and the termination-path line comment at line 18. `Project Guide.md` §5.1 row 1 records this as 4 of 4 with those exact anchors.
- **Business value.** The non-obvious properties of the program are recorded at the point of use rather than inferred by the next reader — why the bare class name works, why `args` exists and is ignored, that one sink is written, and that termination is by normal return.
- **User benefits.** A maintainer editing the file sees the design intent in place, which is what protects the behaviour the rest of this specification depends on; the `javadoc` HTML generated from the same comments "carries both comment blocks and the parameter table" (`Project Guide.md` §4).
- **Technical context.** The change was comment-only: `Project Guide.md` §5.1 row 3 records 15 added and 0 removed lines with the five original code lines byte-identical and debug-free bytecode identical, and `git diff 0726b1d HEAD --stat` confirms `Hello.java +15`. Comment form follows the language's conventions — class block at column 0, member block at four spaces with `@param args` and no `@return`, both line comments at eight spaces (§5.1 row 2). One `javadoc` warning remains by design, at `Hello.java:6`, for the implicit default constructor; as §5.2 divergence 4 explains, "a default constructor can carry no doc comment, and declaring one is a structural change the comment-only constraint forbids." The added lines were re-emitted with CRLF so that all 20 lines remain CRLF, pure ASCII and tab-free — verified directly: 20 of 20 lines carry CR, and the file contains zero non-ASCII bytes and zero tabs.

## 2.2 Functional Requirements

### 2.2.1 Basis, Conventions and Limits of the Requirement Set

The repository declares no requirements document, no service-level objective and no performance target — there is no build descriptor, test suite or CI configuration in which one could be recorded, and `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` Appendix B records that there is "no service, database, broker or cache in this project". Every acceptance criterion below is therefore an **executable verification procedure derived from the artifacts**, phrased so that it can be run against the tree as it stands.

| Convention | Rule applied throughout Section 2.2 |
| --- | --- |
| Requirement ID | `F-XXX-RQ-YYY`, numbered per feature from `001`; 45 requirements across F-001 … F-009 |
| Priority | `Must-Have` = the feature's documented contract fails without it; `Should-Have` = a stated property of the artifact; `Could-Have` = advised by an external instrument or deferred by owner decision |
| Complexity | `Low` = satisfied by one line, one absence or one file; `Medium` = requires a multi-artifact or byte-level procedure; `High` = not used, because no requirement here exceeds a 20-line file or a single document |
| Requirement version | All requirements below are **version 2.0, observed at `HEAD` = `2a78292`** (see Section 2.6.3) |

**Evidence classes.** Criteria are marked in the evidence column by how they were established: *static* — verified directly against the tree while writing this section (file content, `grep`, `git`); *recorded* — executed first-hand by the project's own validation run on a Linux host with OpenJDK 25.0.3 and reported in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md`; *open* — not satisfied or not verified at `HEAD`. No JDK exists in the environment used to produce this specification (`java` and `javac` are absent from `PATH`), so no criterion was executed here that requires a compiler or a JVM.

### 2.2.2 F-001 — JVM Entry-Point Contract

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F-001-RQ-001 | Declare a JVM-launchable entry point with the exact signature `public static void main(String[] args)` | Must-Have | Low |
| F-001-RQ-002 | Declare the class in the default package so that it launches by the bare name `Hello` | Must-Have | Low |
| F-001-RQ-003 | Accept `String[] args` for the signature and never dereference it | Must-Have | Low |
| F-001-RQ-004 | Name the file after the single public class it declares, so the unit compiles standalone | Must-Have | Low |
| F-001-RQ-005 | Hold no instance state: no field, no explicit constructor, no instantiation | Should-Have | Low |

| Requirement ID | Acceptance criterion | Evidence at `HEAD` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| F-001-RQ-001 | `Hello.java` line 15 matches the signature character for character; a launch resolves `main` instead of reporting a missing entry point | static (line 15); recorded — three launch forms verified in `Project Guide.md` §9.5 |
| F-001-RQ-002 | A search for `^\s*package` in `Hello.java` returns zero matches and `java Hello` succeeds with the unqualified name | static (0 matches); `README.md` lines 34–38; `Project Guide.md` §9.8 row 1 |
| F-001-RQ-003 | `args` occurs only on line 11 (Javadoc `@param`) and line 15 (signature), on no executable line; output is unchanged by any argument list | static (2 occurrences); recorded — "no arguments, many arguments, and hostile arguments including shell and injection payloads all produce identical output" (`Project Guide.md` §4) |
| F-001-RQ-004 | `public class Hello` is declared at line 6 of a file named `Hello.java`; exporting the source under another name produces `error: class Hello is public, should be declared in a file named Hello.java` | static (line 6); recorded (`Project Guide.md` §9.8 row 2) |
| F-001-RQ-005 | The only declaration lines in the file are 6 and 15; searches for `\bnew\b` and for field or constructor declarations return zero matches | static; corroborated by the class Javadoc at lines 1–5 ("it has no field, creates no instance") |

| Technical aspect | Specification |
| --- | --- |
| Input parameters | `String[] args` at line 15, accepted and never read. No other input path exists — no stdin read, no file read, no environment variable, no system property |
| Output / response | F-001 produces no output of its own; it yields an invoked `main` frame. A failed resolution produces the platform message `Could not find or load main class Hello` (`Project Guide.md` §9.8) |
| Performance criteria | None is recorded anywhere in the repository. The observable bound is one method frame containing one statement, with no loop, branch or blocking call |
| Data requirements | None. No field, no schema, no record, no serialisation |

| Validation category | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Business rules | The entry point must remain the class's only member; adding a second member would contradict the contract stated in the class Javadoc at lines 1–5 and relied on by Sections 1.2.2.2 and 1.3.1.1 |
| Data validation | Not applicable, and deliberately so — validating `args` would itself breach F-001-RQ-003 |
| Security requirements | Because `args` is never dereferenced there is no argument-injection surface; `Project Guide.md` §6 records that no injection surface exists anywhere in the program |
| Compliance requirements | Each construct carries its explanatory comment (F-008); the file is a covered work under GPL v3 (F-006) |

### 2.2.3 F-002 — Fixed Console Message Emission

| Requirement ID | Description | Priority | Complexity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F-002-RQ-001 | Write exactly the literal `Hello from Java!` to standard output | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-002 | Append exactly one platform line separator to that literal | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-003 | Write to standard output only; write to no other sink | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-004 | Produce byte-identical output on both launch paths and under any argument list | Must-Have | Low |
| F-002-RQ-005 | Emit the greeting exactly once per process run | Must-Have | Low |

| Requirement ID | Acceptance criterion | Evidence at `HEAD` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| F-002-RQ-001 | `Hello.java` line 17 contains the literal as a 16-character ASCII string; captured stdout compares byte-identical to the fenced block at `README.md` lines 59–61 | static (line 17; literal measured at 16 characters); recorded — "the fenced expected-output block compares byte-identical to real standard output" (`Project Guide.md` §4) |
| F-002-RQ-002 | The call is `println`, not `print`; stdout ends with exactly one host separator, giving 17 bytes where the separator is LF | static (one `println`, zero `print(`); recorded (`Project Guide.md` §4: "17 bytes on this host"); `README.md` line 63 |
| F-002-RQ-003 | `System.` appears only on line 17 (the call) and line 18 (a comment); there is no `System.err`, file, socket or stream reference; the error stream is empty after a run | static (2 occurrences, 0 `System.err`); recorded (`Project Guide.md` §4, empty error stream) |
| F-002-RQ-004 | `java Hello` and `java Hello.java` yield identical stdout, and runs with no, many and hostile arguments yield identical stdout | recorded — Runtime behaviour and parity, 6 of 6 checks passed (`Project Guide.md` §3); `README.md` line 46; `Project Guide.md` §9.7 shows `java Hello.java one two three` producing the same line |
| F-002-RQ-005 | Exactly one `println` call exists in the tree and the file contains no loop or conditional (`for (`, `while (`, `if (`, `switch` all return zero matches) | static |

| Technical aspect | Specification |
| --- | --- |
| Input parameters | None. The payload is a compile-time constant; nothing at run time can alter it |
| Output / response | Standard output: `Hello from Java!` plus one platform line separator. Standard error: empty. This is the whole externally observable response of the system |
| Performance criteria | None is recorded. `README.md` line 63 fixes the invariant as the literal and its single trailing separator, explicitly not a byte count, "so the exact byte count varies between platforms" |
| Data requirements | One data element in the entire system — the string constant on line 17 — plus one runtime-derived value, the host line separator. No schema, file format or serialisation |

| Validation category | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Business rules | The literal is the system's contract and may not change without invalidating `README.md` lines 57–63 and the acceptance oracle in `Project Guide.md` §4; the separator must stay host-supplied rather than hard-coded |
| Data validation | No input is validated because none is read; the output is validated by byte comparison against the published fenced block |
| Security requirements | The payload is a constant with no interpolation, so no format-string or injection vector exists; nothing is written to any sink other than stdout |
| Compliance requirements | The output statement carries its own explanatory comment at line 16 (F-008); the published expected output in `README.md` must continue to match byte for byte (F-007-RQ-002) |

| F-003-RQ-002 | Exit with status 0 on every run | Must-Have | Low |
| F-003-RQ-003 | Leave standard error empty; expose no exception or error path | Must-Have | Low |
| F-003-RQ-004 | Run single-threaded and unblocked, so the process always terminates | Should-Have | Low |

| --- | --- | --- |
| F-003-RQ-001 | A search for `System.exit(` in `Hello.java` returns zero matches; control reaches the closing brace of `main` at line 19 | static (0 matches); the line 18 comment states the property; `README.md` line 63 calls it "a deliberate property of the program rather than an omission" |
| F-003-RQ-002 | `java Hello; echo "exit=$?"` prints the greeting followed by `exit=0` | recorded (`Project Guide.md` §9.7, §4); `README.md` line 63 |
| F-003-RQ-003 | The file contains no `try {`, `catch`, `throw` or `new`; a captured error stream is empty and compares byte-identical to the pre-comment build's error stream | static (0 matches each); recorded — parity of stdout, stderr and exit status against a build of the pre-comment source (`Project Guide.md` §3, §4) |

| --- | --- |
| Input parameters | None |
| Output / response | Process exit status 0; empty standard error. No shutdown hook, no finaliser, no diagnostic output |
| Performance criteria | None is recorded. The run is bounded by one statement plus JVM start-up and shutdown; the repository states no start-up or duration target anywhere |
| Data requirements | None; no state survives the process and none is written during it |

| Business rules | Exit status 0 with an empty error stream is the program's only outcome — Section 1.3.2.4 records that treating a non-zero status or stderr content as a program state is unsupported |

| Security requirements | No resource is opened, so nothing can leak on exit; `Project Guide.md` §6 records no resource, port or network use at all |
| Compliance requirements | The termination path carries its own explanatory comment at line 18 (F-008) and is stated in `README.md` line 63 (F-007-RQ-002) |
