### 5.1.3 Data Flow Description

The system has one data flow at build time, one at launch time, and none at all while the program runs. The payload is a single 16-character ASCII string literal, and the entire data domain is that literal plus the host's line separator.

**Build-time flow.** The operator invokes `javac` on the 1,073-byte source file. The compiler reads the unit, resolves nothing — there is no classpath entry to search and no manifest to consult — and emits one class file. The greeting becomes a constant-pool entry in that class file; the archived specification records the compiled artifact as 420 bytes whose `main` body is four bytecode instructions: `getstatic System.out`, `ldc "Hello from Java!"`, `invokevirtual PrintStream.println` and `return`. Where the class file lands is the only branch in the flow: build Path A (`javac Hello.java`) leaves it beside the source inside the checkout, untracked and unignored, while build Path B (`javac -Xlint:all -d "$B" Hello.java` into a `mktemp -d` directory) keeps it outside the working tree entirely.

**Launch-time flow.** The `java` launcher resolves the class by its bare name from the classpath — the repository root after Path A, or the scratch directory via `-cp "$B"` after Path B — and invokes `main` once. Inside the frame, the constant-pool string is pushed and handed to `System.out.println`, which writes the characters and then the host's line separator to file descriptor 1. Control returns from `main`; with no `System.exit` call the JVM shuts down of its own accord and the process reports status 0 with an empty standard error. The single-file source launch `java Hello.java` compresses the two flows into one: the launcher compiles the unit in memory and runs it without materialising a class file, which is why that path leaves no artifact behind and why `README.md` line 40 records it as needing JDK 11 or later.

**Data transformation points.** There are exactly two. The first is compilation, which turns source text into a constant-pool entry and four instructions; it is deterministic, because re-running `javac` re-derives the same class file from the same unchanged unit with zero dependency resolution. The second is the `println` call, which turns a `String` into bytes on a stream and appends the separator — and it is the only point in the system where the output is environment-dependent. `README.md` line 63 states the consequence precisely: the exact byte count varies between platforms while the literal and its single trailing separator do not.

**Flows that do not exist.** No data enters the program. The `args` array is passed and never dereferenced, so arguments — including the shell and injection payloads exercised in `Project Guide.md` §4 — cannot reach any code path. Nothing is read from standard input, from a file, from a socket, from an environment variable or from a secret store. Nothing is written to any sink other than file descriptor 1; the source contains no reference to a file, socket or other stream, and `System.` appears only at line 17 (the call) and line 18 (a comment).

**Key data stores and caches.** There is no runtime data store: the `println` writes to a stream, not to storage. Two durable stores exist outside the program. The **Git object store** holds the five tracked blobs, 14 commits and zero tags; it is the system's only durable, distributable state, and it is also what supplies the pre-comment revision `0726b1d` that the behaviour-parity and additions-only verifications depend on. The **maintainer's working tree** holds the source as edited bytes. Everything else a workflow produces — `Hello.class`, `javadoc` HTML, scratch directories — is ephemeral and explicitly outside the tracked set. No cache of any kind exists: there is no dependency or artifact cache because nothing is resolved or downloaded, no build cache because there is no build system to hold one, and no application cache because there is no state to cache. The per-run `mktemp -d` directory is the deliberate opposite of a cache, being newly generated on every invocation. Section 4.3.1.4 and Section 4.3.1.5 record the full persistence and caching position.

**Documentation data coupling.** One further flow is worth naming because it is validated mechanically: the fenced expected-output block at `README.md` lines 59–61 republishes the literal from `Hello.java` line 17 as the operator-facing oracle, and `Project Guide.md` §4 records that block compared byte-identical against real standard output. The coupling is one-way — the guide reads the code's contract, never the reverse — which is why a drifting guide is a documentation defect rather than a runtime one.

### 5.1.4 External Integration Points

Five external parties participate, and they exhaust the list. Three of them — the JDK toolchain, the operating-system process contract and the GPL v3 instrument — are contracts rather than services; one is a hosted service used only for source distribution; one is a presentation-only renderer. No application-level integration exists in either direction: `Project Guide.md` Appendix B states without qualification that there is "no service, database, broker or cache in this project."

| System | Integration Type | Data Exchange Pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JDK toolchain — `javac`, `java`, `javadoc` (OpenJDK 25.0.3 recorded) | Host-supplied build and runtime tooling; invoked, never embedded | Synchronous one-shot command invocation; source file in, class file or process in and diagnostics out |
| Operating-system process contract | Runtime output and status reporting | Fire-and-forget unidirectional write, then normal return; no reply channel and no acknowledgement |
| Git and the hosting platform (`github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java`) | Version control and the sole distribution channel | Clone, fetch, branch, push and merge on demand; pull-based consumption of source |
| GPL v3 licence instrument (Free Software Foundation, 29 June 2007) | Legal and compliance obligation attached to the covered work | Static conveyance — the verbatim text travels with every copy; no runtime interaction |
| GitHub Flavored Markdown renderer | Presentation of the tracked documentation | Server-side render on view; read-only, presentation only |

| System | Protocol and Format |
| --- | --- |
| JDK toolchain | POSIX process execution from a shell; ASCII/CRLF `.java` source in, JVM class-file bytecode out, diagnostics on standard error |
| Operating-system process contract | POSIX file descriptors 1 and 2 plus the wait-status convention; ASCII payload followed by the platform line separator |
| Git and the hosting platform | Git smart protocol over HTTPS; Git objects — five blobs, 14 commits, zero tags, six refs |
| GPL v3 licence instrument | Verbatim plain text in `LICENSE`, referenced from `README.md` line 77, with the dated modification notice at `README.md` line 5 |
| GitHub Flavored Markdown renderer | GFM over CommonMark, determined by the hosting platform; LF-terminated UTF-8 Markdown source |

**Service-level requirements.** The repository defines none, for any of the five parties, and none is asserted here. The table below records what each integration actually requires in place of an SLA.

| System | Availability or Service-Level Position |
| --- | --- |
| JDK toolchain | No availability requirement: the toolchain is needed only at build and launch time, and no long-running process depends on it. A JDK is the sole prerequisite, unpinned — the compile-then-run path was exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21, while the single-file source launch is documented as needing JDK 11 or later and has not been confirmed on a real JDK 11 runtime |
| Operating-system process contract | No requirement beyond the launching shell connecting standard output and observing the exit status; the only stated contract is the output contract itself (`README.md` lines 57–63) |
| Git and the hosting platform | No uptime, latency or durability commitment is recorded. The dependency is availability-at-clone-time only; once cloned, every documented workflow runs entirely offline with zero network egress |
| GPL v3 licence instrument | Not applicable — a perpetual legal instrument with no operational availability dimension |
| GitHub Flavored Markdown renderer | No requirement: rendering affects presentation only, and `Project Guide.md` §3 records that the guide's structure was asserted against its Markdown source rather than against a rendered page |

Two consequences of this position deserve stating. First, because the JDK is unpinned, a build is reproducible in *behaviour* but not in *toolchain*: two operators on different JDKs both obtain `Hello from Java!` and exit status 0, but nothing records or constrains which JDK either used. Second, because no integration is synchronous with a running service, there is no failure mode in which an external party degrades the program at run time — every recorded failure mode belongs to the build, launch, hygiene or verification stage and is catalogued in Section 4.3.2.2.


## 5.2 Component Details

This sub-section takes each component introduced in Section 5.1.2 and states its purpose, the technologies it actually uses, the interfaces it exposes or consumes, what it persists, and how it scales. Component identifiers (C-1 … C-10) and interface identifiers (I-1 … I-4) are carried forward unchanged.

### 5.2.1 Component Interaction Model

Interaction in this system is entirely synchronous and entirely operator-initiated. There is no message, event, callback, poll or scheduled trigger anywhere: every arrow below is either a shell-initiated invocation, a file read, or a stream write.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Actor["Operator or learner<br/>POSIX shell at repository root"]

    subgraph TrackedSet["Tracked components — inside the boundary"]
        C1["C-1 Hello.java<br/>compilation unit<br/>default package"]
        C2["C-2 Hello.main<br/>entry point, line 15"]
        C3["C-3 stdout write path<br/>line 17"]
        C4["C-4 README.md<br/>operator guide + oracle"]
        C5["C-5 LICENSE<br/>GPL v3"]
        C6["C-6 Project Guide.md<br/>status and verification record"]
        C7["C-7 Technical Specifications.md<br/>baseline archive"]
    end

    subgraph EnvSet["Environment-provided components — outside the boundary"]
        C8a["C-8a javac<br/>-d, -Xlint:all, -Werror, --release"]
        C8b["C-8b java<br/>-cp, class or source launch"]
        C8c["C-8c javadoc<br/>-quiet, -Xdoclint:all"]
        C9["C-9 git 2.51.0 + HTTPS remote<br/>14 commits, 0 tags"]
        C10["C-10 mktemp -d scratch directory<br/>owner-readable, per run"]
    end

    subgraph Sinks["Process contract — I-3"]
        Out["stdout: Hello from Java!<br/>plus platform separator"]
        Err["stderr: empty"]
        Status["exit status 0<br/>by normal return"]
    end

    C4 -.->|"instructs"| Actor
    C6 -.->|"records versions and outcomes"| Actor
    C7 -.->|"historical baseline only"| Actor
    Actor --> C9
    C9 -->|"clone, branch, baseline export"| C1
    Actor -->|"I-1 compile"| C8a
    C1 --> C8a
    C8a -->|"Hello.class, 420 B"| C10
    Actor -->|"I-2 launch"| C8b
    C10 -->|"-cp classpath entry"| C8b
    C1 -.->|"single-file source launch, JDK 11+"| C8b
    C8b --> C2
    C2 --> C3
    C3 --> Out
    C2 --> Err
    C2 --> Status
    Actor -->|"coverage check"| C8c
    C1 --> C8c
    C8c -->|"HTML, never committed"| C10
    C5 -.->|"governs redistribution"| C1
    C4 -.->|"oracle compared byte-for-byte"| Out
```

Three properties of this model are worth naming because they determine everything in Sections 5.3 and 5.4. First, **the only runtime interaction is C-2 → C-3 → stdout**; every other arrow is build-time, documentation-time or distribution-time. Second, **there is no fan-out and no branch inside the boundary** — the runtime chain F-004 → F-001 → F-002 → F-003 is strictly linear because `Hello.java` contains no conditional, loop or exception construct. Third, **the documentation components are pure consumers of the code's contract**: nothing in C-1 reads C-4, C-5, C-6 or C-7, so the dependency is one-way by construction.

### 5.2.2 Application Components

#### 5.2.2.1 C-1 — `Hello` Compilation Unit

| Aspect | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and responsibilities | Holds the whole program. Declares `public class Hello` at line 6 in the default package, with no `package` statement, no `import`, no field, no explicit constructor, no second method and no nested type. It is simultaneously the build input, the deployment unit and the subject of every documentation claim |
| Technologies and frameworks | The Java language at baseline syntax — nothing later than the original language level is used, and no `--release` or `--source` setting is recorded anywhere in the repository. No framework, no annotation, no generated code and no third-party library participates |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Exposes I-1 to `javac`: the file name must match the public class name, which is why exporting the unit under any other name produces `error: class Hello is public, should be declared in a file named Hello.java`. Exposes the public class itself for bare-name resolution under I-2 |
| Data persistence | Permanently persisted as a tracked Git blob (`3fd76ce`, 1,073 bytes, 20 lines, CRLF on every line, pure ASCII, zero tabs). No `.gitattributes` exists, so its stored byte format is preserved by editor discipline alone |
| Scaling considerations | No scaling dimension. The unit is fixed in size, compiles in one invocation with zero dependency resolution, and has no growth path that does not change the architecture — adding a second compilation unit or a first third-party import would introduce build ordering and dependency resolution the project currently has none of |

The comment structure of this component is itself a delivered feature (F-008): the class Javadoc at lines 1–5, the `main` Javadoc with its `@param args` tag at lines 7–14, and the two line comments at lines 16 and 18 constitute four comments for four written functionalities, verified as an additions-only change against the pre-comment revision `0726b1d`.

#### 5.2.2.2 C-2 — `Hello.main` Entry Point

| Aspect | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and responsibilities | The only executable path in the system. Invoked exactly once per process by the JVM launcher; performs the single write and returns. Accepts `String[] args` solely to satisfy the entry-point signature and never dereferences it, so behaviour is identical with no arguments, many arguments, or the shell and injection payloads exercised in `Project Guide.md` §4 |
| Technologies and frameworks | The JVM entry-point convention: `public static void main(String[] args)` at `Hello.java` line 15. `static`, so no instance is ever created; no `throws` clause, so no checked exception is declared |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Consumes I-2 from the `java` launcher, resolved by the bare class name because the class sits in the default package. Its termination behaviour is part of I-3: control returns at the closing brace with no `System.exit` call, and the JVM then shuts down of its own accord |
| Data persistence | None. No field, no instance, no static mutable state, no shutdown hook and no finaliser, so nothing survives the frame and nothing is carried between runs |
| Scaling considerations | Perfectly parallel by construction: with no shared mutable state and no lock, any number of concurrent invocations are independent and cannot contend. Scaling is therefore process-per-invocation and horizontal by definition; the repository records no timing, throughput or startup-cost measurement, so no capacity figure is asserted |

#### 5.2.2.3 C-3 — Standard-Output Write Path

| Aspect | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and responsibilities | Emits the program's sole output. The line comment at `Hello.java` line 16 fixes single-sink behaviour as a design property: one write to standard output, the fixed greeting plus the platform line separator, and "no other sink is written" |
| Technologies and frameworks | `java.base` only, and only the classes actually reached: `java.lang.System` for the `out` field, `java.io.PrintStream` for `println(String)`, and `java.lang.String` for the literal. No logging framework, formatter or encoder participates |
| Key interfaces and APIs | `System.out.println(String)` at line 17 — the single API call in the entire program. Downstream it consumes I-3, writing to file descriptor 1; file descriptor 2 is left untouched, which is what makes the empty standard error a contract rather than a coincidence |
| Data persistence | None. The call writes to a stream, not to storage; the source contains no reference to a file, socket or other stream, and no query of the stream's error state |
| Scaling considerations | Constant work per invocation — one write of a compile-time constant. The only variable is the separator supplied by the host, which makes standard output 17 bytes where the separator is LF and 18 where it is CRLF |

### 5.2.3 Documentation and Governance Components

#### 5.2.3.1 C-4 — Operator Guide (`README.md`)

| Aspect | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and responsibilities | The operator-facing contract. Eight sections in a fixed order — change summary, overview, requirements, build, run, expected output, layout, licence — covering both build paths, all three launch forms, the argument contract, the output contract and the licence reference |
| Technologies and frameworks | GitHub Flavored Markdown over CommonMark, determined by the hosting platform; no generator or renderer is part of the project. Stored LF-only, UTF-8, newline-terminated, 77 lines / 4,053 bytes (blob `3956e03`) |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Human-readable. Two relative links (to `Hello.java` and `LICENSE`), both verified to resolve on disk; two stable-symbol source citations at lines 14 and 53 with zero line-number locators, chosen because inserting comments shifts every line below them; and the fenced expected-output block at lines 59–61 that serves as the published output oracle |
| Data persistence | Permanently tracked. Its dated modification notice at line 5 is the GPL-required record for a modified covered work |
| Scaling considerations | Not applicable in a capacity sense. The maintenance consideration is drift: its layout section at line 67 still describes three tracked files and no subdirectories, which the five-file tracked inventory has overtaken |

| Purpose and responsibilities | Establishes the redistribution terms for the covered work as the verbatim GNU General Public License, Version 3, dated 29 June 2007 — preamble, all numbered terms, end-of-terms marker and the appendix on applying the licence to new programs |
| Technologies and frameworks | Plain text, 674 lines / 35,149 bytes (blob `f288702`). No executable content, no declaration and no dependency |

C-7 (`blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md`, 8,321 lines / 839,724 bytes) retains the prior generation of this specification |
| Technologies and frameworks | Markdown with embedded Mermaid diagrams; LF-only. Together they account for 884,733 of the 925,008 tracked bytes, which is why explaining the program is the larger part of the project's output |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Human-readable through I-4 only. C-6 is the sole durable record of the 49 verification checks, because nothing in the repository re-runs them |

The consideration is currency: C-7 documents `Hello.java` as five lines / 127 bytes and `README.md` as a 41-byte placeholder and anchors its version 1.0 at commit `0726b1d`, so it describes the pre-comment baseline rather than `HEAD`; C-6 repeats C-4's stale three-file layout claim in its Appendix C |

### 5.2.4 Environment-Provided Components

#### 5.2.4.1 C-8 — JDK Toolchain

| Aspect | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and responsibilities | `javac` compiles the single unit and, under `-Xlint:all -Werror`, serves as the project's entire static-analysis surface since no linter is configured. `java` launches either the compiled class or the source file directly. `javadoc` measures comment coverage |
| Technologies and frameworks | OpenJDK 25.0.3 is the recorded version for all three tools; the repository pins nothing. Observed flags across the documented workflows: `-d`, `-Xlint:all`, `-Werror`, `--release`, `--source`, `-cp`, `-quiet`, `-Xdoclint:all` |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Command-line interfaces invoked synchronously from a POSIX shell, consuming I-1 and I-2 and producing I-3. The compile-then-run path was exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21; the single-file source launch requires a launcher implementing source-file mode, documented as JDK 11 or later |
| Data persistence | Writes only outside the tracked set: a class file (beside the source under build Path A, or into the scratch directory under Path B) and `javadoc` HTML that is never committed |
| Scaling considerations | Host-supplied and never vendored, so nothing about it scales with the project. The residual consideration is exposure rather than capacity: because the JDK is unpinned, runtime CVE exposure is a property of the operator's chosen build and is neither recorded nor constrained here |

#### 5.2.4.2 C-9 — Git Repository and Hosting Remote

| Aspect | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and responsibilities | The durable object store, the sole distribution channel, and the supplier of the pre-comment revision `0726b1d` that the behaviour-parity and additions-only verifications compare against |
| Technologies and frameworks | `git` 2.51.0 recorded; the Git smart protocol over HTTPS to `github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java`. Local branches `jr_java1` (checked out) and `main`; six refs in total including `origin/jr_java2`, `origin/jr_java3` and one generated branch |
| Key interfaces and APIs | The `git` CLI and the hosting platform's pull-request merge, consumed through I-4. The platform's Markdown renderer resolves the two relative links in `README.md` |
| Data persistence | Five tracked blobs, 14 commits and **zero tags** — which is why every version reference in this specification is a commit SHA rather than a release identifier |
| Scaling considerations | No capacity dimension at this size. The operative consideration is reachability: `main` sits at `0726b1d` and is 11 commits behind the working branch, so the entire documentation delivery is absent from the default branch until the branch is published and merged |

#### 5.2.4.3 C-10 — Per-Run Scratch Directory

| Aspect | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and responsibilities | Receives class output and `javadoc` HTML outside the checkout, which is the control that keeps the working tree clean in the absence of any `.gitignore` |
| Technologies and frameworks | `mktemp -d`, invoked as `B="$(mktemp -d)"` and quoted consistently for both the compile (`javac -d "$B"`) and the launch (`java -cp "$B"`) |
| Key interfaces and APIs | Acts as the `-d` destination under I-1 and as the `-cp` classpath entry under I-2 |
| Data persistence | Ephemeral by design. Freshly generated on every invocation and removed afterwards; it is the deliberate opposite of a cache |
| Scaling considerations | Trivially parallel: because each run generates a new uniquely named, owner-readable-only directory, repeated or concurrent builds never collide. A fixed, predictable destination would forfeit that property and could be pre-created, replaced or redirected through a symbolic link by another local process before the compiler writes into it |

### 5.2.5 Component State Transitions

The process-level state machine, the build-artifact lifecycle and the repository delivery state are documented in Sections 4.3.1.1 through 4.3.1.3. The machine below is the complementary **component-level** view: the states the `Hello` component passes through as its representation changes from tracked source bytes to an executing frame and back to nothing. It is the state machine that explains why the three launch workflows are equivalent — they differ only in which representation path they take to `Loaded`.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Tracked source bytes, blob 3fd76ce, 1,073 B CRLF" as SourceTracked
    state "Working-tree source, possibly edited" as SourceWorking
    state "Class file on disk, 420 B, main is 4 instructions" as ClassOnDisk
    state "Class compiled in memory, no artifact materialised" as ClassInMemory
    state "Class loaded and resolved by the bare name Hello" as Loaded
    state "main frame active, args never dereferenced" as Frame
    state "Single write completed to file descriptor 1" as Written
    state "Frame returned, no System.exit, JVM shutting down" as Returned
    state "Nothing retained, exit status 0, stderr empty" as Gone
    state "Documentable members measured, 2 of 3 covered" as Measured

    [*] --> SourceTracked : git clone
    SourceTracked --> SourceWorking : checkout, or git show of revision 0726b1d
    SourceWorking --> SourceTracked : commit, additions-only, 15 added 0 removed
    SourceWorking --> ClassOnDisk : javac Hello.java, or javac -d scratch, exit 0 no diagnostics
    SourceWorking --> ClassInMemory : java Hello.java, single-file source launch, JDK 11+
    SourceWorking --> Measured : javadoc -quiet, exactly one expected warning
    Measured --> SourceWorking : coverage recorded, no source change
    ClassOnDisk --> Loaded : java Hello, or java -cp scratch Hello
    ClassInMemory --> Loaded : launcher hands the in-memory class to the JVM
    Loaded --> Frame : public static void main invoked exactly once
    Frame --> Written : line 17 executed exactly once
    Written --> Returned : closing brace at line 19, no System.exit
    Returned --> Gone : JVM shuts down of its own accord
    Gone --> [*]
    note right of Loaded
        Both representation paths converge here,
        which is why README.md line 46 can state
        that both launch paths produce
        byte-identical standard output.
    end note
    note right of Frame
        No field, no instance, no shared mutable
        state, no shutdown hook, no finaliser.
        Nothing to initialise, synchronise or reset.
    end note
```

The machine has one notable structural property: **no state has an error transition out of it that originates inside the component**. Every failure that can interrupt the path — a name mismatch at compilation, an unresolvable class at launch, a launcher without source-file mode — is raised by C-8 before or instead of entering the next state, never by C-1 or C-2. Section 5.4.3 develops that containment property, and the fault catalogue itself is in Section 4.3.2.2.

### 5.2.6 Key Flow Sequence Diagrams

#### 5.2.6.1 Compile-Then-Run — Workflows W-1 and W-2

Both compile-then-run workflows share one sequence and differ only in the class-output destination, shown as the branch after compilation. This is the path with no version floor; it was exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor Op as Operator
    participant Sh as POSIX shell
    participant Jc as javac (C-8a)
    participant Dest as Destination (checkout or C-10)
    participant Jv as java launcher (C-8b)
    participant Main as Hello.main (C-2)
    participant Out as stdout / exit status (I-3)

    Op->>Sh: read README.md build section
    Op->>Sh: javac Hello.java (Path A) or javac -Xlint:all -d "$B" Hello.java (Path B)
    Sh->>Jc: invoke with the single compilation unit
    Jc->>Jc: resolve nothing - no classpath entry, no manifest
    Jc->>Dest: write Hello.class, 420 bytes
    Jc-->>Sh: exit 0, no diagnostics, empty stderr
    Note over Jc,Dest: Path A leaves an untracked, unignored artifact in the checkout.<br/>Path B keeps it outside the working tree entirely.
    Op->>Sh: java Hello (Path A) or java -cp "$B" Hello (Path B)
    Sh->>Jv: invoke the launcher
    Jv->>Dest: resolve class Hello by bare name from the classpath
    Dest-->>Jv: class bytes
    Jv->>Main: invoke main(String[] args) exactly once
    Note over Main: args is accepted and never dereferenced
    Main->>Out: one write - Hello from Java! plus the platform separator
    Main-->>Jv: return normally, no System.exit
    Jv->>Out: exit status 0, stderr empty
    Out-->>Op: 17 bytes on an LF host, 18 on a CRLF host
```

#### 5.2.6.2 Single-File Source Launch — Workflow W-3

This path collapses compilation and launch into one invocation and materialises no artifact, which is the reason `README.md` records it as needing JDK 11 or later while the compile-then-run path carries no such floor.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor Op as Operator
    participant Sh as POSIX shell
    participant Jv as java launcher in source-file mode
    participant Mem as In-memory class
    participant Main as Hello.main (C-2)
    participant Out as stdout / exit status (I-3)

    Op->>Sh: java Hello.java  (arguments optional and never read)
    Sh->>Jv: invoke with a .java path rather than a class name
    Jv->>Jv: require the first top-level class to declare the standard main signature
    Jv->>Mem: compile the unit in memory - nothing written to disk
    Mem-->>Jv: class ready
    Jv->>Main: invoke main(String[] args)
    Main->>Out: one write - identical payload to the compiled path
    Main-->>Jv: return normally
    Jv->>Out: exit status 0, stderr empty, no class file left behind
    Out-->>Op: byte-identical standard output to W-1 and W-2
    Note over Jv,Out: On a launcher without source-file mode this path fails.<br/>The documented fallback is compile-then-run.
```

#### 5.2.6.3 Verification of the Output Contract and Comment Coverage — Workflows W-4 and M-2

This is the only flow in the system that compares one component against another, and it is entirely manual: no CI pipeline, scheduler or gate re-runs it.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor Mt as Maintainer
    participant Git as git (C-9)
    participant Base as Baseline build of revision 0726b1d
    participant Head as Build of HEAD
    participant Cmp as cmp / diff
    participant Jd as javadoc (C-8c)
    participant Rec as Project Guide.md sections 3 and 4 (C-6)

    Mt->>Git: git show 0726b1d:Hello.java into a scratch path named Hello.java
    Git-->>Base: pre-comment source, five code lines
    Mt->>Base: javac, then run and capture stdout and stderr
    Mt->>Head: javac, then run and capture stdout and stderr
    Mt->>Cmp: compare both streams and the exit status
    Cmp-->>Mt: byte-identical - behaviour preserved by the comment-only change
    Mt->>Jd: javadoc -quiet Hello.java
    Jd-->>Mt: exit 0 with exactly one warning - the implicit default constructor
    Note over Jd,Mt: Coverage stands at 2 of 3 documentable members.<br/>The third cannot carry a doc comment without declaring a constructor.
    Mt->>Head: compare README.md lines 59-61 against real stdout
    Head-->>Mt: fenced oracle matches byte for byte
    Mt->>Rec: record 49 of 49 checks passing on OpenJDK 25.0.3
    Note over Rec: This record is the only durable evidence of the checks -<br/>nothing re-runs them on future changes.
```

### 5.2.7 Consolidated Scaling Position

The system has no scaling requirement recorded anywhere, and its structure gives it an unusual scaling profile worth stating once rather than repeating per component:

- **Concurrency is free and unbounded in principle.** With no field, no instance, no static mutable state and no lock, concurrent invocations share nothing and cannot contend. The repository nonetheless records no concurrency requirement and no measurement.
- **Scaling is horizontal by definition and vertical not at all.** The unit of work is one process that executes four bytecode instructions in `main`; there is no heap growth, no thread pool, no connection pool and no queue to enlarge.
- **Build scaling is a non-question.** One compilation unit of 1,073 bytes, zero dependency resolution and zero network egress mean a build neither benefits from caching nor degrades with repetition.
- **There is no scaling infrastructure and none is implied.** No container, orchestrator, cloud service or IaC descriptor exists in the repository; Section 3.7.4 records each absence against a direct verification.
- **The real limit is architectural, not operational.** Growth in any direction — a second compilation unit, a first third-party import, a `package` declaration, a build manifest — changes the architecture rather than scaling it, and Section 3.7.5 enumerates exactly which recorded requirements each such change invalidates.


## 5.3 Technical Decisions

### 5.3.1 Decision Provenance

The repository contains no architecture decision record, design note, RFC or issue tracker, so no decision below is quoted from a stated design rationale unless the source explicitly states one. Three levels of provenance are distinguished throughout this sub-section, and each decision is labelled accordingly:

- **Stated** — the repository explicitly names the choice and its reason. Only four decisions qualify: the default package as the reason for bare-name launch (`Hello.java` lines 3–4), single-sink output as a design property (`Hello.java` line 16), termination by normal return as "a deliberate property of the program rather than an omission" (`README.md` line 63), and the freshly generated compiler-output directory with its threat rationale (`README.md` line 30).
- **Recorded** — the repository states the position without arguing for it, typically in `README.md` §Requirements or a `Project Guide.md` appendix. The unpinned Java version and the absence of any dependency manifest are of this kind.
- **Reconstructed** — the choice is evident only from what the artifacts do and do not contain. These are labelled as such and are never presented as the author's intent.

### 5.3.2 Architecture Style Decision and Tradeoffs

| Decision | Provenance | Tradeoff Accepted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-process, single-module, invoke-and-exit console application | Reconstructed from one compilation unit, one class, one method, one statement | No extension point of any kind: adding a second responsibility means adding the project's first structural decomposition |
| One class in the **default package**, launched by the bare name `Hello` | Stated — `Hello.java` lines 3–4 give the default package as the reason for bare-name launch | Forfeits namespacing and any module system; a later `package` declaration would break every documented command |
| Unit of compilation is the unit of deployment | Reconstructed from the absence of a build descriptor, `module-info.java` and any packaged artifact | Nothing is publishable as a binary; the program is consumed only as source from a checkout |
| No layering, facade, dependency injection or ports-and-adapters arrangement | Reconstructed from zero collaborator objects and zero imports | A future collaborator arrives with no seam to attach to; the first abstraction is also the first architectural change |
| Statelessness by construction rather than by policy | Reconstructed from no field, no constructor, no instance, `static` entry point | Nothing can be carried between runs even if a later requirement wanted it |
| Documentation as the primary deliverable, behaviour frozen | Recorded — `README.md` lines 7–8 and the compliance matrix in `Project Guide.md` §5.1 rows 1–3 | 884,733 of 925,008 tracked bytes explain 1,073 bytes of program, and the documentation can drift from the tree, which it already has in two places |

The style's central tradeoff is that **every property that makes the program valuable also makes it unextendable**. Section 3.7.5 states the consequence in requirement terms: each candidate growth step — a build manifest, a second compilation unit, a first third-party import, a `package` declaration, a `--release` setting — invalidates specific recorded requirements rather than merely adding to them.

### 5.3.3 Communication Pattern Choices

The system communicates in exactly three ways, all synchronous and all operator-initiated. No asynchronous pattern is present anywhere: there is no message, event, callback, queue, broker, poll or scheduled trigger, and `Project Guide.md` Appendix B records that the program "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call."

| Pattern | Where it applies | Why it is the choice observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Synchronous one-shot command invocation | Operator to `javac`, `java` and `javadoc` (I-1, I-2) | The tools are process-scoped; the shell's exit status is the complete reply, so no protocol layer is needed |
| Unidirectional fire-and-forget stream write | `Hello.main` to standard output (I-3) | The program has no reply channel by design — the single write is the whole output contract, and standard error is deliberately left empty |
| Out-of-band human communication | Terminal output, `README.md`, `Project Guide.md`, pull requests | With no CI gate, no logging framework and no notification channel, the operator's terminal and the tracked documents are the only channels that exist |
| Pull-based source distribution | Git clone, fetch and merge over HTTPS (I-4) | Consumers take the source when they want it; nothing is pushed to a consumer and no artifact is published |

Two consequences follow. First, **request/response, publish/subscribe and request/reply are all absent, not merely unused** — there is no component pair between which they could apply. Second, because the only runtime communication is a write with no acknowledgement, the program cannot detect delivery failure and does not try: the source contains no query of the stream's error state.

### 5.3.4 Data Storage Solution Rationale

| Storage decision | Provenance | Rationale and tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No database, no embedded store, no file written by the program | Recorded — `Project Guide.md` Appendix B: "there is no service, database, broker or cache in this project" | The data domain is one compile-time string constant and one host-supplied line separator; a store would have nothing to hold. Tradeoff: no run leaves evidence of itself |
| Git object store as the only durable, distributable state | Reconstructed from five tracked blobs, 14 commits, zero tags | Source-only distribution needs no artifact repository, and history doubles as the verification baseline supplier (`0726b1d`). Tradeoff: with no tags, every version reference must be a commit SHA |
| Build output kept outside the tracked set | Stated for the mechanism (`README.md` line 30); recorded as a deferred hygiene item in `Project Guide.md` §5.2 item 5 | Keeps the distribution source-only. Tradeoff: with no `.gitignore`, the guarantee rests on command discipline, which is why an accidentally committed `Hello.class` is a catalogued failure mode |
| Source stored with CRLF line endings and no `.gitattributes` | Recorded — `Project Guide.md` §5.2 item 5: normalising would rewrite all lines and change the file's content digest | Preserves the historical byte format exactly. Tradeoff: an LF-normalising editor silently rewrites all 20 lines, tracked as a Medium-severity risk "Open — accepted by design" |
| No configuration file, environment variable or secret | Recorded — `Project Guide.md` §9.2 and Appendix E | Nothing to configure means nothing to misconfigure and no credential surface. Tradeoff: behaviour cannot be varied without editing source |

The persistence-point inventory and the durability of each is documented in Section 4.3.1.4 and is not repeated here.

### 5.3.5 Caching Strategy Justification

**The strategy is that there is no cache, and the repository is explicit about it.** Three caching layers a Java project would ordinarily carry are absent for structural rather than configuration reasons:

| Cache that would ordinarily exist | Why it is absent |
| --- | --- |
| Dependency or artifact cache | Nothing is resolved or downloaded at build time — there is no manifest and no lock file of any kind, and the build performs zero network egress |
| Build or incremental-compilation cache | There is no build system to hold one; `javac` is invoked directly on a single 1,073-byte compilation unit |
| Application-level cache | There is no state to cache — one compile-time string constant and one runtime-derived line separator are the entire data domain |

The one piece of ephemeral storage in the workflows is deliberately anti-cached: `mktemp -d` generates a **new** directory on every invocation and the workflows remove it afterwards, which is exactly what makes each destination unique and owner-readable-only. Reusing a fixed, predictable location is the condition `README.md` line 30 warns against, so caching the build destination would trade a security property for a benefit the project has no use for. Section 4.3.1.5 records the same position from the process-flow perspective.

### 5.3.6 Security Mechanism Selection

The security architecture is **attack-surface elimination rather than control selection**. `Project Guide.md` §6 states the basis: the program "reads no input, dereferences no argument, opens no resource, binds no port, makes no network call and has no dependency manifest, so there is no injection surface, no supply-chain exposure, no authentication or authorisation surface and no data-at-rest concern." Only one positive security mechanism is selected anywhere in the repository, and it protects the build rather than the program.

| Mechanism or posture | Selection and provenance | What it addresses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Freshly generated, owner-readable-only compiler-output directory | **Selected mechanism** — stated with its rationale at `README.md` line 30 | A fixed, predictable destination can be pre-created, replaced or redirected through a symbolic link by another local process before the compiler writes into it. `mktemp -d` removes the predictability the attack depends on |
| No input surface | Posture — `args` accepted and never dereferenced; no stdin, file, socket or environment read | Eliminates injection entirely. `Project Guide.md` §4 records runs with no arguments, many arguments and hostile arguments including shell and injection payloads all producing identical output |
| No dependency manifest | Posture — zero imports beyond `java.lang`, no manifest in which a dependency could be declared | Eliminates supply-chain exposure; there is no third-party code to compromise and nothing downloaded at build time |
| No network or port surface | Posture — `Project Guide.md` Appendix B | Eliminates remote attack surface; every documented workflow runs offline after clone |
| No credential or secret surface | Posture — `Project Guide.md` Appendix E: no variable and no secret is read by any tracked file | Nothing to leak, rotate or store; `JAVA_HOME` is not even required |
| `javac -Xlint:all -Werror` | **Selected gate** — `Project Guide.md` Appendix F names it "the project's static-analysis surface, as no linter is configured" | The only automated code-quality control; recorded clean at `HEAD` |
| GPL v3 copyleft | **Selected legal control** — verbatim `LICENSE`, referenced at `README.md` line 77, dated modification notice at `README.md` line 5 | Governs redistribution of the covered work; the per-file notice its appendix advises is absent because no rights holder is recorded |

**Authentication and authorisation are not implemented and cannot be.** The program reads no input, so no principal can be asserted, and there is no resource to protect. The only access control in the system is filesystem ownership on the scratch build directory and whatever the hosting platform enforces on the Git remote.

**Two residual risks are recorded rather than mitigated.** Because the JDK is host-supplied and unpinned, runtime CVE exposure is entirely a property of the operator's chosen build and is neither recorded nor constrained by the repository — the trade accepted in exchange for compiling on any JDK. And because the safe-destination rationale lives in prose rather than in a check, a future edit could reintroduce a predictable compiler-output path; `Project Guide.md` §6 rates that Low/Low and marks it "Mitigated" precisely because the reason is written beside the command where the next editor will see it.

### 5.3.7 Decision Tree

The tree below is the reviewable form of the reasoning above: walking it from the root against the actual artifacts reproduces every architectural decision in force at `HEAD`. Each leaf names the ADR that records the decision.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q1{"Must any state survive<br/>a single run?"}
    Q1 -->|"No — no field, no instance,<br/>no I/O beyond one write"| D1["No database, no file write,<br/>no cache, no config<br/>ADR-004"]
    Q1 -->|"Yes"| X1["Would require a storage component<br/>— none exists in the repository"]

    D1 --> Q2{"Is any code required<br/>from outside java.lang?"}
    Q2 -->|"No — zero import statements"| D2["Zero third-party dependencies;<br/>no manifest, no lock file<br/>ADR-003"]
    Q2 -->|"Yes"| X2["Would require dependency resolution<br/>and a supply-chain surface"]

    D2 --> Q3{"Is more than one<br/>compilation unit needed?"}
    Q3 -->|"No — one class, one method"| D3["No build tool; javac and java<br/>invoked directly<br/>ADR-002"]
    Q3 -->|"Yes"| X3["Would require build ordering<br/>and a build model"]

    D3 --> Q4{"Does the class need<br/>a namespace?"}
    Q4 -->|"No — one class in the system"| D4["Default package;<br/>launch by the bare name Hello<br/>ADR-001"]
    Q4 -->|"Yes"| X4["A package declaration would break<br/>every documented command"]

    D4 --> Q5{"Does the program need<br/>to signal a failure status?"}
    Q5 -->|"No — there is no error path<br/>to report"| D5["Return normally from main;<br/>no System.exit<br/>ADR-005"]
    Q5 -->|"Yes"| X5["Would require an exit code<br/>and an error branch"]

    D5 --> Q6{"Must behaviour vary<br/>with operator input?"}
    Q6 -->|"No — output is a<br/>compile-time constant"| D6["Accept args to satisfy the<br/>signature; never read it<br/>ADR-006"]
    Q6 -->|"Yes"| X6["Would create the project's<br/>first injection surface"]

    D6 --> Q7{"Is a reproducible toolchain<br/>more valuable than<br/>running on any JDK?"}
    Q7 -->|"No — portability preferred"| D7["Record versions, pin none;<br/>no --release or --source<br/>ADR-007"]
    Q7 -->|"Yes"| X7["Would convert an any-JDK source<br/>file into a version-targeted build"]

    D7 --> Q8{"May the documentation change<br/>alter runtime behaviour<br/>or stored bytes?"}
    Q8 -->|"No"| D8["Comment-only, additions-only edit;<br/>byte and behaviour parity proven<br/>ADR-008"]
    Q8 -->|"Yes"| X8["Would invalidate the parity evidence<br/>recorded in Project Guide sections 3 and 4"]

    Q9 -->|"No — repository has<br/>no .gitignore"| D9["Compile into a fresh mktemp -d<br/>directory outside the checkout<br/>ADR-009"]
    Q9 -->|"Yes"| X9["An ignore rule remains an<br/>open owner decision"]

    D9 --> Q10{"Is a named copyright holder<br/>recorded anywhere<br/>in the repository?"}
    Q10 -->|"No"| D10["Verbatim GPL v3 plus a dated<br/>modification notice; no per-file notice<br/>ADR-010"]
    Q10 -->|"Yes"| X10["Would allow the per-file notice<br/>the licence appendix advises"]
```

### 5.3.8 Architecture Decision Records

| ADR | Decision | Status at `HEAD` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ADR-001 | Single class in the default package, launched by the bare name | Accepted — stated |
| ADR-002 | No build tool; `javac` and `java` invoked directly | Accepted — recorded |
| ADR-003 | Zero third-party dependencies; `java.lang` only | Accepted — recorded |
| ADR-004 | No persistence, no cache, no configuration | Accepted — recorded |
| ADR-005 | Terminate by normal return, never `System.exit` | Accepted — stated |
| ADR-006 | Accept command-line arguments and never read them | Accepted — stated |
| ADR-007 | Record toolchain versions; pin none | Accepted — recorded, with one open verification item |
| ADR-008 | Document by comment-only, additions-only edit | Accepted — recorded and verified |
| ADR-009 | Compile into a freshly generated directory outside the checkout | Accepted — stated, mitigating |
| ADR-010 | Verbatim GPL v3 with a dated modification notice | Accepted — with a known coverage gap |

#### 5.3.8.1 ADR-001 — Single Class in the Default Package

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | The system has exactly one type and one behaviour. A namespace would partition nothing |
| Decision | Declare `public class Hello` with no `package` statement, so the launcher resolves it by the bare name `Hello` |
| Evidence | `Hello.java` lines 3–4 and 6; `README.md` line 12; the launch forms at `README.md` lines 37 and 43 |
| Consequences | Every documented command depends on it, and `Project Guide.md` §9.8 lists the bare-name resolution explicitly when diagnosing `Could not find or load main class Hello`. Adding a `package` declaration or a `module-info.java` would invalidate F-001-RQ-002, F-001-RQ-004, F-004-RQ-002 and F-004-RQ-004 |

#### 5.3.8.2 ADR-002 — No Build Tool

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | One compilation unit, no dependency to resolve, no packaging step and no test suite to run |
| Decision | Invoke `javac` and `java` directly from a POSIX shell; commit no `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, wrapper, `Makefile` or CI descriptor |
| Evidence | `README.md` lines 18, 27, 37, 43; `Project Guide.md` §9.3 and §9.4; direct worktree probe confirming every such file absent |
| Consequences | A JDK alone builds and runs the program, and nothing is downloaded at build time. The cost is that **nothing re-runs the verification checks**: the 49 recorded checks were executed by hand and their only durable record is `Project Guide.md` §3 and §4. `javac -Xlint:all -Werror` is consequently the entire static-analysis surface |

#### 5.3.8.3 ADR-003 — Zero Third-Party Dependencies

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | The program's whole behaviour is one write to standard output, which `java.lang` already provides |
| Decision | Declare no `import` statement and no dependency manifest; rely solely on the implicitly imported `java.lang` |
| Evidence | `Hello.java` lines 2–4 ("imports nothing outside `java.lang`, so a JDK alone builds and runs it") and line 17; `README.md` line 18 |
| Consequences | No supply-chain exposure, no resolution step, no lock file and no version-conflict class of problem. The APIs actually reached are `System`, `PrintStream`, `String` and `Object`. Adding a first third-party import would invalidate F-004-RQ-001, F-004-RQ-002 and F-005-RQ-001 at once |

#### 5.3.8.4 ADR-004 — No Persistence, Cache or Configuration

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | The data domain is one compile-time constant and one host-supplied separator |
| Decision | Keep no state within or between runs; write to no store; read no configuration, environment variable or secret |
| Evidence | `Hello.java` lines 1–5; `README.md` line 12; `Project Guide.md` §9.2, Appendix B, Appendix E |
| Consequences | No backup, migration, schema, connection, cache-invalidation or configuration-drift concern exists. Conversely no run leaves any evidence of itself, so verification must compare live streams rather than inspect stored results |

#### 5.3.8.5 ADR-005 — Terminate by Normal Return

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | There is no error path in the program, so there is no failure status to report |
| Decision | Let control return from `main`; make no `System.exit` call anywhere |
| Evidence | `Hello.java` line 18; `README.md` line 63, which calls it "a deliberate property of the program rather than an omission" |
| Consequences | Exit status is 0 on every run and standard error stays empty, which is what makes the output contract verifiable by a byte comparison. No shutdown hook or finaliser is registered, so the JVM shuts down of its own accord once the frame returns |

#### 5.3.8.6 ADR-006 — Accept Arguments, Never Read Them

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | The JVM requires the `String[]` parameter on a launchable entry point, but the program's output is fixed |
| Decision | Declare the parameter to satisfy the signature and never dereference it |
| Evidence | `Hello.java` lines 11–13 and the argument-contract table at `README.md` lines 48–51 |
| Consequences | Output is identical whether or not arguments are supplied, which `Project Guide.md` §4 confirms for no-argument, many-argument and hostile-argument runs including shell and injection payloads. The decision is also the project's principal security property: with nothing read, there is nothing to inject |

#### 5.3.8.7 ADR-007 — Record Versions, Pin None

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | No file exists in which a version could be recorded — no `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `.java-version`, `.sdkmanrc`, CI descriptor or `module-info.java` |
| Decision | Prefer portability over reproducibility: state in `README.md` that no Java version is pinned, record the toolchain actually used in `Project Guide.md` Appendix D, and declare no language level |
| Evidence | `README.md` lines 18 and 20; `Project Guide.md` Appendix D (OpenJDK 25.0.3, language level "None declared"), §9.1 (release targets 11, 17 and 21 exercised) |
| Consequences | The build is reproducible in behaviour but not in toolchain. Two open items follow: the documented JDK 11 floor for the single-file source launch has not been exercised on a real JDK 11 runtime, and runtime CVE exposure is left to the operator's chosen JDK |

#### 5.3.8.8 ADR-008 — Document by Comment-Only, Additions-Only Edit

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | The program's value lies in its predictability, so the documentation upgrade had to leave behaviour untouched |
| Decision | Add four comments — class Javadoc, `main` Javadoc with `@param args`, and line comments on the output and termination paths — delete and modify nothing, and replace the README placeholder with an eight-section guide |
| Evidence | `Hello.java` lines 1–5, 7–14, 16, 18; `README.md` lines 7–8; `Project Guide.md` §5.1 rows 1–4; the commit sequence `3c3af75` → `dabe2c9` → `14ed6db` → `ce8e85c`, with 15 lines added and 0 removed against `0726b1d` |
| Consequences | Behaviour and stored byte format were verified preserved, and debug-information-suppressed class files compared identical. Two costs are recorded: Javadoc coverage stands at 2 of 3 documentable members because the implicit default constructor can carry no doc comment, and the comment census must be given the pre-comment revision as its baseline or it fails vacuously |

#### 5.3.8.9 ADR-009 — Build Outside the Checkout

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | Compiling in place leaves an untracked `Hello.class` beside the source, and the repository has no `.gitignore` to catch it |
| Decision | Document `B="$(mktemp -d)" && javac -d "$B" Hello.java` followed by `java -cp "$B" Hello` as the recommended path, with the threat rationale stated beside the command |
| Evidence | `README.md` line 30; `Project Guide.md` §9.4 Path B, Appendix A, and §5.2 divergence 3 |
| Consequences | The working tree stays clean and the destination is uniquely named and owner-readable only, closing the predictable-path exposure. The control is documentary rather than enforced, so an accidentally committed class file remains a catalogued failure mode and an ignore rule remains an open owner decision |

#### 5.3.8.10 ADR-010 — Verbatim GPL v3 with a Dated Modification Notice

| Field | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Context | The work was licensed under GPL v3 in the initial commit and has since been modified |
| Decision | Keep `LICENSE` verbatim and unmodified, reference it from the guide, and carry a dated modification notice in the guide rather than adding per-file notices |
| Evidence | `LICENSE` (674 lines, 29 June 2007, unchanged since `c537a19`); `README.md` lines 5 and 77; `Project Guide.md` §5.1 row 8 |
| Consequences | Redistribution terms travel with every conveyed copy and the modification is dated as the licence requires. The known gap is the per-file copyright and warranty notice the licence appendix advises: it needs a named holder and year, and no tracked file records either, so it is deferred as an owner decision |


## 5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns

Cross-cutting concerns in a system of this shape are mostly concerns that have been designed out of existence. This sub-section records, for each one, what actually exists, what is verified absent, and what the architectural consequence of that absence is. Where the concern overlaps with process-flow detail already documented, Section 4.3 is cross-referenced rather than repeated.

### 5.4.1 Monitoring and Observability

**No monitoring exists, and no component capable of monitoring is present.** There is no metrics endpoint, health check, readiness probe, dashboard, agent, APM integration or alerting rule anywhere in the repository — consistent with `Project Guide.md` Appendix B, which records that the program "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call." Nor could there be: the process lives for the duration of one write, so there is no steady state to observe.

What the architecture does provide is a **complete and trivially checkable set of process observables**. Because the program's entire contract is expressible in three values, observability is achieved by comparison rather than by instrumentation.

| Observable | Expected signal | How it is observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standard output | The literal `Hello from Java!` followed by exactly one platform line separator | Byte comparison against the fenced oracle at `README.md` lines 59–61 |
| Standard error | Empty on every run | Capture and compare against an empty file |
| Exit status | 0, produced by normal return rather than by `System.exit` | `echo "exit=$?"`, recorded as `exit=0` in `Project Guide.md` §9.7 |
| Compiler diagnostics | None, including under `-Xlint:all -Werror` | `javac` exit status and an empty error stream |
| Comment coverage | Exactly one warning, for the implicit default constructor | `javadoc -quiet`, which exits 0 with that single warning |
| Working-tree cleanliness | `git status --short` prints nothing | Run after any build or verification step |

The instrumentation used to observe these is entirely external and entirely manual: the JDK's own exit statuses, `javadoc -Xdoclint:all` for doc-comment syntax, GNU `grep`, `awk`, `diff`, `tr`, `od`, `cmp` and `iconv` for structural and byte-format assertions, and `git diff` against the pre-comment revision for change-shape assertions. Two limitations follow directly from ADR-002 and are recorded rather than mitigated: **nothing re-runs these checks**, so the 49 recorded results are a point-in-time observation whose only durable record is `Project Guide.md` §3 and §4; and there is no notification channel of any kind on which a failure could be raised, a position Section 4.3.2.6 documents in full.

### 5.4.2 Logging and Tracing Strategy

The strategy is best stated as a distinction: **the program's single write is its product, not its log.** `System.out.println` at `Hello.java` line 17 emits the deliverable payload; it is not a diagnostic channel, and the line comment at line 16 fixes single-sink behaviour as a design property — "no other sink is written."

| Concern | Position at `HEAD` |
| --- | --- |
| Logging framework | None. No `java.util.logging`, SLF4J, Log4j or any other logger appears; the source declares zero imports |
| Log levels, formatters, appenders | Not applicable — there is no logger to configure |
| Diagnostic output to standard error | Deliberately none. Standard error stays empty on every run, which is what makes it a verifiable contract rather than an incidental property |
| Structured or correlated logging | None. No request identifier, correlation identifier or trace context exists, because there is no request and no hop to correlate |
| Distributed tracing | Not applicable. One process, one frame, one write — there is no span boundary anywhere in the system |
| Log persistence, rotation, retention, aggregation | None. Nothing is written to storage; the terminal is the only destination |
| Toolchain diagnostics | The only error-stream traffic in the whole system comes from outside the boundary: `javac` diagnostics (zero at `HEAD`), `java` launch failures, and the single expected `javadoc` warning |
| Durable record of any observation | `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3 and §4, written by hand. This is the system's only durable log, and it is prose rather than machine output |

The architectural consequence is that **auditability is documentary, not automatic**. Any change to `Hello.java` requires a manual `javac -Xlint:all -Werror` re-run and a manual re-record, because nothing will do it on the maintainer's behalf.

### 5.4.3 Error Handling Patterns

Three patterns operate at three different layers, and the division between them is the single most important cross-cutting property of this architecture.

**Pattern 1 — Containment by absence, inside the program.** `Hello.java` contains no error handling of any kind, and this is a specified property rather than an oversight. A keyword census over the five executable lines returns zero occurrences of `try`, `catch`, `throw`, `new`, `System.exit` and `System.err`, and the source contains no query of the output stream's error state. The program therefore performs no error detection whatsoever, and its only outcome is the greeting on standard output, an empty standard error and exit status 0. Whole categories of failure cannot arise because the surfaces they need do not exist: no input is read, no argument is dereferenced, no resource is opened, no port is bound, no network call is made and no dependency is declared.

**Pattern 2 — Fail-fast at the toolchain boundary.** Every fault that can interrupt a workflow is raised by `javac`, `java` or `javadoc` — before or instead of entering the program — and surfaces as a diagnostic on standard error with a non-zero status. The component-level state machine in Section 5.2.5 shows the structural reason: no state in the `Hello` component has an error transition originating inside the component.

**Pattern 3 — Documented manual recovery, in the human layer.** With no CI gate, no scheduler and no loop anywhere in the system, there is no automated retry and no automated escalation. Recovery is an operator re-running a deterministic command, which is safe precisely because the payload is a compile-time constant, both launch paths are equivalent, `javac` re-derives the same class file from the same unchanged unit with zero dependency resolution, and `mktemp -d` yields a fresh directory so a repeated attempt never collides with a previous one. The seven catalogued faults (E-1 … E-7), their causes and their recoveries are enumerated in Section 4.3.2.2, and the recovery procedures in Section 4.3.2.7; the diagram below is the architectural view of where each one is raised and absorbed.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Origin(["Fault arises during a workflow"]) --> Layer{"Which architectural layer<br/>is able to raise it?"}

    subgraph ProgramLayer["Program layer — C-1, C-2, C-3: raises nothing"]
        P1["No try, catch, throw or error branch<br/>exists in the 5 executable lines"]
        P2["No input read and no argument dereferenced,<br/>so no invalid value can reach a code path"]
        P3["Single outcome: greeting on stdout,<br/>stderr empty, exit status 0"]
        P1 --> P2
        P2 --> P3
    end

    subgraph ToolchainLayer["Toolchain layer — C-8: fail-fast, all diagnostics originate here"]
        T1{"Which tool<br/>reported it?"}
        T2["Compile: unit name does not match<br/>the public class — E-2, no class emitted"]
        T3["Launch: class not resolvable on the<br/>classpath — E-1; no source-file mode — E-7"]
        T4["Coverage: exactly one warning for the<br/>implicit default constructor — E-6"]
        T1 -->|"javac"| T2
        T1 -->|"java"| T3
        T1 -->|"javadoc"| T4
    end

    subgraph RepoLayer["Repository layer — C-9 and the working tree"]
        R1{"What did git or the<br/>census surface?"}
        R2["Untracked Hello.class in the<br/>checkout — E-3, no ignore rule exists"]
        R3["Hello.java normalised to LF — E-5,<br/>no .gitattributes exists"]
        R4["Comment census given the wrong<br/>baseline — E-4, fails vacuously"]
        R1 -->|"git status"| R2
        R1 -->|"line-ending census"| R3
        R1 -->|"additions-only diff"| R4
    end

    subgraph HumanLayer["Human layer — the only responder in the system"]
        H1["Operator reads the terminal:<br/>the only signal channel that exists"]
        H2["Consult the troubleshooting table,<br/>Project Guide section 9.8, seven rows"]
        H3["Re-run the deterministic command<br/>by hand, or apply the documented fallback"]
        H4["Escalate to the repository owner<br/>as a recorded open item"]
        H1 --> H2
        H2 --> H3
        H2 --> H4
    end

    Layer -->|"none — containment by absence"| P1
    Layer -->|"javac, java or javadoc"| T1
    Layer -->|"git or the working tree"| R1
    P3 --> Contract(["Contract satisfied: nothing to handle"])
    T2 --> H1
    T3 --> H1
    T4 --> Accepted(["Accepted by design:<br/>coverage stands at 2 of 3 members"])
    R2 --> H1
    R3 --> H1
    R4 --> H1
    H3 --> Resolved(["Resolved: correct stdout, empty stderr,<br/>status 0, clean working tree"])
    H4 --> OpenItem(["Open item: no CI gate and no<br/>notification channel to escalate on"])
```

Two of the catalogued faults are not program defects at all but consequences of deliberate repository decisions, which is why they sit in the repository layer: E-3 exists because no `.gitignore` was added, and E-5 exists because `Hello.java` is stored with CRLF on all 20 lines with no `.gitattributes`, so line-ending preservation depends entirely on editor discipline. Both are tracked in the `Project Guide.md` §6 risk register — the latter as Medium severity, "Open — accepted by design."

### 5.4.4 Authentication and Authorisation Framework

**No authentication or authorisation framework exists, and none can be applied to the program as it stands.** `Project Guide.md` §6 states the basis directly: the program has "no authentication or authorisation surface." Two structural facts make that irreducible rather than incidental — the program reads no input, so no principal can be asserted; and it exposes no resource, so there is nothing to authorise access to.

| Control dimension | Position at `HEAD` |
| --- | --- |
| Identity provider, token, session or credential | None. No credential, key, environment variable or secret is used by anything in this project, and `JAVA_HOME` is not required |
| Authorisation model — roles, scopes, policies | None. There is no protected operation and no caller identity to evaluate |
| Transport security | Not applicable to the program, which makes no network call. The only encrypted channel in the system is Git over HTTPS to the hosting remote |
| Cryptography | None in the program. The only integrity mechanism in use is Git's own content addressing, which is how the source blob `3fd76ce` and the pre-comment baseline `0726b1d` are identified |
| Filesystem access control | The one real access control: the compiler-output directory generated by `mktemp -d` is uniquely named and readable only by its owner, which is the mechanism ADR-009 selects |
| Repository access control | Enforced outside the boundary by the hosting platform — branch refs and the pull-request merge that produced `2a78292`. Nothing in the tracked files configures it |
| Legal rather than technical control | GPL v3 governs who may redistribute the covered work and on what terms; it is enforced by licence, not by code |

The architectural consequence is that **introducing a first input would also introduce the project's first authentication question**. Section 3.7.5 records the corresponding requirement impacts, and ADR-006 records why the argument array is accepted and never read.

### 5.4.5 Performance Requirements and Service Levels

**The repository states no performance requirement, no service-level objective and no service-level agreement.** There is no latency target, no throughput figure, no availability objective, no capacity plan, no error budget and no timing measurement of any kind recorded in any tracked file. None is asserted here.

What exists instead is a set of measured structural baselines. These are quality and size observations, not performance targets, and each is reported as recorded rather than re-derived.

| Baseline | Observed value | Source of observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Executable footprint | 1 source file, 20 lines, 1,073 bytes, 1 class, 1 method, 1 statement; 5 lines of executable code after comment stripping | Direct measurement of `Hello.java` |
| Compiled artifact | 420 bytes, with `main` compiled to four bytecode instructions — `getstatic`, `ldc`, `invokevirtual`, `return` | `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` §5.1.1.1 |
| Standard-output payload | 16 ASCII characters plus one platform line separator — 17 bytes observed on an LF host | `Project Guide.md` §4; `README.md` lines 57–63 |
| Compiler diagnostics | 0, including under `-Xlint:all -Werror` | `Project Guide.md` §3, on OpenJDK 25.0.3 |
| Verification checks | 49 executed, 49 passed, 0 failed — 37 acceptance assertions plus 12 direct toolchain checks | `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Comment coverage | 2 of 3 documentable members; 1 accepted `javadoc` warning | `Project Guide.md` §3, §9.6 |
| Committed automated test coverage | None — no test suite has ever existed in the repository | `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Verified compatibility range | Compile-then-run exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21; single-file source launch documented JDK 11+ but unconfirmed on a JDK 11 runtime | `Project Guide.md` §9.1, §1.6 |

Three architectural performance properties follow from the structure and are stated qualitatively, because the repository provides no measurement to quantify them:

- **Work per invocation is constant and minimal.** Four bytecode instructions, one string constant, no allocation in the program itself, no loop and no branch. Runtime cost is therefore dominated by JVM startup rather than by anything the program does — a characteristic the repository notes nowhere and measures nowhere.
- **The two launch paths differ in cost, not in outcome.** Compile-then-run pays compilation once and launch cost per run; the single-file source launch compiles the unit in memory on every run. Their outputs are byte-identical, which is what makes the choice purely operational.
- **Scalability is unbounded in principle and unspecified in practice.** With no shared mutable state and no lock, concurrent invocations cannot contend, but no concurrency requirement, benchmark or capacity figure exists. Section 5.2.7 states the consolidated position.

### 5.4.6 Disaster Recovery and Continuity

Disaster recovery in this system is unusually simple because **nothing the program does needs recovering**: it persists no state, so there is no data loss scenario, no backup schedule, no snapshot, no restore point and no recovery-point objective to define. Section 4.3.2.7 confirms that no recovery procedure in the repository requires a backup.

Continuity therefore reduces to the durability of the source and its documentation, both of which live entirely in the Git object store — five blobs, 14 commits, zero tags — and in every clone of it.

| Scenario | Impact | Recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Working tree lost or corrupted | None permanent | Re-clone from the remote; the object store holds every tracked byte, including the pre-comment revision `0726b1d` that two verification procedures depend on |
| Build artifact lost or deleted | None | Recompile. `javac` re-derives the same class file from the same unchanged 1,073-byte unit with zero dependency resolution; `rm -f Hello.class` is itself a documented cleanup step |
| Hosting remote unavailable | Distribution halted; local work unaffected | Every clone is a complete replica. All documented workflows run offline after clone, with zero network egress |
| Toolchain unavailable or replaced | Build and launch blocked until a JDK is present | A JDK is the sole prerequisite and is not vendored; nothing pins a version, so any JDK satisfying the documented floor works. No fallback toolchain exists and none is needed |
| Source accidentally normalised to LF | All 20 lines rewritten and the blob digest changed | Restore the file from history and re-apply the edit in byte mode, re-emitting CRLF on every line, then re-run the line-ending census |
| Class file committed by accident | Distribution ceases to be source-only | Revert and remove it from the tracked set; the documented preventive control is building into a `mktemp -d` directory |
| `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` lost | The only durable record of the 49 verification checks is lost | Not reconstructible from the repository — the checks would have to be re-executed by hand, since nothing re-runs them |
| Default branch never advanced | Documentation delivery invisible to anyone cloning the default branch | Push and merge the working branch. `main` sits at `0726b1d`, 11 commits behind; this is the one open continuity item in the system |

Two continuity observations are worth recording explicitly. First, **the program itself is effectively unloseable**: five lines of executable code whose exact contract is published in `README.md`, so it is recoverable from any clone and reconstructible from the guide alone. Second, **the fragile asset is the evidence, not the code**. The verification results, the compliance matrix and the risk register exist only as prose in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md`; because no automated gate reproduces them, their loss is the only scenario in this table with no mechanical recovery path. No recovery-time or recovery-point objective is defined anywhere in the repository, and none is asserted here.
