# 6. SYSTEM COMPONENTS DESIGN

## 6.1 Core Services Architecture

### 6.1.1 Applicability Assessment

**Core Services Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The tracked repository is five files — `Hello.java`, `README.md`, `LICENSE`, `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` and `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` — of which exactly one is executable. `Hello.java` is 20 lines and 1,073 bytes; stripping its comment lines leaves five executable lines, at line 6 (`public class Hello {`), line 15 (`public static void main(String[] args) {`), line 17 (`System.out.println("Hello from Java!");`) and the two closing braces at lines 19 and 20. That single statement at line 17 is the whole of the program's behaviour, and the line comment above it fixes single-sink output as a stated design property: "no other sink is written."

There is therefore no second deployable unit to draw a service boundary against, no network listener, no remote call, no message broker, no persistent store, no scheduler and no process that outlives a single write. Every concern this section would normally specify — service decomposition, inter-service communication, service discovery, load balancing, circuit breaking, auto-scaling, failover and graceful degradation — has no subject matter in this codebase. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` Appendix B states the position for the repository as a whole without qualification: the program "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call; there is no service, database, broker or cache in this project."

The finding is consistent with Section 5.1.1.1, which characterises the runtime architecture as a single-process, single-module, invoke-and-exit console application and records that it has "no tier decomposition, no service boundary, no inter-process communication, no concurrency and no long-running runtime."

This sub-section does not stop at the verdict. Each area required of a core-services specification is addressed in turn in Sections 6.1.2 through 6.1.4, stating what the repository provides in place of the pattern, what is verifiably absent, and what operational consequence the absence carries. Section 6.1.5 records the concrete repository changes that would make this sub-section applicable.

#### 6.1.1.1 Preconditions for a Core-Services Architecture

Five structural preconditions must hold before a core-services architecture has anything to describe. None holds here.

| Precondition | Artifact that would evidence it | Observed state at `HEAD` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two or more independently deployable units | Multiple source roots, modules or build targets | One compilation unit in the default package; no `src/` tree; no `module-info.java`; the only directories are `blitzy/` and `blitzy/documentation/`, which hold Markdown only |
| A remotely reachable interface | Socket, HTTP, gRPC, RMI or broker client code | None. `Hello.java` declares zero imports and contains no socket, HTTP, RPC or messaging construct |
| A resident process that outlives a request | Server loop, listener, scheduler or daemon entry point | None. `main` is invoked once, executes one write and returns; `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.5 states "There is no service to start — the program writes one line and exits" |
| An infrastructure definition on which to place services | Dockerfile, Compose file, Kubernetes manifest, Helm chart or Terraform configuration | None. No container, orchestration or infrastructure file of any kind exists in the tree |
| Shared state that units must coordinate over | Database, cache, queue or file-store configuration | None. No field, no instance, no static mutable state and no persistence configuration; Section 5.1.3 records the absence of any runtime data store |

#### 6.1.1.2 Basis for the Determination

The determination rests on exhaustive inspection rather than sampling, which is practical because the entire executable surface is one 1,073-byte file.

- **Complete file inventory.** `git ls-files` returns exactly the five tracked paths, and a filesystem walk of the checkout adds no further source or configuration file. The repository contains one `.java` file and three `.md` files plus the licence text.
- **Complete configuration inventory.** A recursive search of the whole checkout for `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.xml`, `*.properties`, `*.json`, `*.toml`, `*.ini`, `*.conf`, `*.sh`, `*.jar` and `*.class` returns **zero files**. There is no descriptor anywhere in which a service topology, endpoint, replica count, scaling rule, retry budget or circuit-breaker threshold could be declared.
- **Absence of a build and deployment model.** Direct probes confirm that `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts`, `settings.gradle`, `settings.gradle.kts`, `module-info.java`, `Makefile`, `mvnw`, `gradlew`, `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `Procfile`, `Chart.yaml`, `main.tf`, `serverless.yml`, `.github/`, `Jenkinsfile`, `.gitlab-ci.yml` and `.gitignore` are all absent. `README.md` line 18 states the same thing from the operator's side: a JDK is all that is required, and "nothing has to be resolved or downloaded before building."
- **Keyword inspection of all source.** A case-insensitive scan of `Hello.java` for `Socket`, `ServerSocket`, `HttpClient`, `HttpServer`, `URL`, `Connection`, `DataSource`, `jdbc`, `Thread`, `Runnable`, `Executor`, `CompletableFuture`, `synchronized`, `volatile`, `Registry`, `RMI`, `grpc`, `kafka`, `jms`, `amqp`, `rabbit`, `redis`, `retry`, `circuit`, `timeout`, `fallback`, `cache`, `health` and `metric` matches no executable line. The only hits are two comment lines: the Javadoc at line 3, which records that the class "imports nothing outside `java.lang`", and the line comment at line 18, which records that there is "no `System.exit` call".
- **Independent corroboration in the repository's own records.** `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.1 lists among the prerequisites "No package manager step, no virtual environment, no container, no database, no broker and no bound port," and §6 records that the program "reads no input, dereferences no argument, opens no resource, binds no port, makes no network call and has no dependency manifest."

#### 6.1.1.3 The Execution Model That Exists Instead

What the system has in place of a service topology is a strictly sequential, operator-owned pipeline: clone, compile, run, exit. Nothing in it is resident, replicated, addressable or discoverable, and the operator's shell is the only scheduler and the only orchestrator in the system.

| Stage | Owner | What it produces |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clone | `git` and the hosting remote (component C-9) | A complete local replica of the five tracked blobs |
| Compile | `javac` (component C-8a), per `README.md` line 27 | One 420-byte class file, in the checkout under build Path A or in a `mktemp -d` directory under Path B |
| Run | `java` launcher (component C-8b) invoking `Hello.main` (C-2) | One process whose entire lifetime is one write to file descriptor 1 |
| Exit | The JVM, by normal return from `main` at line 19 | Exit status 0 with an empty standard error |

Component identifiers (C-1 … C-10), interface identifiers (I-1 … I-4) and workflow identifiers (W-1 … W-4) used throughout Section 6.1 are those established in Sections 5.1.2 and 5.2.


### 6.1.2 Service Components

No service component exists in this repository. This sub-section records, for each service-component concern the specification calls for, what plays the corresponding role in a single-process console application and what is verified absent.

#### 6.1.2.1 Service Boundaries and Responsibilities

The only boundary in the system is the operating-system process boundary, and it encloses the entire program. The three code components identified in Section 5.1.2 are not services and cannot be deployed, versioned, scaled or failed over independently of one another: they are a class, a method and a statement inside one compilation unit.

| Candidate service boundary | What occupies the role here | Independently deployable? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deployment boundary | The single compilation unit `Hello.java` (C-1) — simultaneously the build input and the deployment unit, since no packaging step or artifact repository exists | No — the unit of compilation is the unit of deployment |
| Execution boundary | The one JVM process launched by `java`, entered at `Hello.main` (C-2, line 15) and invoked exactly once | No — there is only ever one |
| Interface boundary | The four seams I-1 (compilation), I-2 (JVM entry point), I-3 (process and standard streams) and I-4 (distribution and governance), per Section 5.1.1.3 | Not a service seam — none is a network or API boundary |
| Data boundary | None. `System.out.println` at line 17 writes to a stream, not to storage; no field, instance or static mutable state exists | Not applicable |

Responsibility allocation is therefore trivial and complete: C-1 holds the program, C-2 is the only executable path, and C-3 (the standard-output write path at line 17) emits the only output. The documentation components C-4 through C-7 carry no runtime responsibility at all — Section 5.2.1 records that nothing in `Hello.java` reads `README.md`, `LICENSE` or anything under `blitzy/documentation/`, so the dependency runs one way by construction.

#### 6.1.2.2 Inter-Service Communication Patterns

There is no inter-service communication because there is no second participant. The only "communication" in the running system is a method invocation within a single JVM frame followed by one write to file descriptor 1. Section 5.2.1 records the wider property: interaction across the whole system is synchronous and operator-initiated, with "no message, event, callback, poll or scheduled trigger anywhere."

| Communication mechanism | Observed state | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Synchronous HTTP/REST, gRPC, RMI or SOAP | Absent | No client or server construct and zero imports in `Hello.java`; no bound port per `Project Guide.md` Appendix B |
| Asynchronous messaging — queue, topic, broker, event bus | Absent | "no service, database, broker or cache in this project" (`Project Guide.md` Appendix B) |
| Shared-memory or shared-state coordination | Absent | No field, no instance, no static mutable state, no lock; `README.md` line 12 records that the program "keeps no state" |
| Inter-process communication — pipe, socket, signal, shared file | Absent inside the program | The source contains no reference to a file, socket or other stream; only file descriptor 1 is written |
| In-process invocation | **Present — the only mechanism.** The launcher invokes `main` once; `main` calls `System.out.println` once | `Hello.java` lines 15 and 17; Section 5.2.1 |

The single outbound channel is best understood as fire-and-forget: the process writes to standard output, returns, and receives nothing back. Section 5.1.4 characterises the operating-system process contract in exactly those terms — a unidirectional write with "no reply channel and no acknowledgement." The diagram below is the service-interaction diagram for this system; every arrow is either a shell-initiated invocation, a class-resolution read or a stream write, and none crosses a network.

**Figure 6.1.2-A — Invocation interaction topology (the service-interaction view of a single-process system)**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Op["Operator shell session<br/>the only scheduler and orchestrator<br/>that exists in the system"]

    subgraph BuildStage["Build stage — interface I-1, outside the program"]
        Jc["javac (C-8a)<br/>resolves nothing: no classpath entry,<br/>no manifest, zero dependencies"]
        Art["Hello.class, 420 bytes<br/>checkout under Path A, or the<br/>mktemp -d directory C-10 under Path B"]
        Jc --> Art
    end

    subgraph RunStage["Run stage — one JVM process, whole lifetime is one write"]
        Jv["java launcher (C-8b)<br/>resolves the bare name Hello<br/>because the class is in the default package"]
        Main["Hello.main (C-2), line 15<br/>invoked exactly once<br/>args accepted and never dereferenced"]
        Write["System.out.println (C-3), line 17<br/>the only API call in the program"]
        Jv --> Main
        Main --> Write
    end

    subgraph ProcContract["Process contract — interface I-3, the only outbound seam"]
        Sout["stdout: Hello from Java!<br/>plus one platform line separator"]
        Serr["stderr: empty on every run"]
        Code["exit status 0<br/>by normal return, no System.exit"]
    end

    subgraph AbsentPlane["Verified absent — no service plane of any kind"]
        NoNet["No bound port, listener<br/>or network call"]
        NoPeer["No second deployable unit<br/>to address or call"]
        NoBroker["No broker, queue, database<br/>or cache"]
        NoNet --- NoPeer
        NoPeer --- NoBroker
    end

    Op -->|"javac Hello.java — W-1 / W-2"| Jc
    Op -->|"java Hello or java -cp scratch Hello"| Jv
    Op -.->|"java Hello.java — W-3, compiled in memory, no artifact"| Jv
    Art -->|"class bytes on the classpath"| Jv
    Write --> Sout
    Main --> Serr
    Main --> Code
    Sout -.->|"read by the operator; compared byte for byte<br/>against the oracle at README.md lines 59-61"| Op
```

#### 6.1.2.3 Service Discovery Mechanisms

No service discovery mechanism exists, and none is needed: there is no address to resolve because there is no remote endpoint, and no registry to consult because there is no second unit to register. No Eureka, Consul, ZooKeeper, DNS-based discovery or client-side registry appears anywhere in the repository, and — as Section 6.1.1.2 records — there is no configuration file of any kind in which such a client could be configured.

Two name-resolution mechanisms do operate, both supplied by the JDK and both purely local:

| Resolution mechanism | How it works here | Failure behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compilation-unit resolution (I-1) | `javac` requires the file name to match the public class name, so `Hello.java` must declare `public class Hello` | Fails fast with `error: class Hello is public, should be declared in a file named Hello.java`; no class is emitted |
| Class resolution at launch (I-2) | The `java` launcher resolves the bare name `Hello` from the classpath — the repository root under build Path A, or the scratch directory via `-cp "$B"` under Path B — which works only because no `package` statement exists | Fails fast when the class is not on the classpath; catalogued as fault E-1 in Section 4.3.2.2 |

The operative constraint is recorded in Section 5.1.2 under C-2: the bare-name launch depends on the absence of a `package` declaration, so adding one would invalidate every launch command documented in `README.md`.

#### 6.1.2.4 Load Balancing Strategy

No load balancing exists and none can be applied, because there is no admission point in front of the program and no pool of instances behind one. No load balancer, reverse proxy, ingress controller, service mesh sidecar or DNS round-robin arrangement appears in the repository, and no infrastructure descriptor exists in which one could be declared.

Work arrives only when a human types one of the three documented launch commands, so distribution of load is an operator decision made outside the system boundary. Each invocation creates its own JVM process, and Section 5.2.2.2 records why those processes cannot interfere: with no shared mutable state and no lock, concurrent invocations "are independent and cannot contend." The practical consequence is that concurrency is bounded only by host capacity, and the repository records no measurement of that bound.

#### 6.1.2.5 Circuit Breaker Patterns

No circuit breaker exists, and there is nothing for one to protect. A breaker guards a caller against a failing remote dependency by tripping after a threshold of failures; this program has no remote dependency, no declared dependency of any kind, and no failure it can detect. Section 5.4.3 states the governing property as "containment by absence": a keyword census over the five executable lines returns zero occurrences of `try`, `catch`, `throw`, `new`, `System.exit` and `System.err`, and the source contains no query of the output stream's error state, so the program performs no error detection whatsoever.

| Breaker element | Requirement it would need | Observed state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Protected call | An outbound call that can fail or hang | None — the only call is `System.out.println` on an already-open stream |
| Failure detection | An exception, error code or timeout to count | None — no `try`/`catch`, no timeout, no stream error check |
| Threshold and state store | Configurable counters and a half-open timer | None — no configuration file and no state that survives the frame |
| Fallback path | An alternative response when open | None — the program has exactly one path through it (Section 5.2.1) |

What operates in place of a breaker is fail-fast at the toolchain boundary, which is Section 5.4.3's Pattern 2: every fault that can interrupt a workflow is raised by `javac`, `java` or `javadoc` before or instead of entering the program, and Section 5.2.5 confirms the structural reason — no state in the `Hello` component has an error transition originating inside the component.

#### 6.1.2.6 Retry and Fallback Mechanisms

There is no programmatic retry anywhere: no loop, no backoff, no retry budget, no timeout and no idempotency key exists in `Hello.java`, and with no CI gate and no scheduler in the repository there is nothing that could re-drive a failed step automatically. Section 5.4.3 records the resulting position as Pattern 3 — recovery is an operator re-running a deterministic command by hand.

That manual retry is safe rather than risky, and for reasons that are properties of the artifacts: the payload is a compile-time constant, both launch paths are documented as producing byte-identical standard output (`README.md` line 46), `javac` re-derives the same class file from the same unchanged unit with zero dependency resolution, and `mktemp -d` yields a fresh directory on every run so a repeated attempt never collides with a previous one. Re-running any documented command is therefore idempotent in effect.

Three genuine fallbacks are documented in the repository. They are operator-level substitutions, not automated failover paths.

| Documented fallback | Trigger | Substitute path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compile-then-run in place of the single-file source launch | The launcher does not implement source-file mode; `README.md` line 20 records that `java Hello.java` needs JDK 11 or later | `javac Hello.java` then `java Hello` — a path with no stated version floor, exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21 |
| Out-of-tree compiler output in place of in-place compilation | Keeping the working tree clean where no `.gitignore` exists, so `Hello.class` would otherwise appear as untracked content | `B="$(mktemp -d)" && javac -d "$B" Hello.java`, then `java -cp "$B" Hello` (`README.md` line 30) |
| Baseline export in place of the default comparison baseline | The comment-census verification, run with its default baseline, reports failures against a correct tree | Supply the pre-comment revision `0726b1d` explicitly as the baseline (`Project Guide.md` §9.8) |

No fallback exists for the one dependency the system genuinely has: if no JDK is present, no documented workflow can proceed. Section 5.1.4 states that position directly — a JDK is the sole prerequisite, it is not vendored, and "No fallback toolchain exists and none is needed."


### 6.1.3 Scalability Design

The repository contains no scaling design, no scaling requirement and no measurement against which one could be designed. What it has instead is a structural scaling profile that follows unavoidably from a stateless, invoke-and-exit process. Section 5.2.7 states the consolidated position; this sub-section addresses each scalability concern the specification calls for and records the evidence for it.

#### 6.1.3.1 Horizontal and Vertical Scaling Approach

**Scaling is horizontal by definition and vertical not at all.** The unit of work is one process that executes four bytecode instructions in `main` — `getstatic`, `ldc`, `invokevirtual`, `return` — and then exits. Adding capacity means starting another process; there is no long-running instance to enlarge.

| Scaling dimension | Position at `HEAD` | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Horizontal | Unbounded in principle, entirely manual in practice | Each launch is an independent process; Section 5.2.2.2 records that with no shared mutable state and no lock, concurrent invocations "cannot contend". Nothing dispatches them but the operator's shell |
| Vertical | Not applicable | There is no heap growth, no thread pool, no connection pool and no queue to enlarge (Section 5.2.7); the program allocates nothing itself |
| Build-time | A non-question | One 1,073-byte compilation unit, zero dependency resolution and zero network egress, so a build neither benefits from caching nor degrades with repetition |
| Data/storage | Not applicable | Nothing is persisted at run time; `README.md` line 12 records that the program "keeps no state" |

**Figure 6.1.3-A — Scalability architecture: process-per-invocation with nothing shared**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Demand["Demand side — concurrency is an operator choice, never elastic"]
        Sh1["Shell invocation 1<br/>java Hello"]
        Sh2["Shell invocation 2<br/>java -cp scratch Hello"]
        ShN["Shell invocation N<br/>java Hello.java"]
    end

    subgraph Instances["Execution side — N independent JVM processes that share nothing"]
        P1["JVM process 1<br/>4 bytecode instructions in main<br/>one write, then exit 0"]
        P2["JVM process 2<br/>no field, no lock, no pool,<br/>nothing to contend over"]
        PN["JVM process N<br/>no state carried in or out<br/>of the frame"]
    end

    subgraph HostCap["Host capacity — the only real limit in the system"]
        CPU["CPU and memory consumed by JVM startup<br/>no timing or footprint figure<br/>is recorded anywhere in the repository"]
        FD["One file descriptor per process:<br/>fd 1 written once, fd 2 left untouched"]
    end

    subgraph AbsentElastic["Verified absent — there is no elastic control plane"]
        NoLB["No load balancer, reverse proxy<br/>or ingress in front of anything"]
        NoASG["No autoscaler, replica count<br/>or scaling rule, and no file to declare one in"]
        NoPool["No thread pool, connection pool,<br/>queue or cache to size"]
        NoInfra["No container, orchestrator<br/>or infrastructure descriptor"]
        NoLB --- NoASG
        NoASG --- NoPool
        NoPool --- NoInfra
    end

    Sh1 --> P1
    Sh2 --> P2
    ShN --> PN
    P1 --> CPU
    P2 --> CPU
    PN --> CPU
    P1 --> FD
    P2 --> FD
    PN --> FD
```

#### 6.1.3.2 Auto-Scaling Triggers and Rules

**No auto-scaling exists, and there is no artifact in the repository in which a trigger could be expressed.** The recursive configuration census in Section 6.1.1.2 found zero YAML, JSON, XML, TOML, INI and properties files across the whole checkout, so there is no manifest, chart, task definition or scaling policy to carry a rule. There is equally nothing to trigger on: Section 5.4.1 records that no metrics endpoint, health check, readiness probe, dashboard, agent, APM integration or alerting rule exists, and that the process "lives for the duration of one write, so there is no steady state to observe."

| Trigger class | Where it would be declared | Observed state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Utilisation-based — CPU, memory, saturation | Orchestrator or autoscaler manifest | Absent; no manifest and no metric emitter exist |
| Queue-depth or backlog-based | Broker or consumer configuration | Absent; "no service, database, broker or cache in this project" (`Project Guide.md` Appendix B) |
| Request-rate or latency-based | Ingress, gateway or service-mesh policy | Absent; the program binds no port and serves no request |
| Schedule-based | Cron, timer or scheduled-task definition | Absent; no scheduler, timer or CI descriptor exists in the tree |

#### 6.1.3.3 Resource Allocation Strategy

Resource allocation is entirely delegated to the host, and no tracked file attempts to influence it. A grep across `Hello.java`, `README.md` and `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` finds no `-Xmx`, `-Xms` or `-XX:` flag, no `JAVA_OPTS`, `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` or `_JAVA_OPTIONS` reference, and no `ulimit`, cgroup, quota, `nice` or `taskset` usage. The JVM therefore runs with host defaults on every invocation, and Section 5.4.4 records that no environment variable or secret is used by anything in this project — `JAVA_HOME` is not required.

The only allocation decisions the repository actually makes are about *where bytes land*, not about how much resource a run may consume:

| Allocation decision | Documented choice | Rationale recorded in the repository |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compiler output destination | Either beside the source (build Path A) or a per-run `mktemp -d` directory (Path B, component C-10) | Keeps the working tree clean where no `.gitignore` exists; the unique owner-readable directory also prevents a predictable destination being pre-created or symlink-redirected by another local process (`README.md` line 30) |
| Classpath composition | The repository root, or `-cp "$B"` pointing at the scratch directory | Only the one class is ever resolved; there is no dependency to place on the path |
| Toolchain provisioning | Host-supplied and unpinned; OpenJDK 25.0.3 is recorded, never enforced | `README.md` line 18 — "This repository pins no Java version"; the compile-then-run path was exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21 |
| Process count | One per operator invocation | No pool, no supervisor and no orchestrator exists to allocate more |

#### 6.1.3.4 Performance Optimization Techniques

**No optimization technique is applied, and none has a subject to act on.** Work per invocation is constant and minimal: one string constant, four bytecode instructions, no allocation in the program itself, no loop and no branch. Section 5.4.5 records the consequence — runtime cost is dominated by JVM startup rather than by anything the program does, a characteristic the repository notes nowhere and measures nowhere.

| Optimization technique | Applicability here |
| --- | --- |
| Caching — application, dependency, artifact or build cache | None exists. Section 5.1.3 records that nothing is resolved or downloaded, there is no build system to hold a cache, and there is no state to cache; the per-run `mktemp -d` directory is "the deliberate opposite of a cache" |
| Connection pooling, keep-alive, multiplexing | Not applicable — no connection of any kind is opened |
| Concurrency, parallelism, batching | Not applicable inside the program; parallelism exists only as independent whole-process invocations |
| Lazy initialisation, warm-up, ahead-of-time compilation | Not applicable — no initialisation path and no `--release`, `--source` or AOT setting is recorded in any tracked file |
| Payload reduction or compression | Not applicable — the payload is 16 ASCII characters plus one platform line separator |
| Launch-path selection | The one genuine cost choice available: compile-then-run pays compilation once, while the single-file source launch recompiles in memory on every run. Section 5.4.5 records that their outputs are byte-identical, which makes the choice purely operational |

Two properties make optimization moot rather than merely unnecessary. The output is a compile-time constant, so there is no computation to speed up; and the repository records no timing, throughput or startup-cost measurement of any kind, so any change would be unverifiable against a baseline that does not exist.

#### 6.1.3.5 Capacity Planning Guidelines

**The repository defines no capacity plan, no throughput figure, no latency target and no availability objective, and none is asserted here.** Section 5.4.5 states that position for the specification as a whole. What can be stated are the measured per-invocation footprints, which are the only capacity-relevant quantities the repository actually records.

| Quantity | Observed value | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source footprint | 1 file, 20 lines, 1,073 bytes, 1 class, 1 method, 1 statement; 5 executable lines after comment stripping | Direct measurement of `Hello.java` |
| Compiled artifact | 420 bytes; `main` is four bytecode instructions | Section 5.4.5, citing the archived specification |
| Output per invocation | 16 ASCII characters plus one platform line separator — 17 bytes on an LF host, 18 on a CRLF host | `README.md` lines 57–63; Section 5.2.2.3 |
| Process footprint per invocation | One JVM process, one written file descriptor, zero threads created by the program, zero bytes persisted | `Hello.java` lines 15–19; `README.md` line 12 |
| Concurrency ceiling | Not defined by the system; bounded only by host capacity, since invocations share nothing | Section 5.2.7 |

For an operator, capacity planning therefore reduces to two host-level questions that the repository leaves entirely open: how many JVM startups per unit time the host can absorb, and how much terminal or pipeline throughput the accumulated standard output requires. Neither has a recorded answer, and nothing in the tracked files constrains either. The only growth path that would change this picture is architectural rather than operational — Section 5.2.7 notes that a second compilation unit, a first third-party import, a `package` declaration or a build manifest each changes the architecture rather than scaling it, and Section 6.1.5 records what that would oblige this sub-section to specify.


### 6.1.4 Resilience Patterns

Resilience in this system is a property of what cannot fail rather than of machinery that recovers from failure. No fault-tolerance library, supervisor, health check, standby instance or backup schedule exists in the repository. This sub-section records the mechanisms that do operate, the layers they operate in, and the concerns that have no subject matter.

**Figure 6.1.4-A — Resilience model: where a fault is raised, absorbed and recovered**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Start(["Operator initiates a documented workflow<br/>W-1, W-2, W-3 or W-4"]) --> Attempt["One synchronous attempt<br/>no timeout, no retry budget, no breaker,<br/>no supervisor watching it"]
    Attempt --> Outcome{"Which layer produced<br/>the outcome?"}

    subgraph ProgramPlane["Program plane — tolerance by absence of a failure surface"]
        Pa["No try, catch, throw or error branch<br/>in the 5 executable lines"]
        Pb["No input read, no argument dereferenced,<br/>no resource opened, no port bound,<br/>no dependency declared"]
        Pc["Exactly one outcome: greeting on stdout,<br/>empty stderr, exit status 0"]
        Pa --> Pb
        Pb --> Pc
    end

    subgraph ToolPlane["Toolchain and repository plane — fail-fast; all diagnostics originate here"]
        Ta["javac, java or javadoc raises the fault<br/>before or instead of entering main"]
        Tb["git and the working tree surface hygiene<br/>and byte-format faults after the fact"]
        Ta --- Tb
    end

    subgraph HumanPlane["Human plane — the only responder and the only retry mechanism"]
        Ha["Operator reads the terminal:<br/>the only signal channel that exists"]
        Hb["Apply the documented recovery and re-run<br/>the deterministic command by hand"]
        Hc["Escalate as a recorded open item —<br/>no CI gate and no notification channel"]
        Ha --> Hb
        Ha --> Hc
    end

    subgraph RedundancyPlane["Redundancy plane — the only replicated asset is the source"]
        Ra["Every git clone is a complete replica:<br/>5 blobs, 14 commits, 0 tags"]
        Rb["Artifacts are re-derived, never restored:<br/>javac re-emits the same class<br/>from the same unchanged unit"]
        Ra --> Rb
    end

    Outcome -->|"program: nothing to raise"| Pa
    Outcome -->|"toolchain, git or working tree"| Ta
    Pc --> Ok(["Contract satisfied — nothing to recover"])
    Tb --> Ha
    Hb --> Attempt
    Hc --> OpenItem(["Open item: manual escalation only"])
    Rb -.->|"supplies the source bytes for any re-attempt"| Attempt
```

#### 6.1.4.1 Fault Tolerance Mechanisms

Three mechanisms operate, at three different layers, and Section 5.4.3 develops each in full. Summarised from the service-architecture perspective:

| Mechanism | Layer | What it actually guarantees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Containment by absence | The program (C-1, C-2, C-3) | The failure surfaces themselves do not exist: no input is read, no argument dereferenced, no resource opened, no port bound, no network call made and no dependency declared, so whole categories of fault cannot arise |
| Fail-fast at the toolchain boundary | `javac`, `java`, `javadoc` (C-8) | Every interrupting fault is raised outside the program and surfaces as a diagnostic on standard error with a non-zero status. Section 5.2.5 confirms that no state in the `Hello` component has an error transition originating inside the component |
| Documented manual recovery | The operator | A deterministic command re-run by hand. There is no automated retry and no automated escalation, because no CI gate, scheduler or loop exists anywhere in the system |

The catalogued faults E-1 through E-7, their causes and their recoveries are enumerated in Sections 4.3.2.2 and 4.3.2.7; the seven-row troubleshooting table an operator would actually use is `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.8. Two of those faults are consequences of deliberate repository decisions rather than program defects — an untracked `Hello.class` appearing because no `.gitignore` was added, and `Hello.java` being normalised to LF because no `.gitattributes` constrains its CRLF storage format.

There is no retry, timeout, bulkhead, rate limiter, supervisor or watchdog in the system, and no process manager to restart anything. Because the program's entire lifetime is one write, a "crash" and a "completion" are the same event from the outside: the process is gone either way, and the only durable evidence of which occurred is the terminal output the operator saw.

#### 6.1.4.2 Disaster Recovery Procedures

Disaster recovery is unusually simple here because **nothing the program does needs recovering**: it persists no state, so there is no data-loss scenario, no backup schedule, no snapshot and no restore point. Section 5.4.6 carries the full scenario table and records that no recovery procedure in the repository requires a backup, and that no recovery-time or recovery-point objective is defined anywhere. The service-relevant consequences are:

| Scenario | Recovery procedure | Recovery source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Working tree lost or corrupted | Re-clone; every tracked byte, including the pre-comment baseline revision `0726b1d`, is in the object store | Any clone of the Git repository (C-9) |
| Build artifact lost or deleted | Recompile — `rm -f Hello.class` is itself a documented cleanup step, and `javac` re-derives the identical class file with zero dependency resolution | `Hello.java` plus a JDK |
| Hosting remote unavailable | No recovery needed for execution: every documented workflow runs offline after clone, with zero network egress. Only distribution is halted | The local clone |
| Toolchain unavailable | Install any JDK satisfying the documented floor; nothing pins a version and no fallback toolchain exists | The host, not the repository |
| Verification evidence lost | Not mechanically reconstructible — the 49 recorded checks would have to be re-executed by hand, since nothing in the repository re-runs them | Manual re-execution |

Section 5.4.6 names the one open continuity item: `main` sits at `0726b1d`, eleven commits behind the working branch, so the documentation delivery is absent from the default branch until the branch is published and merged.

#### 6.1.4.3 Data Redundancy Approach

There is no runtime data and therefore no runtime redundancy question. `System.out.println` at line 17 writes to a stream, not to storage; Section 5.1.3 records that no data store, cache or persistence tier exists in the running system. Redundancy applies only to the repository's own assets, and it is Git's distributed model rather than anything the project configures.

| Asset | Redundancy model | Loss consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source and documentation (5 tracked blobs) | Distributed replication — every clone is a complete replica, and the remote is one replica among them | None while any clone survives |
| Compiled class file and `javadoc` HTML | None, deliberately. Re-derivable from source rather than replicated; explicitly outside the tracked set | None — recompile |
| Per-run scratch directory (C-10) | None. Freshly generated per run and removed afterwards | None — regenerated on the next invocation |
| Verification record (`Project Guide.md` §3, §4) | Only the Git replication above; no automated gate reproduces its contents | The single non-reconstructible loss in the system (Section 5.4.6) |

The asymmetry is worth stating plainly: the program is effectively unloseable — five executable lines whose exact contract is published in `README.md` — while the evidence that it was verified exists only as hand-written prose.

#### 6.1.4.4 Failover Configurations

**No failover configuration exists, and no element required for one is present.** Failover needs a second instance to fail over to, a health signal to trigger the switch, and an addressing layer to redirect. None of the three exists: there is no standby process, no active-passive or active-active pair, no leader election, no heartbeat, no readiness or liveness probe (Section 5.4.1), and no load balancer or DNS record to repoint (Section 6.1.2.4).

What stands in for failover is operator substitution between documented equivalents, already tabulated in Section 6.1.2.6: compile-then-run substitutes for the single-file source launch where the launcher lacks source-file mode, and an out-of-tree `mktemp -d` destination substitutes for in-place compilation. Both are chosen by a human before the run, not switched to automatically during one, and both produce byte-identical output — which is exactly why they are interchangeable.

#### 6.1.4.5 Service Degradation Policies

**There is no degraded mode, and the architecture admits none.** The outcome of a run is binary: either the full contract is met — the literal `Hello from Java!` plus one platform line separator on standard output, an empty standard error and exit status 0 — or the workflow never reaches the program at all, having been stopped by a toolchain fault. There is no intermediate state in which the program does less.

| Degradation technique | Applicability here |
| --- | --- |
| Partial response or reduced payload | Not applicable — the payload is a single compile-time constant; a partial write is not a documented or reachable state |
| Feature flags or kill switches | Absent. No configuration file exists, and the argument array is accepted and never dereferenced, so nothing external can alter behaviour |
| Load shedding, throttling, queueing | Not applicable — there is no admission point, no queue and no request to shed |
| Read-only or cached-response mode | Not applicable — no data store and no cache exist |
| Graceful shutdown or drain | Not applicable — termination is by normal return from `main` with no `System.exit`, no shutdown hook and no in-flight work to drain |

The one environment-dependent element in the entire output contract is not a degradation: `README.md` line 63 records that the platform line separator makes the exact byte count vary between hosts, while the literal and its single trailing separator never do.


### 6.1.5 Reassessment Triggers and Cross-Section References

#### 6.1.5.1 Changes That Would Make This Sub-Section Applicable

The determination in Section 6.1.1 is a statement about the repository at `HEAD`, not a permanent property. Each change below would introduce the first genuine core-services concern of its kind and would oblige this sub-section to be rewritten rather than amended.

| Repository change | First core-services concern it creates | Sub-section that would need content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A second compilation unit, source root or module descriptor | A service boundary and a build-ordering question where none exists today | 6.1.2.1 boundaries; 6.1.3.1 build-time scaling |
| Any socket, HTTP, gRPC, RMI or broker construct in source | A remotely reachable interface, and with it addressing, timeouts and error semantics | 6.1.2.2 communication; 6.1.2.5 circuit breakers; 6.1.2.6 retry |
| A server loop, listener, scheduler or daemon entry point | A resident process, a steady state to observe and a lifecycle to supervise | 6.1.3.2 auto-scaling triggers; 6.1.4.4 failover; 6.1.4.5 degradation |
| A Dockerfile, Compose file, Kubernetes manifest or Helm chart | A placement and replica model, and the first file capable of declaring a scaling rule | 6.1.2.3 discovery; 6.1.2.4 load balancing; 6.1.3.2 auto-scaling |
| A database, cache, queue or file-store configuration | Shared state to coordinate over, plus a persistence and redundancy question | 6.1.4.2 disaster recovery; 6.1.4.3 data redundancy |
| A first third-party dependency or build manifest | An external failure surface and a supply-chain dependency the program currently has none of | 6.1.2.6 fallback; 6.1.4.1 fault tolerance |
| A `package` declaration on `Hello.java` | Invalidation of bare-name class resolution — every launch command documented in `README.md` would change | 6.1.2.3 discovery |

Section 5.2.7 makes the same point from the architecture side: growth in any of these directions changes the architecture rather than scaling it, and Section 3.7.5 enumerates which recorded requirements each such change invalidates.

### 6.1.6 References

#### 6.1.6.1 Repository Files Examined

A comment-stripping census confirmed exactly five executable lines (6, 15, 17, 19, 20), and a keyword scan for socket, HTTP, RPC, messaging, threading, retry, circuit-breaker, cache, health and persistence constructs matched no executable line.

- `LICENSE` — the verbatim GNU General Public License v3 text that governs redistribution; establishes that the only governance control over the work is legal rather than technical.
- `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` — first-hand operational evidence recorded on Linux with OpenJDK 25.0.3: no credential, key or network egress anywhere (§1.4); external services and registries not applicable (§2); the program as "a console application with no user interface, no hosted page, no bound port and no external integration" (§4); the absent-risk-category statement covering input, resource, port, network and dependency surfaces (§6); prerequisites recording "No package manager step, no virtual environment, no container, no database, no broker and no bound port" (§9.1); "There is no service to start — the program writes one line and exits" with the three verified launch forms (§9.5); the seven-row troubleshooting table (§9.8); and Appendix B, which states that "there is no service, database, broker or cache in this project".
- `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` — the archived prior generation of this specification, consulted only to confirm that its Section 6.1 reached the same not-applicable determination; it is stale by construction, describing three tracked files and a 127-byte source, so no figure in this sub-section is taken from it.

- Filesystem and tracked-file enumeration (`git ls-files`, recursive `find`) — confirmed five tracked files, one `.java` source and zero subdirectories containing code.
- Recursive configuration census across the checkout for `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.xml`, `*.properties`, `*.json`, `*.toml`, `*.ini`, `*.conf`, `*.sh`, `*.jar` and `*.class` — returned zero files, establishing that no descriptor exists in which a service topology, replica count, scaling rule, retry budget or breaker threshold could be declared.
- Existence probes for build, container, orchestration, IaC and CI artifacts — all absent, as listed in Section 6.1.1.2.
- Resource-flag grep across `Hello.java`, `README.md` and `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` for `-Xmx`, `-Xms`, `-XX:`, `JAVA_OPTS`, `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, `_JAVA_OPTIONS`, `ulimit`, cgroup, `nice` and `taskset`, and for throughput, latency, benchmark and replica figures — no match, supporting Sections 6.1.3.3 and 6.1.3.5.
- Line and byte measurement of `Hello.java` (`wc`) — 20 lines, 1,073 bytes; `cat -A` confirmed CRLF storage on every line.
