## 6.2 Database Design

### 6.2.1 Applicability Assessment

**Database Design is not applicable to this system.**

The repository contains one compilation unit, `Hello.java`, whose entire executable body is five lines and whose only input/output operation is a single `System.out.println` call on line 17. There is no datastore, no persistent entity, no schema, no connection configuration and no runtime path that reaches durable media. This finding is not an inference from the program's small size — it is the result of an exhaustive artifact-level, source-level and full-history-level search for persistence, all three of which returned nothing.

This sub-section states the determination and the evidence behind it. The remaining sub-sections do not abandon the prompt's areas; each one is addressed on its own terms, distinguishing what is genuinely absent from the system from what does exist in the one durable substrate the project actually relies on — the Git object store — which Section 3.5.4 identifies as the system's only durable store while Section 1.3.1.2 places the hosting platform itself outside the system boundary.

#### 6.2.1.1 Preconditions for a Database Design

A Database Design sub-section is meaningful only when a system satisfies the preconditions below. Each was tested directly against the checkout at commit `2a78292` on branch `jr_java1`. All five fail.

| # | Precondition | Verified Result |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | A datastore exists to design against — an engine, driver, DSN, connection URI or credential appears in a tracked file | **Fails.** `Hello.java` declares zero `import` statements and zero `package` statement; no driver coordinate, engine name, DSN, URI or credential appears in any of the five tracked files |
| P2 | Persistent entities exist — types whose state outlives a single method invocation | **Fails.** `Hello` declares no field, no constructor, no instance, no static mutable state, no `Serializable` or `Externalizable` type and no mapping annotation of any kind |
| P3 | A schema or schema-evolution history exists | **Fails.** Zero `*.sql`, `*.ddl`, `*.dbml`, `*.prisma` or `schema.*` files; no `migrations/`, `db/`, `flyway/`, `liquibase/` or `alembic/` directory; the checkout contains exactly three directories — `.`, `blitzy/` and `blitzy/documentation/` |
| P4 | A place exists to configure a connection | **Fails.** Zero configuration files of any format anywhere in the checkout — no `*.properties`, `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.json`, `*.xml`, `*.toml`, `*.ini` or `.env`. There is also no build manifest (`pom.xml`, `build.gradle`) into which a driver dependency could be declared |
| P5 | The running program can reach durable media | **Fails.** The five executable lines were isolated by stripping comments and then searched for 38 distinct persistence, file-I/O, NIO, JDBC, serialisation, collection and state-holding API patterns. Zero matched. The sole API call is `PrintStream.println` on a stream, not a store |

#### 6.2.1.2 Persistence-Surface Census

Absence was established at three independent levels, so that a negative result at one level cannot be an artifact of where the search was pointed.

| Level of Search | What Was Tested | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Artifact level | Approximately 47 named database and persistence artifacts were existence-tested at the repository root, followed by a recursive search of the whole checkout for 25 data, schema and configuration file extensions | Zero present, zero files found |
| Source level | `Hello.java` reduced to its 5 executable lines (L6, L15, L17, L19, L20), then matched against 38 persistence/I/O/state API patterns including `java.sql`, `java.io`, `java.nio`, `DataSource`, `Serializable`, `Preferences`, `FileWriter`, `Files`, `Map`, `List` and `static` field declarations | Zero matches |
| History level | `git log --all --diff-filter=A --name-only` enumerated every path ever added on any branch across all 14 commits, then filtered for `sql`, `db`, `schema`, `migrat`, `data`, `store`, `cache` and `persist` | No such path has ever existed. Only the five known tracked files have ever been added |

The history-level result is the decisive one: a database was not removed, deprecated or deferred. No persistence artifact has ever been present in this repository's recorded history.

#### 6.2.1.3 Basis for the Determination

The repository's own documentation states the same conclusion independently, in three separate places, so the determination is corroborated rather than merely derived.

- `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` line 426 (Appendix B) records that the program "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call; there is no service, database, broker or cache in this project."
- The same file at line 252 (§9.1) records the absence of a "package manager step, no virtual environment, no container, no database, no broker and no bound port."
- Line 188 (§6) records that the program "reads no input, dereferences no argument, opens no resource, binds no port, makes no network call and has no dependency manifest," concluding there is "no data-at-rest concern."
- `README.md` line 12 states that the program "reads no input, opens no resource and keeps no state."

Section 3.5 of this specification reaches the identical stack-level finding — "No database, cache or storage service is part of this system" — and Section 4.3.1.3 records the application data store as persistence point `P-5`, present in the inventory precisely so that its non-existence is explicit rather than unstated.

One nuance is worth stating plainly, because it is the most likely source of a mistaken "this system writes data" reading. The documented workflow does produce a durable file: `Hello.class`, the 420-byte compiler output. That file is a **build artifact, not application data**. It is derived deterministically from `Hello.java`, it is never read by the program, it holds no state that the program mutates, and Section 3.5.4 confirms that zero `*.class` blobs have ever been tracked in the repository. Treating it as persisted data would misclassify a compilation output as a datastore.

#### 6.2.1.4 How the Remainder of This Sub-Section Is Organised

Declaring non-applicability does not discharge the prompt. Every area it enumerates is addressed below, in one of two ways, and each sub-section makes clear which applies:

1. **Genuinely absent from the system.** Query optimization, connection pooling, read/write splitting, caching policy and partitioning have no counterpart anywhere in the repository. These are stated as absent, with the reason the concern cannot arise and the condition under which it would.
2. **Present in the durable substrate the project does depend on.** Entity relationships, indexing, replication, backup, migration, versioning, retention, audit and access control all have concrete, measurable analogues in the Git object store that holds the five tracked files. These are documented with real measured values, and each is explicitly flagged as belonging to a substrate that Section 1.3.1.2 places outside the system boundary.

This second category is documented deliberately. The repository's data-governance properties — what is retained, what is replicated, what is recoverable, who can change what and what record survives — are real and load-bearing even though no database implements them. Omitting them would leave the specification silent on questions a reader legitimately needs answered.

#### 6.2.1.5 Verification Environment

Two constraints on the evidence in this sub-section should be stated so that its claims can be weighted correctly.

| Constraint | Consequence for This Sub-Section |
|---|---|
| No JDK is installed in the environment used to verify the repository | Every runtime figure quoted here — the 420-byte class file, the four bytecode instructions in `main`, the observed absence of any file written during a run — is attributed to `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` as recorded evidence. None is asserted first-hand |
| Git and standard text tooling are present | All repository-state figures — object counts, blob sizes, byte sizes, index sizes, ref targets, commit metadata, delta-chain depths, `git fsck` results — were measured directly and are first-hand observations |

The one untracked file in the working tree, `tech_spec.md`, is an authoring artifact of the documentation process. It is not a system file, is not tracked, and is excluded from every figure below.

### 6.2.2 Schema Design

No schema exists in this system, because no datastore exists to hold one. There is no DDL, no entity-relationship model over application data, no index definition, no partitioning scheme and no configured replication of any database.

What does exist, and what this sub-section documents, is the structure of the Git object store that holds the five tracked files. That store has a genuine, well-defined content-addressed schema with real entities, real relationships, real integrity constraints and real index structures — all of which were measured directly at commit `2a78292`. It is documented here as the project's de-facto persistence substrate, with the standing qualification that Section 1.3.1.2 places the hosting platform outside the system boundary: this is the schema of the repository, not of the application.

#### 6.2.2.1 Entity Relationships

The Git object model is a directed acyclic graph of four object kinds. The counts below are the measured contents of this repository's single pack file, not generic Git description.

**Figure 6.2.2-A — Entity-relationship model of the repository's object store**

```mermaid
erDiagram
    REF ||--|| COMMIT : "resolves to"
    COMMIT ||--|| TREE : "has root tree"
    COMMIT }o--o{ COMMIT : "has parent"
    TREE ||--o{ TREE : "contains subtree"
    TREE ||--o{ BLOB : "contains file entry"
    REF {
        string ref_name PK "8 refs: 2 local heads, 6 remote-tracking, 0 tags"
        string target_sha "mutable pointer to a commit"
    }
    COMMIT {
        string sha1 PK "14 commits reachable from HEAD"
        string author_and_date "name plus ISO-8601 timestamp, immutable"
        string signature_status "4 status E, 10 status N unsigned"
    }
    TREE {
        string sha1 PK "13 tree objects, 1 nested for blitzy/documentation"
        string entry_mode "every tracked entry is mode 100644"
    }
    BLOB {
        string sha1 PK "10 blobs, 5 reachable from the HEAD tree"
        int size_bytes "41 B smallest to 839,724 B largest"
    }
```

Three properties of this model are worth calling out because they differ from a relational schema in ways that matter to every later sub-section:

| Property | Observed Behaviour Here |
|---|---|
| Identity is content, not a surrogate key | Every `COMMIT`, `TREE` and `BLOB` is keyed by the SHA-1 of its own content. `git rev-parse --show-object-format` confirms `sha1`. A change of one byte produces a new object rather than mutating an existing row |
| Only refs are mutable | `REF` rows are the sole mutable structure. All 37 objects are append-only; there is no `UPDATE` or `DELETE` equivalent reachable through normal operation |
| Relationships are embedded, not joined | A `TREE` stores its children's hashes inline; a `COMMIT` stores its parent hashes inline. There is no foreign-key table, no join, and consequently nothing for a query planner to optimise |

#### 6.2.2.2 Data Models and Structures

Two distinct data models are present in the project, and neither is a database model.

**The application's data model.** `Hello` declares no field, no constructor and no nested type. Its single method `main(String[] args)` receives an array parameter that is referenced only in the Javadoc `@param` tag on line 11 and in the method signature on line 15 — it is provably never dereferenced in the body. The only datum in the program is the string literal on line 17: 16 ASCII characters, held in the class file's constant pool and pushed onto the operand stack by one `ldc` instruction. The application's data model is therefore a single immutable constant with no owner, no lifecycle and no representation outside one process frame.

**The repository's data model.** Five tracked paths totalling 925,008 bytes at HEAD, all mode `100644`, arranged across exactly two directory levels.

| Tracked Path | Current Blob | Size at HEAD |
|---|---|---|
| `Hello.java` | `3fd76ce8` | 1,073 bytes |
| `README.md` | `3956e03d` | 4,053 bytes |
| `LICENSE` | `f288702d` | 35,149 bytes |
| `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` | `888336e8` | 45,009 bytes |
| `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` | `231e2f19` | 839,724 bytes |

The distribution is heavily skewed: the two documentation artifacts account for 884,733 bytes, or 95.6% of tracked content, while the source that the whole specification describes is 1,073 bytes — roughly 0.1%. Section 3.5.5 draws the operational consequence, that clone size grows with each documentation generation round rather than with the program.

A second structural fact matters for the retention discussion in 6.2.3.3. The pack holds **10 blobs, but only 5 are reachable from the HEAD tree.** The other five are superseded revisions retained indefinitely:

| Path | Retained Revisions | Blob Chain, Oldest First |
|---|---|---|
| `Hello.java` | 3 | `3b131a99` 127 B → `48653e2e` 2,059 B → `3fd76ce8` 1,073 B |
| `README.md` | 4 | `adeeab69` 41 B → `43b7a9f3` 3,720 B → `5ea2c6f1` 3,687 B → `3956e03d` 4,053 B |
| `LICENSE`, and each of the two `blitzy/documentation/` files | 1 each | Never modified since first commit |

Section 4.3.1.4 states the figure "five blobs, 14 commits, zero tags"; that is the HEAD tree's reachable set. The 10-blob figure here is the pack's full retained set including history, and refines rather than contradicts it.

#### 6.2.2.3 Indexing Strategy

No database index exists — there is no B-tree, hash, covering, partial, composite or full-text index over application data, and no query planner to serve. Four real index structures do exist, all belonging to Git, and all measured directly:

| Index Structure | Measured Size | Function |
|---|---|---|
| `.git/index` | 574 bytes, 5 entries | The staging index: a sorted path-to-blob mapping covering exactly the five tracked paths, used to compute status and stage changes |
| Pack `.idx` | 2,108 bytes | Primary lookup: SHA-1 to byte-offset within the pack, giving O(log n) object retrieval by hash without scanning the pack |
| Pack `.rev` | 200 bytes | Reverse index: pack-order to SHA-1, supporting the inverse traversal |
| `.git/packed-refs` | 427 bytes | Ref index: resolves symbolic ref names to commit SHAs without opening loose ref files |

The pack in question is `pack-ad68250ec2e74bdf98de672082a8e788fe4af318.pack`, 307,997 bytes. Its internal storage strategy is delta compression, and `git verify-pack -v` reports the exact composition: **24 objects stored non-delta, 10 objects at delta chain length 1, and 3 objects at chain length 2** — 37 objects total, with a maximum chain depth of 2. The pack verifies `ok`. No `pack.*` or `gc.*` configuration is set anywhere, so Git's defaults govern packing and repacking entirely; the project has made no tuning decision here.

The practical reading is that all lookup in this system is by exact content hash or by exact path. Nothing in the repository requires a range scan, a sort, a secondary access path or a selectivity estimate, which is why no index-design decision exists to document.

#### 6.2.2.4 Constraints and Integrity Rules

Eight constraints genuinely govern this system. They are not database constraints; they are enforced by the compiler, the JVM launcher, Git's own integrity model, or — in two cases — by nothing at all. The enforcement column is the important one.

| Constraint | Enforced By |
|---|---|
| The public class name must match the filename: `Hello` in `Hello.java` | `javac`, at compile time — a hard failure |
| The class is in the default package, so the launch command is the bare `java Hello` | `javac` and the JVM launcher; changing this breaks the documented command |
| The entry point must be exactly `public static void main(String[] args)` (line 15) | The JVM launcher, at startup — a hard failure |
| Every object's SHA-1 must equal the hash of its content | Git; `git fsck --no-progress` ran clean with exit status 0 and reported no dangling, missing or corrupt object |
| Path names within a tree must be unique | Git's tree-object format, structurally |
| All five tracked entries carry mode `100644` — no executable bit, no symlink, no submodule, no gitlink | Git records the mode; nothing in the project asserts it. Verified uniform at HEAD |
| Stored line endings: `Hello.java` is CRLF on all 20 lines, `README.md` is LF-only | **Nothing.** No `.gitattributes` exists. Section 3.5.6 classifies stored byte format as "Unmanaged and load-bearing"; `Project Guide.md` line 193 records the CRLF-with-no-policy risk as "Open — accepted by design", because normalising would rewrite all five code lines and change the file's content digest |
| Requirement F-005-RQ-002: no compiled artifact may be tracked | **Documented, not enforced.** No `.gitignore` exists; `.git/info/exclude` is present at 240 bytes but contains no active pattern; `git check-ignore -v Hello.class` matches no rule. The requirement holds today only because contributors follow the documented workflow of building into a scratch directory |

The last two rows are the only integrity gaps in the system, and both are gaps of enforcement rather than of definition.

#### 6.2.2.5 Partitioning Approach

No partitioning exists and none is possible. There is no table to partition, no shard key, no time-series dimension, no tablespace and no horizontal or vertical split of any kind. The single pack file is not a partitioning decision — it is Git's default consolidation of all 37 objects, reached with no `pack.*` configuration set.

Two divisions of the repository do exist and are worth naming so they are not mistaken for partitioning. The first is the single nested tree for `blitzy/documentation/`, the only hierarchical subdivision in a checkout that contains exactly three directories. The second is the logical separation of data domains described in Section 3.5.5 — 1,073 bytes of source against 884,733 bytes of generated documentation. Both are organisational, not distributional: they do not affect where data is stored, how it is addressed, or how it is retrieved.

#### 6.2.2.6 Replication Configuration

No database replication is configured. There is no primary, no replica, no writer/reader pair, no write-ahead-log shipping, no change-data-capture stream, no quorum, no replication lag to monitor and no consistency level to select.

Replication of the repository itself, however, is real, and its topology was read directly from the ref database. Eight refs exist — two local heads and six remote-tracking refs — and zero tags.

**Figure 6.2.2-B — Replication topology of the repository's object store**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Upstream["Hosting remote — one replica among equals, reached over HTTPS"]
        RMain["origin/main and origin/HEAD at 0726b1d<br/>default branch, 11 commits behind the delivery"]
        RWork["origin/jr_java1 at 2a78292<br/>carries the full documentation delivery"]
        ROther["origin/jr_java2 and origin/jr_java3 at 0726b1d<br/>origin/blitzy-6d6c8680 at b4a1188"]
    end

    subgraph LocalClone["This clone — a complete replica, 37 objects in one 302.84 KiB pack"]
        LHead["refs/heads/jr_java1 at 2a78292<br/>the checked-out branch"]
        LMain["refs/heads/main at 0726b1d<br/>an ancestor, 11 commits behind"]
        LObj["Object database: 10 blobs, 14 commits, 13 trees<br/>SHA-1 content addressing, git fsck clean"]
        LHead --> LObj
        LMain --> LObj
    end

    subgraph PeerClones["Any further clone — the same guarantee by construction"]
        Peer["Full history and every reachable object<br/>no shallow, partial or sparse replica is configured"]
    end

    subgraph AbsentRepl["Database replication machinery — verified absent"]
        AR1["No primary/replica or writer/reader pair"]
        AR2["No WAL shipping, log-based CDC or snapshot restore"]
        AR3["No quorum, lag metric or consistency level to tune"]
        AR1 --- AR2
        AR2 --- AR3
    end

    RMain -->|"git clone or git fetch"| LObj
    RWork -->|"git fetch, the only inbound path"| LObj
    ROther -->|"fetched into the same object database"| LObj
    LHead -.->|"git push and merge, not yet performed for main"| RMain
    LObj -->|"git clone"| Peer
```

The replication model is symmetric full replication: every clone receives the complete history and every reachable object, since no shallow, partial or sparse-checkout configuration is set. Section 5.4.6 draws the continuity conclusion — every clone is a complete replica, so no dedicated replica provisioning is required.

One divergence is open and is the single consistency issue in the topology. `refs/heads/main` and all four `origin` refs other than `origin/jr_java1` point at `0726b1d`, which is an **ancestor** of the delivery commit: `git rev-list --left-right --count main...HEAD` returns `0 11`, meaning `main` is strictly 11 commits behind with no divergent commits of its own. The documentation delivery exists only on `jr_java1`. Section 5.4.6 records this as the one open continuity item.

The remote is the GitHub repository `github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java`. Its configured URL resides in the untracked `.git/config` and embeds an ephemeral access token, which is deliberately not reproduced anywhere in this specification.

#### 6.2.2.7 Backup Architecture

There is no database to back up, and correspondingly no backup architecture in the conventional sense: no dump schedule, no snapshot policy, no point-in-time recovery window, no RPO and no RTO. Section 3.5.6 states the position exactly — "no backup policy, retention rule or recovery target exists in any tracked file" — and Section 4.3.2.7 adds that no recovery procedure in the system requires a backup, a snapshot or a restore point.

What stands in for a backup architecture is the durability of a content-addressed, fully replicated object store, together with the fact that almost everything in the system is derivable.

| Asset | Recovery Posture |
|---|---|
| The five tracked files and all history | Recoverable from any clone. The store is append-only and hash-verified; `git fsck` is clean and reports zero garbage and zero loose objects |
| `Hello.class`, the 420-byte build artifact | Not backed up and not required to be. It is deterministically regenerable from `Hello.java`, which is why the documented workflow builds it into a `mktemp -d` scratch directory |
| The `.git/logs` reflog, 3 entries on HEAD with `core.logallrefupdates` set to `true` | Local only. Reflogs are untracked and are **not conveyed by a clone**, so this is the one structure in the store that replication does not protect |
| The verification-outcome record in `Project Guide.md` §3 and §4 | The single non-reconstructible loss in the system, per Section 6.1.4.3: nothing in the repository re-runs those checks, so the record cannot be regenerated — only re-earned by repeating the verification |

Two residual exposures follow from what was measured rather than from what is written down. First, no `gc.*` configuration is set, so Git's default pruning behaviour governs unreachable objects; the project has made no explicit decision to preserve or expire anything. Second, Section 3.5.6 classifies sensitive content entering the immutable store as "Unguarded" — clean today, but with no mechanism preventing it, and with the content-addressed, append-only design meaning that any such content would be effectively permanent across every replica.

### 6.2.3 Data Management

There is no data to manage in the database sense: no schema to migrate, no schema version to track, no records to archive, no store to read from or write to, and no cache anywhere in the system. This sub-section addresses each area on its own terms, documenting the real mechanisms that occupy the equivalent position — Git commits in place of migrations, commit SHAs in place of schema versions, indefinite object retention in place of an archival tier — and identifying precisely where nothing exists at all.

#### 6.2.3.1 Migration Procedures

No database migration capability exists. There is no migration tool (no Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic or equivalent), no `migrations/` directory, no versioned change script, no `up`/`down` pair and no baseline. Section 6.2.1.2 established the stronger fact: no such path has ever existed across all 14 commits on any branch, so there is no legacy migration history either.

The only change-management procedure in the project operates on files, not on schemas, and it is Git itself. Two observed properties define its semantics:

| Property | Observed Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Change unit | A commit. All 14 commits are append-only additions to the object store; a content change produces a new blob rather than mutating the existing one, so no in-place migration step is ever performed |
| Rollback | Achieved by moving a ref to an earlier commit, not by executing a reverse script. Section 4.3.1.6 records that the system has "no transactional resource… no commit protocol, no two-phase coordination and no rollback log" |

Two related mechanisms recorded elsewhere in this specification are the closest the project comes to a data-movement procedure, and neither is a migration. Persistence point `M-1` in Section 4.3.1.4 is the baseline export performed with `git show`, which materialises a historical blob for comparison. `M-2` is generated Javadoc HTML. Both are read-only derivations from the object store; neither alters stored structure.

#### 6.2.3.2 Versioning Strategy

There is no schema version, because there is no schema. No `schema_version` table, no migration checksum, no compatibility matrix and no forward/backward-compatibility contract exist anywhere in the repository.

Three genuine versioning mechanisms are in use, and they operate at different levels:

| Level | Versioning Mechanism | Observed State |
|---|---|---|
| Content | SHA-1 content addressing. Every distinct byte sequence has a permanent identity; `Hello.java` has three such identities in the store and `README.md` has four | 10 blobs for 5 current paths |
| History | Linear commit sequence on `jr_java1`, each commit carrying author and ISO-8601 timestamp | 14 commits, HEAD at `2a78292` |
| Requirements | Requirement versions anchored to commit SHAs rather than to release labels, per Section 3.5.6. Features F-001 through F-009 and their 45 requirements are recorded at version 2.0, anchored at `2a78292` | Authoritative, SHA-anchored |

The notable absence is release tagging. **Zero tags exist** in the repository — `git show-ref` returns eight refs, all of which are branch or remote-tracking refs. There is therefore no semantic version, no release marker and no immutable named point in history; every reference to a version in this specification necessarily resolves through a mutable branch ref to a commit SHA. Combined with the `main`-is-11-commits-behind divergence documented in Section 6.2.2.6, the practical consequence is that the authoritative state of the project is identified only by a SHA on a non-default branch.

#### 6.2.3.3 Archival Policies

No archival policy exists. There is no data lifecycle tier, no cold or nearline storage, no TTL, no expiry, no truncation and no time-based rollover — and no such concept is referenced in any tracked file.

The de-facto policy in the object store is **indefinite retention of everything ever committed**, which was verified rather than assumed:

- Five superseded blobs are retained with no expiry: three revisions of `Hello.java` (`3b131a99` at 127 B, `48653e2e` at 2,059 B, and the current `3fd76ce8` at 1,073 B) and four of `README.md` (`adeeab69` at 41 B, `43b7a9f3` at 3,720 B, `5ea2c6f1` at 3,687 B, and the current `3956e03d` at 4,053 B).
- `git count-objects -vH` reports 37 objects in-pack, 1 pack, 302.84 KiB, **0 loose objects and 0 garbage** — nothing is awaiting cleanup and nothing has been pruned.
- No `gc.*` configuration is set. Git's default pruning behaviour therefore governs unreachable objects by omission; the project has never made a retention decision.

The growth characteristic follows directly from this. Because 95.6% of tracked content is generated documentation and nothing is ever expired, the store's size is driven by documentation regeneration rather than by program change — the observation Section 3.5.5 makes when it notes that clone size grows with each documentation generation round, not with the program. The single largest blob, `231e2f19` at 839,724 bytes, is a documentation artifact that is 783 times the size of the source it describes.

#### 6.2.3.4 Data Storage and Retrieval Mechanisms

The application has no storage or retrieval mechanism at all. It stores nothing, reads nothing and queries nothing; its single datum travels from a compile-time constant to a file descriptor without touching durable media at any point. The diagram below traces that path end to end and marks every candidate persistence point that was tested and found absent.

**Figure 6.2.3-A — Data flow for the system's only datum, with verified-absent persistence points**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph SourceStage["Authoring — the only durable home of the datum"]
        Lit["String literal Hello from Java!<br/>Hello.java line 17, 16 ASCII characters"]
        Blob["Git blob 3fd76ce, 1,073 bytes<br/>content-addressed, effectively immutable"]
        Lit --> Blob
    end

    subgraph BuildStage["Compilation — transient artifact, never committed"]
        Pool["Constant-pool entry inside Hello.class<br/>420 bytes total, deleted or discarded after use"]
    end

    subgraph RunStage["Execution — in memory only, one process frame"]
        Ldc["ldc pushes the constant<br/>1 of 4 bytecode instructions in main"]
        Call["invokevirtual PrintStream.println<br/>the only API call in the program"]
        Ldc --> Call
    end

    subgraph SinkStage["Egress — a stream, not storage"]
        Fd1["File descriptor 1<br/>17 bytes on an LF host, 18 on a CRLF host"]
        Term["Operator terminal or pipe<br/>consumer chosen outside the system boundary"]
        Fd1 --> Term
    end

    subgraph NoStore["Candidate persistence points — all verified absent"]
        NS1["No database, embedded engine or file write"]
        NS2["No cache, queue, broker or session store"]
        NS3["No serialisation, journal, WAL or temp file"]
        NS1 --- NS2
        NS2 --- NS3
    end

    Blob -->|"javac reads the single compilation unit"| Pool
    Pool -->|"class loader, resident only for the run"| Ldc
    Call --> Fd1
    Call -.->|"no branch reaches any store"| NS1
```

The figures for the 420-byte class file and the four bytecode instructions in `main` are recorded evidence from `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md`, since no JDK was available in the verification environment. The same source records that three successive runs left the working directory, `HOME` and `java.io.tmpdir` byte-identical, with no performance-data file, lock file, journal or serialised object produced — which is the direct runtime confirmation of the `NoStore` subgraph above.

At the repository level, retrieval mechanisms do exist and were measured. They are exact-match lookups, not queries:

| Retrieval Path | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| By path, current state | `.git/index` (574 bytes, 5 entries) maps each tracked path to its blob for checkout and status |
| By content hash | The pack `.idx` (2,108 bytes) resolves a SHA-1 to a byte offset in the 307,997-byte pack, with `.rev` (200 bytes) providing the inverse |
| By ref name | `.git/packed-refs` (427 bytes) resolves a ref to a commit SHA |
| By history | Commit-graph traversal from a ref, following embedded parent hashes; `git show` materialises any historical blob |

#### 6.2.3.5 Caching Policies

No cache exists at any layer, and this is the result of design rather than of omission. Section 3.5.3 records caching as None, and Section 4.3.1.5 confirms that no cache exists anywhere in the system while enumerating the caches a comparable system would have as explicitly absent.

Each absence has a structural cause that can be traced to something observable:

| Cache That Would Normally Exist | Why It Cannot Arise Here |
|---|---|
| Application or query cache | There is no store to cache in front of, no repeated read, and no state. `Hello` holds no field and no static mutable data |
| Dependency cache | There is no build manifest of any kind in the repository, so no dependency is ever resolved or downloaded, and nothing is ever cached locally |
| Incremental build cache | Section 3.5.3 states there is "no incremental-build or caching concern because there is no second compilation unit" — a single-unit build has nothing to reuse |

The strongest evidence that cache avoidance is deliberate is the scratch-directory pattern. The documented workflow compiles into a fresh `mktemp -d` directory (component `C-10`), and Section 4.3.1.5 characterises this per-run scratch directory as "the deliberate opposite of a cache": it guarantees that every verification run starts from nothing and reuses no prior output, so results are reproducible rather than fast. There is consequently no invalidation policy, no TTL, no eviction strategy and no cache-coherence concern to document — and no cache-related failure mode appears among the faults `E-1` through `E-7` catalogued in Section 4.3.2.2.

### 6.2.4 Compliance Considerations

No database compliance surface exists, because no database exists and the program processes no data. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` line 188 states the position directly: the program "reads no input, dereferences no argument, opens no resource, binds no port, makes no network call and has no dependency manifest," and therefore has "no data-at-rest concern." No regulatory regime — GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, SOX or any other — is referenced in any tracked file, and no data classification, consent, residency or erasure requirement appears anywhere in the repository.

What follows documents the compliance-relevant properties that do exist, all of which attach to the repository rather than to the application. Two of them are genuine, verified gaps and are stated as such.

#### 6.2.4.1 Data Retention Rules

No retention rule exists. Section 3.5.6 states that "no backup policy, retention rule or recovery target exists in any tracked file," and direct inspection confirms no `gc.*` or `pack.*` configuration is set, so nothing expires by policy and nothing expires by configuration.

| Retained Content | Effective Retention |
|---|---|
| All 37 objects in the pack, including 5 superseded blobs not reachable from HEAD | Indefinite. Append-only and content-addressed; no expiry mechanism is configured |
| Commit metadata for all 14 commits, including author identity and timestamp | Indefinite and immutable — rewriting it would change every descendant commit SHA |
| `.git/logs` reflog, 3 HEAD entries under `core.logallrefupdates` = `true` | Governed by Git defaults only; untracked and local to this clone |
| `Hello.class`, the build artifact | Zero retention by design. The documented workflow builds into a `mktemp -d` scratch directory, and zero `*.class` blobs have ever been tracked |

The only formal obligation the repository does carry is a licensing one, not a data one: `LICENSE` is the GNU General Public License v3 dated 29 June 2007, 35,149 bytes across 674 lines, and it is 34 times the size of the source it governs.

#### 6.2.4.2 Backup and Fault Tolerance Policies

There is no database backup or failover policy, and Section 4.3.2.7 records that no recovery procedure in the system "requires a backup, a snapshot or a restore point." Section 5.4.6 reaches the corresponding conclusion that nothing in the system needs recovering, because continuity rests on object-store durability and every clone is a complete replica.

Fault tolerance is therefore a property of derivability rather than of redundancy. Of the seven faults catalogued in Section 4.3.2.2 as `E-1` through `E-7`, none is a data-loss fault: there is no corruptible store, no partial write and no torn transaction, and Section 4.3.1.6 confirms the absence of any commit protocol, two-phase coordination or rollback log.

Three exposures remain, and they are precise:

| Exposure | Status |
|---|---|
| Reflog loss | The reflog is untracked and **not conveyed by a clone**, so ref-movement history local to this checkout is unprotected by replication |
| Loss of the verification record | `Project Guide.md` §3 and §4 hold the only durable record of verification outcomes. Section 6.1.4.3 identifies this as the single non-reconstructible loss in the system, since nothing in the repository re-runs the checks |
| Single-branch delivery | The delivery exists only on `jr_java1`; `main` is 11 commits behind with no divergent commits, per Section 6.2.2.6. Section 5.4.6 records this as the one open continuity item |

Against these, the store's integrity was positively verified: `git fsck --no-progress` exits 0 with no dangling, missing or corrupt object, and `git verify-pack -v` reports the single pack as `ok`.

#### 6.2.4.3 Privacy Controls

No privacy control exists in the application, and none is required of it. The program accepts no input — `args` is referenced only in the Javadoc `@param` on line 11 and in the signature on line 15, and is provably never dereferenced — so it is structurally incapable of ingesting personal data. `README.md` line 12 records that it "reads no input, opens no resource and keeps no state." There is no user, no identity, no session, no PII field and no authentication or authorisation surface anywhere in the system.

Two genuine privacy-relevant facts do exist in the repository, and both concern the immutable store rather than the program.

**Contributor identity is permanently embedded.** Every one of the 14 commits carries an author name and an ISO-8601 timestamp inside the commit object. Because commit SHAs are computed over that metadata, the identities cannot be redacted without rewriting history and invalidating every descendant SHA — and because every clone is a full replica, they are distributed to every copy of the repository. This is normal Git behaviour, but it is the only personal data the system holds, and it is irrevocable in practice.

**Nothing prevents sensitive content from entering the store.** Section 3.5.6 classifies this risk as "Unguarded": the tracked content is clean today, but no mechanism — no secret scanner, no pre-commit hook, no `.gitignore` — stands between a contributor and the append-only store. Given content addressing and full replication, any secret committed once would be effectively permanent across all replicas. A live illustration of the general hazard already exists adjacent to the checkout: the configured remote URL in the untracked `.git/config` embeds an ephemeral GitHub access token. It is outside the tracked content and is deliberately not reproduced in this specification, but it demonstrates why the unguarded status matters.

#### 6.2.4.4 Audit Mechanisms

No database audit exists — no audit table, no trigger, no change-data-capture stream, no access log and no application-level logging of any kind (the program writes only to standard output and never to standard error). The audit capability that does exist is the commit history, and it was examined in full.

| Audit Property | Verified State |
|---|---|
| Change attribution | Complete. All 14 commits carry an author and a timestamp: `c537a19`, `f1847fa` and `0726b1d` by `rjhonsi` on 2026-09-16 (+0530); nine commits by `Blitzy Agent` on 2026-09-16 and 2026-09-17; and `2a78292` by `blitzy-qa[bot]` at 2026-09-22 08:51:44 |
| Tamper evidence | Strong. SHA-1 content addressing chains every commit to its parent, so altering any historical content or metadata changes all subsequent SHAs |
| Cryptographic signing | **Partial and unenforced.** The signature histogram is 4 commits with status `E` — a signature is present but unverifiable in this environment, covering the three `rjhonsi` commits and the merge — against 10 with status `N`, meaning unsigned. No configuration requires signing |
| Ref-movement audit | Local only. `core.logallrefupdates` is `true` and `.git/logs/HEAD` holds 3 entries, but reflogs are untracked and not transferred by clone or fetch |

Two consequences follow. First, *what* changed and *who* changed it are fully auditable from any clone; *when a ref moved* is auditable only from the clone where it happened. Second, because 10 of 14 commits are unsigned and signing is not enforced, authorship metadata is self-asserted for the majority of the history — it establishes attribution, not cryptographic proof of identity.

#### 6.2.4.5 Access Controls

No access control exists in the application layer, and none can: there is no database to grant privileges on, no role, no principal, no credential, no `GRANT` equivalent and no authentication surface, as `Project Guide.md` line 188 records.

At the repository layer, the observable access-control surface is notable chiefly for what is missing. Each of the following was existence-tested directly:

| Control | Observed State |
|---|---|
| `CODEOWNERS` and `.github/CODEOWNERS` | **Absent.** No review ownership is declared for any path, including `Hello.java` |
| `SECURITY.md` | **Absent.** No vulnerability-disclosure or security-contact policy exists |
| `.gitignore` | **Absent.** `.git/info/exclude` exists at 240 bytes but contains no active pattern, and `git check-ignore -v Hello.class` matches no rule — so the build artifact is unignored and can be committed by accident, which is why requirement F-005-RQ-002 is documented-but-unenforced (Section 6.2.2.4) |
| `.gitattributes` | **Absent.** No line-ending, diff or merge policy is asserted, leaving the CRLF/LF divergence in Section 6.2.2.4 unmanaged |
| File permission model | Uniform. All five entries at HEAD are mode `100644` — no executable bit, no symlink, no submodule and no gitlink |

Write access to the hosting remote is mediated by the ephemeral token in the untracked `.git/config`, which is a credential of the automation session rather than a project-defined control. Branch protection, required reviews and organisation-level permissions, if any are configured on the GitHub remote, are not observable from a clone and are therefore neither confirmed nor documented here; the one piece of indirect evidence available is that `main` has not been advanced to the delivery commit, which is consistent with a deliberate review gate but does not establish one.

### 6.2.5 Performance Optimization

No database performance optimization exists, and none of the five areas below has a counterpart in the system. There is no query to tune, no cache to warm, no connection to pool, no read/write asymmetry to exploit and no batch to size. The program executes four bytecode instructions in `main`, writes 17 bytes to a stream and exits.

Each area is nonetheless documented, because the reason a concern cannot arise is itself specification-relevant, and because a small number of real performance characteristics were measured in the object store.

#### 6.2.5.1 Query Optimization Patterns

No query language, query planner, execution plan, statistics collector or `EXPLAIN` facility exists in this system. `Hello.java` declares zero imports and contains no query construct of any kind; the 38-pattern source search described in Section 6.2.1.2 found no data-access API at all.

Every lookup that does occur in the project is an exact-match resolution against a pre-built index, which is why there is nothing to optimise — the access path is determined by the structure, not chosen by a planner:

| Lookup | Access Path and Cost Characteristic |
|---|---|
| Path to current content | Linear scan of 5 sorted entries in the 574-byte `.git/index` — bounded by the tracked-file count, which is five |
| Content hash to object | Binary search in the 2,108-byte pack `.idx`, then a direct seek to a byte offset in the 307,997-byte pack. Logarithmic in object count, with the object count being 37 |
| Ref name to commit | Direct resolution through the 427-byte `.git/packed-refs` |

Two measured properties characterise the store's read efficiency. First, delta-chain depth is minimal: `git verify-pack -v` reports 24 objects stored non-delta, 10 at chain length 1 and 3 at chain length 2, so reconstructing any object requires at most two delta applications. Second, compression is effective — the 10 blobs total 934,642 bytes of raw content, stored in a 307,997-byte pack alongside all 14 commits and 13 trees, a ratio of roughly 3:1. Neither figure is the result of a tuning decision: no `pack.*` configuration is set anywhere, so both follow entirely from Git's defaults.

#### 6.2.5.2 Caching Strategy

There is no caching strategy because there is no cache, at any layer. Section 6.2.3.5 documents this in full, including the structural reason each normally-expected cache cannot arise and the deliberate anti-caching posture of the `mktemp -d` scratch directory that Section 4.3.1.5 describes as "the deliberate opposite of a cache."

The only point to add in a performance context is the trade-off direction: the scratch-directory pattern optimises for reproducibility and verifiability, not for speed. A run always starts from nothing and reuses no prior output. With a single 1,073-byte compilation unit and no dependency resolution step, the cost of that choice is negligible, which is why no cache has ever been justified.

#### 6.2.5.3 Connection Pooling

Nothing in this system opens a connection, so there is no pool, no pool size, no minimum or maximum, no acquisition timeout, no validation query, no idle eviction and no leak detection. There is no connection string to point a pool at, and no configuration file in which to define one.

Two connection-adjacent facts are worth recording so the absence is unambiguous:

| Connection-Like Resource | Observed Reality |
|---|---|
| File descriptor 1 | **Inherited from the parent process, never opened.** The program acquires no handle and releases none; there is no lifecycle to manage and no `close()` call in the source |
| HTTPS to the hosting remote | Used only by `git clone`, `git fetch` and `git push` (component `C-9`). These are Git's own transient transport connections, entirely outside the application and not configured by the project |

The program binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call, as `Project Guide.md` line 252 records, so no socket resource exists on either the inbound or outbound side.

#### 6.2.5.4 Read/Write Splitting

No read/write splitting exists, and there is no primary/replica pair to split traffic across — Section 6.2.2.6 established that no database replication of any kind is configured.

The application's I/O profile makes the concept inapplicable rather than merely unimplemented: it performs **exactly one write and zero reads** per invocation. The single write is `System.out.println` on line 17, producing 17 bytes on an LF host or 18 on a CRLF host. There is no read path to route, no staleness window to reason about and no consistency level to select.

At the repository layer a read/write asymmetry does exist naturally, but it is a property of Git's design rather than a configured optimisation. Reads are served locally from the clone's own complete object database and require no network round-trip at all; writes to shared state are `git push` operations against the single hosting remote. The asymmetry is extreme — the delivery history comprises 14 write operations in total against an unbounded number of possible local reads — but nothing in the project routes, balances or tunes it.

#### 6.2.5.5 Batch Processing Approach

No batch processing exists. There is no scheduled job, no cron entry, no worker, no queue, no bulk-insert path, no ETL stage and no CI workflow — the checkout contains exactly three directories (`.`, `blitzy/` and `blitzy/documentation/`), so there is no `.github/workflows/` and no automation definition of any kind.

The execution model is the opposite of batch: one invocation processes one datum and terminates. Section 4.3.1.6 makes the related distinction precise for the documented workflow, noting that the primary path `W-1` "is two invocations, not one" — a `javac` step followed by a `java` step. That is a sequence of two single-item operations, not a batch with a size, a window or a flush policy.

Two bulk operations in the project are performed by tooling rather than by the system, and are noted only to forestall misreading:

- Git's consolidation of all 37 objects into a single pack file, which occurred under Git's default packing behaviour with no `gc.*` or `pack.*` configuration set by the project.
- `javadoc` HTML generation, persistence point `M-2` in Section 4.3.1.4, which processes the one compilation unit in the repository.

Neither has a configurable batch size, a parallelism setting or a throughput target, and no performance requirement, SLA or KPI for any of them appears in any tracked file.

### 6.2.6 Reassessment Triggers and Cross-Section References

The determination in Section 6.2.1 is a statement about the repository at commit `2a78292`, not a permanent property. This sub-section records the specific, observable changes that would invalidate it, so that a future reader can test the verdict rather than re-derive it, and then maps the related material elsewhere in this specification.

#### 6.2.6.1 Changes That Would Make Database Design Applicable

Each trigger below maps to one of the five failed preconditions in Section 6.2.1.1. Any single one occurring would require this sub-section to be rewritten as a substantive database design.

| Trigger | Failed Precondition It Would Satisfy |
|---|---|
| A build manifest appears (`pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts`) declaring any JDBC driver, JPA provider, embedded engine or client library | P1 — a datastore exists to design against |
| `Hello.java` gains an `import` of `java.sql`, `javax.sql`, `java.io`, `java.nio.file` or any persistence framework package, or a second compilation unit introduces one | P1 and P5 — a data-access path enters the source |
| Any type acquires persistent state: an instance or static field, a `Serializable`/`Externalizable` implementation, or a mapping annotation such as `@Entity` | P2 — a persistent entity exists |
| A `*.sql`, `*.ddl` or `schema.*` file appears, or a `migrations/`, `db/`, `flyway/`, `liquibase/` or `alembic/` directory is added | P3 — a schema and an evolution history exist |
| Any configuration file appears (`*.properties`, `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.json`, `*.xml`, `*.toml`, `*.ini`, `.env`) carrying a connection URI, DSN or credential | P4 — a place exists to configure a connection |
| The program writes to a file, a socket or any sink other than standard output | P5 — the runtime reaches durable media |

Two further changes would not make database design applicable but would require the object-store material in Sections 6.2.2 through 6.2.4 to be revised, because they would alter the substrate this sub-section documents:

- A `.gitattributes` or `.gitignore` file appearing, which would close one or both of the two enforcement gaps identified in Section 6.2.2.4.
- `gc.*` or `pack.*` configuration being set, or the first tag being created, either of which would convert the de-facto indefinite-retention and SHA-anchored-versioning positions in Sections 6.2.3.2 and 6.2.3.3 into explicit policy.

| Section 4.3 Technical Implementation | The seven-point persistence inventory including `P-5` (the application data store, none exists) and `M-1` through `M-3`; the no-cache finding; and the absence of any transactional resource, commit protocol or rollback log |

## 6.3 Integration Architecture

### 6.3.1 Applicability Assessment

**Integration Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

The system integrates with no external system or service at run time. The repository at commit `2a78292` on branch `jr_java1` tracks five files, of which exactly one is executable: `Hello.java`, 20 lines and 1,073 bytes, declaring one public class in the default package whose only member is `main(String[] args)`. The body of that method is a single statement at line 17 — `System.out.println("Hello from Java!")` — and the line comment above it at line 16 makes single-sink output a stated design property: "no other sink is written." There is no port, no listener, no socket, no HTTP or RPC client, no broker, no datastore connection, no webhook, no gateway and no third-party SDK anywhere in the tree.

`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` states the position for the repository as a whole without qualification. Line 130 records the implementation as "a console application with no user interface, no hosted page, no bound port and no external integration," and Appendix B at line 426 adds that the program "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call; there is no service, database, broker or cache in this project."

The determination is consistent with the parallel findings already recorded elsewhere in this specification: Section 6.1 concludes that Core Services Architecture is not applicable because there is no second deployable unit to draw a boundary against, and Section 6.2 concludes that Database Design is not applicable because no runtime path reaches durable media. Section 5.1.1.3 records the corresponding architectural fact directly — of the four boundary categories an integration architecture would cross, the network boundary, the persistence boundary and the trust boundary are all verified absent.

This sub-section does not stop at the verdict. Every area the specification calls for — protocol, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, versioning, documentation standards, event processing, queueing, stream and batch processing, error handling, third-party patterns, legacy interfaces, gateway configuration and external contracts — is addressed in turn in Sections 6.3.2 through 6.3.4, distinguishing what is genuinely absent from what does exist at the four non-network seams the system really has. Section 6.3.5 records the observable changes that would invalidate the verdict.

#### 6.3.1.1 Preconditions for an Integration Architecture

An integration architecture is meaningful only when a system satisfies the preconditions below. Each was tested directly against the checkout. All six fail.

| # | Precondition | Verified Result |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | An inbound interface exists that a foreign caller can reach — a bound port, listener, route, handler or entry endpoint | **Fails.** `Hello.java` contains no `ServerSocket`, `HttpServer`, servlet, route or handler construct. `Project Guide.md` line 426 records that the program "binds no port, starts no listener"; no `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `0.0.0.0` or port-like `:NNNN` pattern appears in `Hello.java` or `README.md` |
| P2 | An outbound call exists to a system the program does not own — HTTP, gRPC, RMI, JDBC, SMTP or a vendor SDK | **Fails.** The file declares **zero `import` statements and zero `package` statement**, so the only library surface is the implicitly available `java.lang`. The sole API call in the program is `PrintStream.println` |
| P3 | A message, event or stream substrate exists — a broker, queue, topic, log or event bus | **Fails.** No broker client, no queue or topic name, no consumer group, no offset and no serialisation format appears in any tracked file. `Project Guide.md` line 252 records "no database, broker and no bound port" |
| P4 | A contract artifact exists that describes an interface to a counterparty — OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, WSDL, Protobuf, Avro or GraphQL schema | **Fails.** Twenty-one named contract, gateway and proxy artifacts were existence-tested and all are absent, and a recursive census for 26 interface and configuration file extensions returned zero files across the whole checkout |
| P5 | A place exists to configure an endpoint, credential or connection | **Fails.** There is no configuration file of any format anywhere, no dependency manifest into which a client library could be declared, and no environment variable or secret read by any tracked file (`Project Guide.md` line 262 and Appendix E) |
| P6 | The running program can reach a foreign process or host | **Fails.** `Project Guide.md` line 49 records that "no credential, key, network egress, environment variable or secret is used by anything in this project," and line 188 that the program "reads no input, dereferences no argument, opens no resource, binds no port, makes no network call and has no dependency manifest" |

#### 6.3.1.2 Integration-Surface Census

Absence was established at three independent levels, so that a negative result at one level cannot be an artifact of where the search was pointed.

| Level of Search | What Was Tested | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Artifact level | Twenty-one named integration artifacts existence-tested at the repository root — `openapi.yaml`/`.yml`/`.json`, `swagger.yaml`/`.json`, `asyncapi.yaml`, `nginx.conf`, `Caddyfile`, `envoy.yaml`, `kong.yml`, `haproxy.cfg`, `ingress.yaml`, `api-gateway.yml`, `.well-known`, `postman_collection.json`, `requests.http`, `Procfile`, `serverless.yml`, `template.yaml`, `apigateway.tf`, `schema.graphql` — followed by a recursive census of the whole checkout for 26 extensions (`yml`, `yaml`, `json`, `xml`, `proto`, `wsdl`, `avsc`, `thrift`, `graphql`, `gql`, `http`, `rest`, `toml`, `ini`, `conf`, `cfg`, `properties`, `env`, `sh`, `bat`, `ps1`, `jar`, `war`, `class`, `har`, `raml`) | **Zero present, zero files found** for every artifact and every extension |
| Source level | All `.java` content searched for `package` and `import` declarations, then for the full integration marker set: `java.net`, `java.io`, `java.nio`, `HttpClient`, `HttpServer`, `Socket`, `ServerSocket`, `URL`, `URLConnection`, `InetAddress`, `DatagramPacket`, RMI and `Remote`, `JDBC`, `DataSource`, `Connection`, `JMS`, Kafka, RabbitMQ, AMQP, MQTT, gRPC, Protobuf, Thrift, REST, SOAP, WSDL, OpenAPI, Swagger, webhook, OAuth, JWT, API key, `Serializable`, `ObjectOutputStream`, `BufferedReader`, `Scanner`, `FileWriter` and `Files.` | **Zero declarations and zero functional matches.** The only textual hits anywhere were the word `System.exit` inside the termination comment at `Hello.java` line 18 and descriptive prose in `README.md` |
| History level | `git log --all --diff-filter=A --name-only` enumerated every path ever added on any branch across the full history, then filtered for `api`, `http`, `rest`, `grpc`, `proto`, `swagger`, `openapi`, `wsdl`, `soap`, `queue`, `broker`, `kafka`, `mq`, `event`, `webhook`, `gateway`, `nginx`, `ingress`, `client`, `sdk`, `integration` and every configuration extension | **No such path has ever existed.** Only the five known tracked files have ever been added on any branch |

The history-level result is the decisive one: an integration was not removed, stubbed out or deferred. No integration artifact has ever been present in this repository's recorded history.

A fourth census is worth stating separately because it bounds the system's entire network vocabulary. A URL and URI scheme search across every tracked file for `http`, `https`, `ftp`, `ws`, `wss`, `jdbc`, `amqp`, `mqtt`, `redis`, `mongodb`, `kafka`, `file`, `git` and `ssh` returns **zero occurrences in `Hello.java`, zero in `README.md` and zero in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md`.** The only four URLs in the tracked tree are in `LICENSE`: `https://fsf.org/` at line 4, `https://www.gnu.org/licenses/` at lines 648 and 667, and `https://www.gnu.org/licenses/why-not-lgpl.html` at line 674. All four are licence-text references addressed to a human reader; none is an endpoint any tracked file resolves, requests or depends on. Section 3.4.1 reaches the same conclusion independently.

#### 6.3.1.3 What Exists Instead — The Four Interface Seams

The system is not hermetic. Five external parties participate, and Section 5.1.4 records that they exhaust the list; three of them are contracts rather than services, one is a hosted service used only for source distribution, and one is a presentation-only renderer. They are reached across the four interface seams established in Section 5.1.1.3 — none of which is a network or API boundary.

| Seam | What crosses it | Why it is not an integration |
|---|---|---|
| **I-1 Compilation** | One compilation unit in, one class file out; no dependency to resolve and no `--release`/`--source` setting | A local toolchain invocation from a shell, not a call to a counterparty. `README.md` line 18 records that "nothing has to be resolved or downloaded before building" |
| **I-2 JVM entry point** | The launcher resolves the bare name `Hello` and invokes `main` exactly once; `args` is accepted and never dereferenced | An in-process method invocation inside a single JVM frame. Nothing is marshalled, addressed or transported |
| **I-3 Process and standard streams** | The greeting plus one platform line separator on file descriptor 1; empty file descriptor 2; exit status 0 by normal return | A fire-and-forget unidirectional write to an inherited descriptor. Section 5.1.4 records it has "no reply channel and no acknowledgement" |
| **I-4 Distribution and governance** | Git objects over HTTPS to and from `github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java`, plus the verbatim GPL v3 terms in `LICENSE` | Source conveyance and legal obligation, exercised by `git` and by human readers. Section 3.4.2 records the runtime coupling as **none** — the program never contacts the platform |

#### 6.3.1.4 How the Remainder of This Sub-Section Is Organised

Declaring non-applicability does not discharge the specification's areas. Each is addressed below in one of three ways, and each sub-section makes clear which applies:

1. **Genuinely absent with no counterpart anywhere.** Rate limiting, authorization, message queueing, stream processing, event processing, API gateway configuration and legacy system interfaces have no analogue in the repository. These are stated as absent, with the structural reason the concern cannot arise.
2. **Present at a non-network seam, and documented as such.** Protocol specification, authentication, versioning, documentation standards, batch flows and error handling all have concrete counterparts at seams I-1 through I-4 — the process contract, the Git transport, and the operator-facing command surface. These are documented with measured values and explicitly flagged as belonging to a seam that is not an API.
3. **Present outside the system boundary.** The GitHub remote's access control and the operator's JDK installation are real dependencies that the repository neither configures nor controls. Section 1.3.1.2 places the hosting platform outside the boundary; they are documented here so the reader is not left to infer them.

#### 6.3.1.5 Verification Environment

Two constraints on the evidence in this sub-section should be stated so its claims can be weighted correctly.

| Constraint | Consequence for This Sub-Section |
|---|---|
| **No JDK is installed** in the environment used to verify the repository (`javac`, `java`, `javap` and `javadoc` are absent from `PATH`, and no `/usr/lib/jvm` exists) | Every runtime observation quoted here — that a run writes only to file descriptor 1, leaves standard error empty, exits 0, and produces no socket, file or network activity — is attributed to `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` as recorded evidence. None is asserted first-hand |
| Git and standard text tooling are present | All repository-state findings — the tracked inventory, the full-history path census, the extension and artifact censuses, the URL census, ref and remote topology — were measured directly and are first-hand observations |

The one untracked file in the working tree, `tech_spec.md`, is an authoring artifact of the documentation process. It is not a system file, is not tracked, and is excluded from every figure and census above.


### 6.3.2 API Design

**No API exists in this system, in any sense the term ordinarily carries.** There is no inbound interface, no outbound client, no route table, no resource path, no request or response schema, no media type, no status-code vocabulary and no interface-definition artifact. The one API call the program makes is `PrintStream.println`, on a stream it inherited rather than opened.

What stands in the position an API would occupy is an **invocation contract**: a documented set of commands an operator types, an argument array the program accepts and never reads, and a three-part process outcome. That contract is specified precisely in `README.md` and is the only interface specification the repository publishes. It is documented below in place of an API specification, and each of the six areas the specification calls for is then addressed against it.

| Interface element | Contract at `HEAD` | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Invocation form | `java Hello` after an in-place compile; `java -cp "$B" Hello` after a scratch-directory compile; `java Hello.java` as a direct source launch | `README.md` lines 37, 30, 43; the three forms are recorded as verified at `Project Guide.md` lines 305-308 |
| Request payload | `String[] args` — accepted only to satisfy the entry-point signature the JVM requires, and never dereferenced anywhere in the body | `Hello.java` lines 11-13, 15; `README.md` lines 48-51 |
| Response payload | The literal `Hello from Java!` followed by one platform line separator, on file descriptor 1; 16 ASCII characters plus the host's separator | `Hello.java` line 17; `README.md` lines 57-63 |
| Error channel | File descriptor 2 stays empty on every run; there is no diagnostic output of any kind | `README.md` line 63; `Project Guide.md` line 130 |
| Status channel | Exit status 0, produced by normal return from `main` with no `System.exit` call | `Hello.java` line 18; `README.md` line 63 |
| Idempotence and determinism | Both launch paths produce byte-identical standard output, and output is identical whether or not arguments are supplied | `README.md` lines 46, 51 |
