#### 6.3.2.1 Protocol Specifications

No application protocol is specified, because no application protocol is spoken. There is no wire format, no framing, no handshake, no content negotiation and no transport security configuration in any tracked file. Section 6.3.1.2 records that the tracked tree contains no `http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`, `jdbc`, `amqp`, `mqtt`, `redis`, `mongodb` or `kafka` URI anywhere outside the four licence-text URLs in `LICENSE`.

Three protocols genuinely operate, all of them at seams that predate the application and none of them chosen or configured by the repository. Section 5.1.4 records the same three from the architecture side.

| Seam | Protocol in force | Payload and encoding |
|---|---|---|
| I-1 Compilation | POSIX process execution from a shell — `javac` addressed by `argv`, with no network step and no dependency resolution | ASCII source stored with CRLF on all 20 lines in, JVM class-file bytecode out, diagnostics on standard error |
| I-2 JVM entry point | The JVM launcher's class-resolution and entry-point convention: a bare-name lookup on the classpath, then one invocation of the required `main` signature | A `String[]` argument array, passed by the launcher and never dereferenced by the program |
| I-3 Process and streams | POSIX file descriptors 1 and 2 plus the wait-status convention — the system's only outbound channel | 16 ASCII characters followed by the platform line separator; empty standard error; status 0 |
| I-4 Distribution | Git smart protocol over HTTPS to `github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java` — exercised by `git`, never by the program | Git objects and refs: five tracked blobs, 14 commits, zero tags, eight refs |

Two properties of this protocol set are worth stating because they are the reason no integration architecture follows from it. First, the outbound channel at I-3 is **fire-and-forget and unidirectional**: Section 5.1.4 records that it has "no reply channel and no acknowledgement," so no request/response, correlation, retry or timeout semantics can exist. Second, the only network protocol in the system — Git over HTTPS at I-4 — is exercised by a separate tool at clone, fetch, push and merge time; Section 3.4.2 records the program's runtime coupling to the platform as **none**, and Section 5.1.4 records that once cloned, every documented workflow runs entirely offline with zero network egress.

#### 6.3.2.2 Authentication Methods

**The application performs no authentication of any kind, and is structurally incapable of it.** There is no credential handling, no identity concept, no session, no token parsing and no `OAuth`, `JWT` or API-key construct in `Hello.java`. The absence is not a configuration choice: because the program reads no input and never dereferences `args`, there is no channel through which a principal could be asserted in the first place. `Project Guide.md` line 49 records that "no credential, key, network egress, environment variable or secret is used by anything in this project," and Appendix E at lines 447-452 records `JAVA_HOME` as not required and adds that no other variable and no secret is read by any tracked file.

Authentication exists only around the distribution seam I-4, and only outside the tracked tree. Section 3.4.3 documents this in full; the two findings that bound the system's entire credential surface are:

| Finding | Consequence for integration |
|---|---|
| No secret is conveyed by a clone. A pattern search across all tracked files for token, key and credential forms matches only documentation prose and the GPL text itself, never a value | Cloning the repository transfers no credential material, so no integration credential needs provisioning, rotating or revoking |
| The only credential observed is untracked and local: the clone reaches the remote over HTTPS using a short-lived token-bearing URL held in the clone's own `.git/config`, which `git ls-files` confirms is outside the tracked tree | The token is an artifact of the checkout environment, not of the repository, and is deliberately not reproduced in this specification |

#### 6.3.2.3 Authorization Framework

**No authorization framework exists at any layer of the application.** There is no role, no permission, no scope, no policy document, no access-control list and no `GRANT` equivalent, because there is no protected resource and no principal to evaluate. Section 6.2.4.5 records the same finding for the data layer, and Section 5.1.1.3 records that the system has no trust or authentication boundary at all.

The only authorization that governs anything in this system sits at seam I-4 and belongs to parties the repository does not control:

| Control point | Who enforces it | Observed state |
|---|---|---|
| Push and merge rights on the remote | The GitHub platform | The repository "defines no roles, accounts or permissions of its own" (Section 3.4.2). Branch protection and required reviews, if configured, are not observable from a clone and are therefore not documented as facts here |
| Review ownership for changes to the interface | Nothing | `CODEOWNERS`, `.github/CODEOWNERS` and `SECURITY.md` are all absent (Section 6.2.4.5); no path, including `Hello.java`, has a declared reviewer |
| File-level capability in the tracked tree | Git's mode field | All five tracked entries are mode `100644` — no executable bit, no symlink, no submodule and no gitlink |
| Redistribution rights over the work | The GPL v3 instrument in `LICENSE`, 674 lines and 35,149 bytes | The only authorization control the repository itself carries is legal rather than technical, and it grants rather than restricts |

#### 6.3.2.4 Rate Limiting Strategy

**No rate limiting exists, and there is no admission point at which any could be applied.** There is no quota, token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window, concurrency cap, backpressure signal, `429`-equivalent response or retry-after hint anywhere in the repository — and, as Section 6.3.1.2 establishes, no configuration file of any format in which one could be declared.

The structural reason is that work never arrives: it is initiated. A run begins only when a human types one of the three documented launch commands, so the request rate is an operator decision made entirely outside the system boundary. Each invocation creates its own JVM process, and Section 6.1.2.4 records why those processes cannot interfere — with no shared mutable state and no lock, concurrent invocations are independent and cannot contend. The practical consequence, recorded in Section 6.1.3.5, is that concurrency is bounded only by host capacity, and the repository records no measurement of that bound. No throughput figure, latency target or availability objective appears in any tracked file, and none is asserted here.

#### 6.3.2.5 Versioning Approach

**No interface version exists, because no interface is published to a consumer that could be broken by a change.** There is no URI version segment, no version header, no versioned media type, no deprecation policy and no compatibility matrix. Section 6.2.3.2 records the repository-level position: **zero tags exist** across the whole history, so there is no semantic version, no release marker and no immutable named point in history — every version reference resolves through a mutable branch ref to a commit SHA, and the authoritative state is identified only by a SHA on a non-default branch, with `main` sitting 11 commits behind the delivery.

Three genuine compatibility statements do exist, and they are properties of the invocation contract rather than of an API version:

| Compatibility statement | Observed position |
|---|---|
| Toolchain floor for the direct source launch | `README.md` line 20 records that `java Hello.java` is a single-file source-code launch needing **JDK 11 or later**, while the compile-then-run path "carries no such floor and works on considerably older releases." Section 5.1.4 notes the floor was corroborated only by compiling at release targets 11, 17 and 21, never on a real JDK 11 runtime |
| Toolchain pinning | None. `README.md` line 18 records that the repository pins no Java version and carries no `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `.java-version`, `.sdkmanrc`, CI descriptor or `module-info.java` in which one could be recorded. OpenJDK 25.0.3 is recorded as observed, never enforced |
| The one breaking-change vector in the contract | Bare-name class resolution depends on the **absence** of a `package` declaration. Section 6.1.2.3 records that adding one would invalidate every launch command documented in `README.md` — the only way a consumer of this interface can be broken |

#### 6.3.2.6 Documentation Standards

No interface-definition artifact exists — Section 6.3.1.2 records that OpenAPI, Swagger, AsyncAPI, WSDL, Protobuf, Avro, Thrift and GraphQL descriptors are all absent, and that no generated reference site is published. Interface documentation in this system is prose and in-source comments, and it follows four observable conventions.

| Convention in force | Observed implementation |
|---|---|
| The operator guide is the interface specification | `README.md` is 77 lines across eight sections — summary of changes, overview, requirements, build, run, expected output, project layout and licence — publishing the requirement set, both build paths, all three launch forms, the argument contract and the output contract |
| The output contract is published as an executable oracle | The fenced block at `README.md` lines 59-61 republishes the literal from `Hello.java` line 17 verbatim, so the specification can be compared byte for byte against real output rather than read. Section 5.1.3 records that `Project Guide.md` confirms that comparison as byte-identical |
| Claims are cited to a stable source symbol | `README.md` carries `Source: Hello.java (class Hello)` at line 14 and `Source: Hello.java (Hello.main)` at line 53, anchoring prose to a named symbol rather than to a line number |
| In-source documentation is Javadoc plus targeted line comments | `Hello.java` carries a class Javadoc at lines 1-5, a `main` Javadoc with an `@param args` tag at lines 7-14, and two line comments recording the single-sink output property (line 16) and the no-`System.exit` termination path (line 18) |

Two limits on the documentation standard are recorded in the repository rather than inferred. First, coverage is measured but incomplete: `Project Guide.md` records `javadoc` reporting one remaining warning, for the implicit default constructor, which "can carry no doc comment" without declaring a constructor — a structural change the comment-only constraint forbade. Second, the rendered form has never been reviewed. The dialect is determined by the hosting platform — GitHub Flavored Markdown over CommonMark, with no generator or renderer part of the project — and Section 3.4.2 records the rendered review of the guide as an open item, since its structure was asserted against the Markdown source rather than a rendered page.

One drift in the documentation is worth naming because it concerns the interface description itself: the project-layout table at `README.md` line 67 still describes the repository as "three tracked files at the root, and no subdirectories," whereas the tracked inventory is five files and `blitzy/documentation/` exists. Section 5.1.2 records the same discrepancy against component C-4.


### 6.3.3 Message Processing

**No message processing exists in this system.** There is no message, no envelope, no topic, no queue, no broker, no consumer, no offset, no serialisation format and no delivery guarantee. Section 6.1.2.2 records the wider property already established for the architecture: interaction across the whole system is synchronous and operator-initiated, with "no message, event, callback, poll or scheduled trigger anywhere."

One datum moves through the system per invocation, and it is not a message in any transported sense. It begins as a 16-character string literal at `Hello.java` line 17, becomes a constant-pool entry at compile time, is pushed onto the operand stack by a single `ldc` instruction, is handed to `System.out.println` by the one API call in the program, and leaves as bytes on file descriptor 1. It is never framed, addressed, routed, acknowledged, retried or persisted.

**Figure 6.3.3-A — Message flow: the only datum in the system, and the messaging substrate that does not exist**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph OriginStage["Origin — the payload is a compile-time constant, not a produced message"]
        Lit["String literal at Hello.java line 17<br/>16 ASCII characters, immutable"]
        Pool["Constant-pool entry inside the class file<br/>pushed by one ldc instruction"]
        Lit --> Pool
    end

    subgraph TransportStage["Transport — one in-process invocation, no broker in the path"]
        CallNode["invokevirtual PrintStream.println<br/>the only API call in the program<br/>synchronous, in-frame, no marshalling"]
    end

    subgraph SinkStage["Sink — a byte stream, not a queue"]
        Fd1["File descriptor 1, inherited from the parent process<br/>written exactly once per invocation"]
        Consumer["Consumer chosen outside the system boundary:<br/>terminal, pipe or shell redirect"]
        Fd1 --> Consumer
    end

    subgraph AbsentMsgStage["Verified absent — no messaging substrate of any kind"]
        NoBroker["No broker, queue, topic, partition,<br/>consumer group, offset or subscription"]
        NoEvent["No event, callback, listener, observer,<br/>poll loop, timer or scheduled trigger"]
        NoStreamOps["No windowing, watermark, checkpoint,<br/>ordering key or delivery guarantee"]
        NoDlq["No dead-letter queue, redelivery, replay log<br/>or poison-message handling"]
        NoBroker --- NoEvent
        NoEvent --- NoStreamOps
        NoStreamOps --- NoDlq
    end

    Pool --> CallNode
    CallNode --> Fd1
    CallNode -.->|"no branch in the program reaches a broker, queue or peer"| NoBroker
```

**Figure 6.3.3-B — Sequence of the primary flow: the complete message path from command to consumed line**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Op as Operator shell
    participant Jc as javac (C-8a)
    participant Jv as java launcher (C-8b)
    participant Hm as Hello.main (C-2)
    participant Os as Process contract (I-3)

    Note over Op,Os: Workflows W-1 and W-2 — compile then run. No step in this flow crosses a network.
    Op->>Jc: javac Hello.java — one file path on argv
    Jc->>Jc: Resolve nothing: no classpath entry, no manifest, zero dependencies
    Jc-->>Op: Exit 0 with no diagnostics, class file emitted
    Op->>Jv: java Hello — bare name, resolvable only because no package is declared
    Jv->>Hm: Invoke main(String[] args) exactly once
    Note right of Hm: args is accepted and never dereferenced,<br/>so no inbound payload can influence the flow
    Hm->>Os: One write to fd 1 — greeting plus platform line separator
    Hm-->>Jv: Normal return, no System.exit call
    Jv-->>Os: JVM shuts down of its own accord, wait status 0, fd 2 empty
    Os-->>Op: Operator reads the line and compares it to the oracle at README.md lines 59-61
```

#### 6.3.3.1 Event Processing Patterns

**No event processing pattern is implemented.** There is no publish/subscribe arrangement, no event bus, no observer registration, no callback, no listener interface, no poll loop, no timer, no shutdown hook and no event-sourcing or CQRS structure. `Hello.java` declares no field and creates no instance, so there is no subscriber to hold a registration and no state for an event to mutate.

Exactly one thing in the system resembles an event, and it originates outside the boundary:

| Candidate event | What actually happens | Why it is not an event pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Operator invocation | A human types one of three documented commands; the shell forks a process and the launcher calls `main` once | Synchronous and blocking, with no producer, no dispatcher and no subscription. The operator's shell is the only scheduler in the system (Section 6.1.1.3) |
| Process termination | `main` returns; the JVM shuts down of its own accord and reports status 0 | No shutdown hook, no finaliser, no `System.exit` and no lifecycle callback — `Hello.java` line 18 records termination as a deliberate property |
| Standard-output write | `System.out.println` emits the greeting and the host's line separator to a descriptor the process inherited | Fire-and-forget with no reply channel and no acknowledgement (Section 5.1.4). Nothing is emitted for a consumer to react to programmatically |

#### 6.3.3.2 Message Queue Architecture

**No message queue architecture exists.** No broker, queue, topic, exchange, partition, consumer group, offset store, subscription, routing key or dead-letter destination appears in any tracked file, and no client library for one is declared — `Hello.java` has zero imports and the repository has no dependency manifest at all. `Project Guide.md` line 252 records the absence among the prerequisites: "No package manager step, no virtual environment, no container, no database, no broker and no bound port," and Appendix B at line 426 repeats it as a categorical statement for the project.

The census behind that finding is exhaustive rather than sampled. Section 6.3.1.2 records that a source-level search for `JMS`, Kafka, RabbitMQ, AMQP, MQTT, gRPC, Protobuf, Thrift and every related marker returned zero functional matches; that a recursive census for 26 interface and configuration extensions returned zero files; and that the full-history path census confirms no broker or queue artifact has ever been added on any branch.

One durable structure in the project could be mistaken for a queue and is named here to forestall that reading. The **Git object store** holds the repository's five tracked blobs, 14 commits and 13 trees in a single pack, and Section 5.1.3 identifies it as the system's only durable, distributable state. It is an append-only, content-addressed object database consumed by exact-hash and exact-path lookup, not a queue: it has no consumer, no ordering semantics for delivery, no acknowledgement, no visibility timeout and no expiry. Section 6.2.3.1 records the corresponding property that all commits are append-only additions with no in-place migration step.

#### 6.3.3.3 Stream Processing Design

**No stream processing design exists.** There is no windowing, watermark, checkpoint, state store, join, aggregation, ordering key, exactly-once semantic or backpressure mechanism anywhere in the repository — and no framework in which to express one, since nothing is declared as a dependency.

The distinction that matters here is between a *byte stream* and a *stream-processing substrate*. The system has exactly one of the former and none of the latter:

| Aspect | Observed reality |
|---|---|
| The stream that exists | `System.out`, a `PrintStream` the process **inherits rather than opens**. Section 6.2.5.3 records that the program acquires no handle and releases none, and that there is no `close()` call in the source |
| Cardinality | One write per invocation, then the process exits. There is no continuous or unbounded input to process, and no second element for a window to span |
| Direction | Write-only. Section 6.2.5.4 records exactly one write and zero reads per invocation, so there is no input stream to consume, transform or partition |
| Environment dependence | The only environment-dependent element in the payload is the terminator: `README.md` line 63 records that the exact byte count varies between platforms while "the literal and its single trailing separator do not" |
| Downstream composition | Whatever the launching shell attaches — a terminal, a pipe or a redirect. The consumer is chosen entirely outside the system boundary and is not configured, negotiated or discovered |

#### 6.3.3.4 Batch Processing Flows

**No batch processing flow exists, and no automation of any kind schedules work.** There is no cron entry, timer, worker, job definition, bulk path, ETL stage or CI workflow; the checkout contains exactly three directories — the root, `blitzy/` and `blitzy/documentation/` — so there is no `.github/workflows/` and no automation descriptor anywhere. Section 6.3.1.2 records that no such path has ever been added in the repository's recorded history.

The execution model is the structural opposite of batch: one invocation processes one datum and terminates. Section 6.2.5.5 makes the precise distinction for the documented workflow — the primary path `W-1` "is two invocations, not one," a `javac` step followed by a `java` step, which is a sequence of two single-item operations rather than a batch with a size, a window or a flush policy.

Three multi-item operations do occur in the project, and none is a batch flow the system defines:

| Bulk operation | Who performs it | Why it is not a batch flow |
|---|---|---|
| Consolidation of all pack objects into a single pack file | `git`, under its default packing behaviour | No `gc.*` or `pack.*` configuration is set anywhere, so the project has made no batching, sizing or scheduling decision (Section 6.2.2.3) |
| `javadoc` HTML generation over the one compilation unit | The operator, by hand, as a documentation-coverage measurement | One input unit, no schedule, no parallelism setting and no throughput target; recorded as persistence point `M-2` in Section 4.3.1.4 |
| Baseline export and comparison against the pre-comment revision | The operator, using `git show` during verification | A read-only derivation from the object store performed once per verification, not a recurring job. Nothing in the repository re-runs it (Section 6.1.4.2) |

#### 6.3.3.5 Error Handling Strategy

There is no message-level error handling, because there is no message and no failure the program can detect. The strategy that operates instead has three layers, developed in full in Sections 5.4.3 and 6.1.4.1 and summarised here from the integration perspective.

| Layer | Mechanism | What it guarantees for this flow |
|---|---|---|
| Program | **Containment by absence.** A keyword census over the five executable lines returns zero occurrences of `try`, `catch`, `throw`, `new`, `System.exit` and `System.err`, and the source contains no query of the output stream's error state | The failure surfaces themselves do not exist. No input is read, no argument dereferenced, no resource opened, no port bound, no network call made and no dependency declared, so no integration fault can arise |
| Toolchain | **Fail-fast at the boundary.** Every interrupting fault is raised by `javac`, `java` or `javadoc` before or instead of entering the program, surfacing as a diagnostic on standard error with a non-zero status | Section 6.1.2.5 records that no state in the `Hello` component has an error transition originating inside the component; a fault stops the workflow rather than degrading the output |
| Operator | **Documented manual recovery.** A deterministic command re-run by hand, guided by the seven-row troubleshooting table at `Project Guide.md` §9.8 | Re-running any documented command is idempotent in effect: the payload is a compile-time constant, `javac` re-derives the same class from the same unchanged unit, and `mktemp -d` yields a fresh directory so a repeat never collides with a previous attempt |

Four error-handling constructs that an integration architecture would normally require are absent, and each absence is structural rather than an omission:

- **No dead-letter path, redelivery or replay.** There is no queue to park a failed message in, and nothing in the flow can partially fail: the write either happens or the process never reached it.
- **No timeout, retry budget, circuit breaker or bulkhead.** Section 6.1.2.5 records that a breaker has nothing to protect — the only call is `println` on an already-open stream, with no failure, error code or timeout to count.
- **No compensating action or rollback.** Section 6.2.3.1 records that the system has no transactional resource, no commit protocol, no two-phase coordination and no rollback log.
- **No notification or escalation channel.** Section 4.3.2.6 records the absence; with no CI gate and no scheduler, escalation is a recorded open item in `Project Guide.md` rather than an automated signal, and the terminal is the only channel on which the operator ever learns an outcome.

The observable outcome of a run is therefore binary and fully specified. `Project Guide.md` §9.7 records the contract as directly observed: `java Hello; echo "exit=$?"` prints the greeting followed by `exit=0` (lines 391-393), and line 388 records `java Hello.java one two three` producing the identical single greeting, confirming that hostile or unexpected arguments cannot reach any code path. The seven faults catalogued as `E-1` through `E-7` in Section 4.3.2.2 all belong to the build, launch, hygiene or verification stage; none is a message-processing or integration fault, because there is no such stage to fail in.

### 6.3.4 External Systems

**No external system is integrated with at run time.** Five external parties participate in the project's lifecycle and Section 5.1.4 records that they exhaust the list, but only one of them is a service, and that one is never contacted by the program. Section 3.4 states the position at stack level: "Exactly one third-party service participates in this system: the Git hosting platform that holds the remote refs. It serves the source-distribution channel and the Markdown rendering; it is not reached by the program at runtime."

The distinction that organises this sub-section is between a *dependency* and an *integration*. The system has real external dependencies — a JDK, a Git client, a hosting platform, a POSIX shell, a licence instrument — every one of which is invoked by an operator or applies to a human reader. It has no integration, because no tracked file opens a connection, resolves an endpoint, authenticates to a counterparty or exchanges a payload with a system it does not own.

**Figure 6.3.4-A — Integration flow: the complete external exchange across the project lifecycle**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Dev as Maintainer or operator
    participant Gitc as git 2.51.0 — client (C-9)
    participant Hub as GitHub remote — service (C-9)
    participant Tool as JDK toolchain 25.0.3 (C-8)
    participant Proc as Process contract (I-3)

    Note over Dev,Hub: Seam I-4 — the only network-bearing exchange in the system, and the program takes no part in it
    Dev->>Gitc: git clone
    Gitc->>Hub: Git smart protocol over HTTPS
    Hub-->>Gitc: 5 tracked blobs, 14 commits, 13 trees, 8 refs, 0 tags
    Gitc-->>Dev: Complete local replica — no credential is conveyed by tracked content

    Note over Dev,Proc: Seams I-1 to I-3 — from here every documented workflow runs offline with zero network egress
    Dev->>Tool: javac Hello.java, then java Hello
    Tool->>Tool: Resolve nothing — no manifest, no classpath entry, no download
    Tool->>Proc: Greeting on fd 1, fd 2 empty, wait status 0
    Proc-->>Dev: Output compared byte for byte against the oracle at README.md lines 59-61

    Note over Dev,Hub: Publication — an operator action, not an application behaviour
    Dev->>Gitc: git commit, then git push
    Gitc->>Hub: Ref update on branch jr_java1
    Hub-->>Dev: Pull-request merge facility — HEAD 2a78292 merged pull request 1
    Note over Hub: Open item — main is 11 commits behind, so the delivery is absent from the default branch
```

#### 6.3.4.1 Third-Party Integration Patterns

**No third-party integration pattern is implemented.** There is no adapter, no anti-corruption layer, no facade over a vendor SDK, no client wrapper, no saga or orchestrator, no ESB, no file-drop exchange and no shared-database integration. The reason is prior to any design choice: `Hello.java` declares **zero `import` statements**, so there is no third-party code in the program to wrap, and the repository has **no dependency manifest** at all, so there is no third party to resolve. `Project Guide.md` line 252 records the consequence directly: "There are no dependencies to resolve: the source imports nothing outside `java.lang`."

Two patterns do genuinely govern how the project relates to the outside world, and both are lifecycle patterns rather than integration patterns:

| Pattern in force | How it operates | Coupling it creates |
|---|---|---|
| **Host-supplied tool invocation** | `javac`, `java` and `javadoc` are invoked from a POSIX shell by the commands `README.md` publishes. Nothing is embedded, vendored or version-pinned | Build-time and launch-time only. `Project Guide.md` line 442 records the version as observed (25.0.3), never enforced, and line 443 records that no `--release` or `--source` setting exists anywhere |
| **Pull-based source conveyance** | Consumers obtain the work by `git clone` from the HTTPS remote; no artifact is published to any registry, and no packaging step exists | Availability-at-clone-time only. Section 5.1.4 records that once cloned, every documented workflow runs entirely offline |

Because there is no third-party code in the program, `Project Guide.md` line 188 records the security consequence as a category that simply does not arise: with no dependency manifest there is "no supply-chain exposure." The one residual supply-chain surface is the operator's own JDK build, which the repository neither records nor constrains, and which Section 3.4.6 identifies as one of only two places where residual third-party risk is concentrated.

#### 6.3.4.2 Legacy System Interfaces

**No legacy system interface exists.** There is no mainframe or midrange connector, no EDI, no fixed-width or COBOL copybook format, no FTP or SFTP file drop, no scheduled extract, no SOAP or WSDL endpoint, no CORBA or RMI stub, no ODBC or JDBC bridge and no screen-scraping or terminal-emulation layer. Section 6.3.1.2 records that the corresponding artifact, source and history censuses all returned zero, and that no such path has ever been added on any branch.

Two things in the repository could be misread as legacy interfaces, and are named here so they are not:

| Artifact | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Backward compatibility with older toolchains** | A property of the invocation contract, not an interface to a legacy system. `Project Guide.md` line 249 records that the compile-then-run path "works on considerably older releases — it was exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21," while `README.md` line 20 records the JDK 11 floor that applies only to the direct source launch. Nothing older is *integrated with*; older runtimes are merely *supported* |
| **`blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md` (component C-7)** | A historical record, not a legacy interface. Section 5.1.2 records it as stale by construction — it documents `Hello.java` as five lines and `README.md` as a 41-byte placeholder, anchoring version 1.0 at commit `0726b1d` — and notes it is "not read by code or tooling" |

#### 6.3.4.3 API Gateway Configuration

**No API gateway, reverse proxy or edge component exists, and there is nothing for one to front.** Every one of the twenty-one named gateway, proxy and contract artifacts existence-tested in Section 6.3.1.2 is absent, including `nginx.conf`, `Caddyfile`, `envoy.yaml`, `kong.yml`, `haproxy.cfg`, `ingress.yaml`, `api-gateway.yml`, `apigateway.tf`, `serverless.yml`, `template.yaml` and `.well-known`. The recursive census for 26 configuration and interface extensions returned zero files across the whole checkout, so there is no descriptor anywhere in which a route, upstream, listener, TLS certificate, CORS policy, auth plugin or rate-limit rule could be declared.

Each capability a gateway would supply is absent for a structural reason that can be traced to an observed fact:

| Gateway capability | Why it cannot apply here |
|---|---|
| Routing and upstream selection | There is no upstream. `Project Guide.md` line 426 records that the program "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call," and Section 6.1.1.1 records that there is no second deployable unit to route to |
| TLS termination and transport security | No listener exists to terminate a connection on. The only TLS in the project is the HTTPS transport `git` itself uses at seam I-4, configured by the Git client rather than by the repository |
| Authentication, authorization and policy enforcement | No principal, credential or protected resource exists (Sections 6.3.2.2 and 6.3.2.3), so there is no decision for a policy engine to make |
| Quota, throttling and traffic shaping | There is no admission point. Section 6.3.2.4 records that work is initiated by an operator rather than arriving, so there is no traffic to shape |
| Observability, request logging and tracing | Section 3.4.4 records that no logging framework, metrics client, tracing instrumentation or APM agent exists anywhere; standard error is empty by design, so there is no request to log |
| Load balancing and health checking | Section 6.1.2.4 records that no load balancer, reverse proxy, ingress controller, service mesh sidecar or DNS arrangement exists, and Section 5.4.1 records that no health, readiness or liveness probe exists |

The only edge in the entire system is the operator's shell session, which Section 6.1.1.3 identifies as "the only scheduler and the only orchestrator in the system."

#### 6.3.4.4 External Service Contracts

Only one of the five external parties is a service; the other four are contracts, tools or legal instruments. The complete external dependency inventory is below, and it is exhaustive at `HEAD` — there is no transitive dependency, no lock file and no vendored library, because there is no manifest to declare one in.

| External dependency | Version observed | Pinned or vendored? |
|---|---|---|
| **JDK toolchain** — `javac`, `java`, `javadoc` (component C-8) | OpenJDK **25.0.3** recorded at `Project Guide.md` lines 255-257 and 442, observed on a Linux host | Neither. `README.md` line 18 records that the repository pins no Java version and carries no file in which one could be recorded |
| **Git client** (component C-9, client side) | **2.51.0**, recorded at `Project Guide.md` line 445 | Neither; needed for cloning and for the baseline comparisons in the verification steps (line 250) |
| **GitHub hosting platform** (component C-9, service side) — `github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java` | Not applicable — a hosted service with no version the repository can observe | Not applicable. The repository "defines no roles, accounts or permissions of its own" (Section 3.4.2) |
| **POSIX shell with GNU `grep`, `diff`, `awk` and `coreutils`** | No version recorded | Neither. Required only "if you intend to run the structural verification commands" (`Project Guide.md` line 251) |
| **GPL v3 licence instrument** — Free Software Foundation, 29 June 2007 | Version 3, carried verbatim in `LICENSE`: 674 lines, 35,149 bytes | **Vendored and pinned** — the verbatim text travels with every copy, with the dated modification notice at `README.md` line 5 |
| **GitHub Flavored Markdown renderer** | GFM over CommonMark, "determined by the hosting platform; no generator or renderer is part of the project" (`Project Guide.md` line 444) | Not applicable — presentation only, read-only, never invoked by the project |
| **Java library dependencies** | **None.** Only the implicitly available `java.lang`; zero imports, zero transitive dependencies, no lock file | Not applicable — nothing is resolved or downloaded before building (`README.md` line 18) |

**No service-level agreement, uptime commitment, latency target or durability guarantee is defined for any of these parties, and none is asserted here.** Section 5.1.4 records that position explicitly for all five. What each contract actually requires, in place of an SLA, is the following:

| External party | What the contract actually requires |
|---|---|
| JDK toolchain | Presence on `PATH` at build and launch time only. No long-running process depends on it, so there is no availability requirement. `javac -Xlint:all -Werror` is the project's entire static-analysis surface, as `Project Guide.md` line 458 records that no linter is configured. **No fallback toolchain exists and none is needed** (Section 6.1.2.6) — if no JDK is present, no documented workflow can proceed |
| Operating-system process contract | That the launching shell connect standard output and observe the exit status. The only stated contract is the output contract itself at `README.md` lines 57-63 |
| GitHub hosting platform | That it hold the branch refs and accept the merge that moves `main` forward — recorded as an open High-priority item, since `main` is 11 commits behind the delivery. Availability is required at clone, fetch and push time only |
| GPL v3 instrument | Verbatim conveyance with every copy and a dated modification notice. A perpetual legal instrument with no operational availability dimension |
| Markdown renderer | Correct presentation of the three Markdown documents, including `README.md`'s two relative links, four fenced blocks and two tables. Never verified against a rendered page; recorded as an open item in Section 3.4.2 |

Two consequences of this contract set bound the system's entire external risk, and both are recorded rather than inferred. First, because the JDK is unpinned, Section 5.1.4 records that a build is reproducible in *behaviour* but not in *toolchain*: two operators on different JDKs both obtain the same greeting and exit status 0, but nothing records or constrains which JDK either used. Second, because no integration is synchronous with a running service, **there is no failure mode in which an external party degrades the program at run time** — every recorded failure mode belongs to the build, launch, hygiene or verification stage and is catalogued as `E-1` through `E-7` in Section 4.3.2.2. Section 3.4.6 concludes that residual third-party risk is therefore concentrated in exactly two places the repository does not control: the hosting platform's own access control, and the unpinned JDK build the operator installs.

### 6.3.5 Reassessment Triggers and Cross-Section References

The determination in Section 6.3.1 is a statement about the repository at commit `2a78292` on branch `jr_java1`, not a permanent property of the project. This sub-section records the specific, observable changes that would invalidate it, so that a future reader can test the verdict rather than re-derive it, and then maps the related material elsewhere in this specification.

#### 6.3.5.1 Changes That Would Make Integration Architecture Applicable

Each trigger below maps to one of the six failed preconditions in Section 6.3.1.1. Any single one occurring would require this sub-section to be rewritten as a substantive integration architecture rather than amended.

| Trigger | Failed precondition it would satisfy | Sub-section that would need content |
|---|---|---|
| Any listener construct enters the source — `ServerSocket`, `HttpServer`, a servlet, a framework route or a handler registration | P1 — an inbound interface a foreign caller can reach | 6.3.2.1 protocols; 6.3.2.2 authentication; 6.3.2.4 rate limiting; 6.3.4.3 gateway |
| `Hello.java`, or a second compilation unit, gains an `import` of `java.net`, `java.net.http`, `javax.net`, `java.rmi`, `java.sql` or any client SDK package | P2 — an outbound call to a system the program does not own | 6.3.2.1 protocols; 6.3.2.5 versioning; 6.3.3.5 error handling |
| A broker, queue or stream client appears — JMS, Kafka, RabbitMQ, AMQP, MQTT, Redis Streams or a cloud messaging SDK | P3 — a message, event or stream substrate | 6.3.3.1 event patterns; 6.3.3.2 queue architecture; 6.3.3.3 stream processing |
| A contract artifact appears — `openapi.*`, `swagger.*`, `asyncapi.*`, `*.wsdl`, `*.proto`, `*.avsc`, `*.thrift` or `schema.graphql` | P4 — a described interface to a counterparty | 6.3.2.6 documentation standards; 6.3.4.4 external service contracts |
| Any configuration file appears (`*.properties`, `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.json`, `*.xml`, `*.toml`, `*.ini`, `.env`) carrying an endpoint, host, port or credential, **or** any tracked file begins reading an environment variable | P5 — a place to configure an endpoint, credential or connection | 6.3.2.2 authentication; 6.3.2.3 authorization; 6.3.4.4 external contracts |
| A proxy, gateway or ingress descriptor appears — `nginx.conf`, `envoy.yaml`, `kong.yml`, `haproxy.cfg`, `ingress.yaml` — or a container or orchestration manifest that publishes a port | P1 and P6 — an edge component and a reachable host | 6.3.4.3 gateway configuration; 6.3.2.4 rate limiting |
| A dependency manifest appears (`pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts`) declaring any client, transport or serialisation library | P2 — a third-party integration surface and the project's first supply-chain exposure | 6.3.4.1 third-party patterns; 6.3.4.4 external contracts |
| A scheduler, timer, daemon loop or CI workflow definition appears | P3 and P6 — an automated trigger and a resident process | 6.3.3.1 event patterns; 6.3.3.4 batch flows |

Two further changes would not make integration architecture applicable but would require material in this sub-section to be revised, because they would alter the seams it documents:

- **A `package` declaration on `Hello.java`.** Bare-name class resolution depends on its absence, so adding one would invalidate every launch command in `README.md` and therefore every invocation form specified in Section 6.3.2. Section 6.1.2.3 records the same constraint from the discovery perspective.
- **A `.gitignore`, `.gitattributes` or first tag.** These would convert the currently documented-but-unenforced hygiene and SHA-anchored versioning positions referenced in Sections 6.3.2.5 and 6.3.2.6 into explicit policy; Section 6.2.6.1 records the equivalent effect on the data-layer material.

### 6.3.6 References

No external or web source was consulted for this sub-section. Every claim above derives from the repository checkout at commit `2a78292` on branch `jr_java1`, from direct measurement of that checkout, or from an explicitly attributed statement in a tracked documentation file.

## 6.4 Security Architecture

### 6.4.1 Applicability Assessment

**Detailed Security Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

At commit `2a78292` on branch `jr_java1` the repository tracks five files, of which exactly one is executable code: `Hello.java`, 20 lines and 1,073 bytes, declaring one public class in the default package whose only member is `main(String[] args)`. Stripping comments leaves five executable lines, and the entirety of the program's behaviour is the single statement at line 17 — `System.out.println("Hello from Java!")`. There is consequently no principal to authenticate, no session to maintain, no token to validate, no role to assign, no resource to authorise access to, no secret to hold, no confidential datum to encrypt and no network interface to defend.

A single case-insensitive census over `Hello.java` covering more than sixty authentication, authorisation, cryptographic, credential, reflection, deserialisation, process-spawning, logging and input-reading markers returned exactly **two** matches, both incidental English words inside comments — "console" in the class Javadoc at line 2 and "signature" in the `@param` text at line 11 — and **zero** matches over the five executable lines. The same file declares zero `import` statements and no `package` statement, so the only library surface available to it is the implicitly imported `java.lang`.

The determination denies a *bespoke* security architecture. It does not claim the absence of security-relevant behaviour, and this sub-section documents the behaviour that genuinely exists: a set of controls inherited from the operating system, the JVM, the Git hosting platform and a licence instrument; exactly one mechanism deliberately selected by the repository; one machine credential that lives outside the tracked tree; and one legal obligation that travels with every copy. Section 5.3.6 records the design position that produces this shape — the security architecture is "attack-surface elimination rather than control selection" — and `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §6, line 188, states the basis in the repository's own words: the program "reads no input, dereferences no argument, opens no resource, binds no port, makes no network call and has no dependency manifest, so there is no injection surface, no supply-chain exposure, no authentication or authorisation surface and no data-at-rest concern."

Declaring non-applicability does not discharge the areas the specification calls for. Each is addressed in turn in Sections 6.4.2 through 6.4.5 and labelled as exactly one of:

- **Genuinely absent** — no corresponding surface exists anywhere in the system, so the control cannot be applied and its absence is structural rather than an omission.
- **Inherited** — the control is in force but supplied by the host, the JVM, the hosting platform or the licence, not implemented by anything in the repository.
- **Selected** — the repository itself chose the mechanism and states the reason; only one control and one gate fall into this class.
- **Absent and expected** — a control a reviewer would reasonably expect of a maintained project that is missing; each is carried into the residual-risk register in Section 6.4.5.3.

Section 6.4.6 records the observable changes that would invalidate this verdict.

#### 6.4.1.1 Preconditions Tested

Each precondition for a conventional security architecture was tested against the checkout rather than assumed absent. All six fail.

| # | Precondition | Verified result |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | A principal exists whose identity the system can receive and evaluate | **Fails.** There is no input channel of any kind. `args` appears only in the Javadoc `@param` at line 11 and in the signature at line 15 — never in an executable statement — and the census found no `System.in`, `Scanner`, `BufferedReader`, `System.getenv`, `System.getProperty`, file read or socket anywhere |
| P2 | A protected resource exists that an authorisation decision could govern | **Fails.** The program's only sink is standard output, a descriptor it inherits rather than opens; the comment at line 16 fixes this as a design property — "no other sink is written." Nothing is written to a file, a port or a store |
| P3 | A secret, key or credential exists that the system must hold or present | **Fails.** A recursive search for `*.jks`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.crt`, `*.cer`, `*.der`, `*.asc`, `*.gpg`, `*.sig`, `id_rsa*`, `*.keystore` and `*.truststore` returns zero files; `Project Guide.md` Appendix E records that "No other variable and no secret is read by any tracked file" and that `JAVA_HOME` is not required |
| P4 | A confidential, personal or regulated datum is processed | **Fails.** The sole datum is a 16-character public compile-time string literal, republished verbatim as an operator-facing oracle in the fenced block at `README.md` lines 59–61. No personal, payment, health or customer datum is read, derived, stored or transmitted |
| P5 | A place exists in which a security policy could be expressed | **Fails.** There is no configuration file of any format anywhere in the checkout, no `SECURITY.md`, no `CODEOWNERS`, no policy file and no dependency manifest. On the toolchain the repository records as used, the JVM's own policy mechanism is permanently disabled (Section 6.4.3.4) |
| P6 | A trust boundary is crossed while the program runs | **Fails.** Section 5.1.1.3 records the trust and authentication boundary as verified absent, alongside the network and persistence boundaries. The only network-bearing exchange in the whole project is Git conveyance, performed by a separate tool before and after the program runs |

#### 6.4.1.2 Security-Surface Census

Absence was established at three independent levels, so that a negative result at one level cannot be an artifact of where the search was pointed.

| Level of search | What was tested | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Artifact level | Thirty-two existence probes for governance, disclosure, review, scanning and secret-bearing artifacts — `SECURITY.md`, `.github/SECURITY.md`, `CODEOWNERS`, `.github/CODEOWNERS`, `.github/dependabot.yml`, `.github/workflows`, `.github`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `.snyk`, `.semgrep.yml`, `.trivyignore`, `sonar-project.properties`, `.gitleaks.toml`, `.secrets.baseline`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `bom.xml`, `sbom.json`, `sbom.spdx.json`, `.well-known`, `.well-known/security.txt`, `.mailmap`, `.allowed_signers`, `.gitsigners`, `GOVERNANCE.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`, `NOTICE`, `.npmrc`, `.netrc`, `.env`, `.env.example` — followed by a recursive key-material search over seventeen filename patterns | **All thirty-two absent; zero key-material files.** The checkout contains exactly three directories (root, `blitzy/`, `blitzy/documentation/`), no hidden dotfile other than `.git`, and zero symbolic links |
| Source level | All `.java` content searched for `package` and `import` declarations, then for the full security marker set: `java.security`, `javax.crypto`, `javax.net`, `javax.security`, `SecureRandom`, `MessageDigest`, `Cipher`, `KeyStore`, `KeyPair`, `SecretKey`, `Signature`, `SSLContext`, `SSLSocket`, `TrustManager`, `HttpsURLConnection`, `Base64`, `Principal`, `Subject`, `LoginContext`, `LoginModule`, `Callback`, `AccessController`, `doPrivileged`, `SecurityManager`, `Permission`, `Policy`, `ProtectionDomain`, `Class.forName`, `getDeclaredField`, `setAccessible`, `Method.invoke`, `Proxy`, `ObjectInputStream`, `ObjectOutputStream`, `readObject`, `writeObject`, `Serializable`, `Runtime.getRuntime`, `ProcessBuilder`, `exec(`, `System.getenv`, `System.getProperty`, `Properties`, `Logger`, `log4j`, `slf4j`, `java.util.logging`, `Console`, `readPassword`, `Scanner`, `System.in`, `BufferedReader`, `InputStream`, `char[]`, `password`, `secret`, `token`, `credential`, `api_key`, `auth` | **Zero declarations and zero functional matches.** The only hits were the two incidental comment words named above |
| History level | `git log --all --diff-filter=A --name-only` enumerated every path ever added on any branch, then `git grep` ran a fourteen-pattern credential set (`ghp_`, `gho_`, `ghu_`, `ghs_`, `ghr_`, `github_pat_`, `x-access-token`, `AKIA`, `ASIA`, `AIza`, `xox[baprs]-`, `sk-…`, `-----BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY-----`, `Bearer …`, `eyJ…`) across **every blob of every commit** | **Only the five known paths have ever been added on any branch, and no credential value exists in any blob of any commit.** The pattern set matches only prose in `blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications.md`, where the archived specification names the pattern classes without reproducing a value |

The history-level result is the decisive one: no security control was removed, stubbed out or deferred. No security, key, policy or scanner artifact has ever been present in this repository's recorded history.

#### 6.4.1.3 Standard Security Practices Followed Instead

These are the practices the system relies on in place of a designed security architecture. None is implemented by code in the repository; each was verified in the state described.

| Standard practice | How it is satisfied here | Evidence class |
|---|---|---|
| Least privilege by default | The process requests no privileged resource: no port, no file write, no environment read, no elevated capability. No setuid, setgid or executable regular file exists anywhere in the worktree | Measured here; runs as an unprivileged account recorded in the archived specification |
| Minimal attack surface by design | Every inbound channel is inert, so there is no parser, decoder or interpreter to attack. Arguments containing shell metacharacters, command substitution, path traversal, format specifiers, a script tag, a SQL tautology, a template expression and NUL bytes all produced byte-identical output with exit status 0 | Recorded — `Project Guide.md` §4; archived specification §6.4.6.1 |
| No secrets in version control | The tracked tree carries source, licence and documentation only; the working credential lives in the clone's untracked `.git/config`. No credential pattern occurs in any blob of any commit | Measured here (Section 6.4.1.2) |
| Encryption in transit on the only network channel | Git conveyance runs over HTTPS with server-certificate verification left at the client default (`http.sslVerify` unset) | Measured here for configuration; TLS 1.3 handshake recorded in the archived specification |
| Content-addressed integrity and tamper evidence | Every object is identified by its SHA-1 content hash; re-hashing `Hello.java` reproduces the stored blob id `3fd76ce8…` exactly, and `git fsck` reports no error and exits 0 | Measured here |
| Discretionary access control on artifacts | Standard POSIX permissions with no privilege-escalation bit: all five tracked files are mode `644` on disk and `100644` in the index; there is no symlink and no submodule entry | Measured here |
| Attributable, append-only change history | Fourteen commits, each carrying author identity and an ISO-8601 timestamp, in a content-addressed store that every clone replicates in full | Measured here (Section 6.4.3.5) |
| Dependency-free, offline-capable build | Nothing is fetched at build time, so there is no resolution step to compromise: no manifest exists in which a dependency could be declared, and `README.md` line 18 records that "nothing has to be resolved or downloaded before building" | Measured here; `README.md` line 18 |
| Safe-by-construction operator commands | The one command that writes to the filesystem directs its output into a freshly generated, owner-readable-only directory, with the threat rationale stated beside it | Selected mechanism — `README.md` line 30 (Sections 6.4.3.3 and 6.4.5.2) |
| Explicit warranty and liability position | GPL v3 §§15–17 disclaim warranty, limit liability and govern the interpretation of both | `LICENSE` lines 589, 600 and 612 |

Four practices a reviewer would expect are **absent and expected**, and each is carried forward as a residual risk in Section 6.4.5.3: there is **no vulnerability-disclosure path** (no `SECURITY.md` and no contact address in any tracked file), **no code-review or ownership gate** expressed in the repository (no `CODEOWNERS`, and no branch-protection artifact is observable from a clone), **no dependency or toolchain pinning** (ADR-007 records versions and pins none), and **no automated scanning, SBOM or patch-management configuration** of any kind.

#### 6.4.1.4 Security Zones and Trust Boundaries

The system spans five zones. None of them is a network zone in the conventional sense, and only one boundary crossing carries traffic off the host.

| Zone | Contents | Isolation mechanism in force |
|---|---|---|
| **Z-1 Public distribution zone** | The hosting remote `github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java` holding 8 refs at 3 distinct commits and zero tags, plus the platform's Markdown renderer | Owned entirely by the hosting platform. The repository "defines no roles, accounts or permissions of its own" (Section 3.4.2); read is anonymous, write is token-gated |
| **Z-2 Operator host** | The shell session, the `git` client that holds the only credential in its untracked `.git/config`, and the host-supplied JDK | Operating-system process and account isolation. The program requests no privilege and no capability |
| **Z-3 Checkout working tree** | The five tracked files, all mode `644` on disk and `100644` in the index, in three directories | POSIX discretionary access control under umask `0022`. No executable bit, no symlink, no setuid or setgid file |
| **Z-4 Per-run scratch build directory** | The compiler's output `Hello.class` — untracked, re-derivable, never committed and never published | `mktemp -d`, verified here to create the directory with mode `2700`, owner-only access. This is the system's one selected security mechanism (ADR-009) |
| **Z-5 JVM process** | One frame of `Hello.main`, one string constant, one write to file descriptor 1 | Process boundary only. No in-JVM sandbox exists or can exist on the recorded toolchain (Section 6.4.3.4) |

| Crossing | What crosses it | Control in force |
|---|---|---|
| **B-1 Z-2 ⇄ Z-1 — Git conveyance** | Git objects and refs: five tracked blobs, 14 commits, 13 trees | The only network crossing in the system. HTTPS with client-default certificate verification; anonymous read; write presents a machine token (Section 6.4.2.4). Performed by `git`, never by the program |
| **B-2 Z-3 → Z-2 — compilation input** | One compilation unit read by `javac` | Filesystem read permission only. Nothing is resolved, downloaded or executed from the tree |
| **B-3 Z-2 → Z-4 — artifact emission** | The 420-byte class file written outside the checkout | The unique owner-readable-only destination; removes the predictable-path exposure that `README.md` line 30 names |
| **B-4 Z-4 → Z-5 — class loading** | The class bytes placed on the classpath and resolved by bare name | JVM class resolution. One class is loaded from the application classpath; there is no agent, plug-in, service loader or reflective load |
| **B-5 Z-5 → Z-2 — process output** | 16 ASCII characters plus one platform line separator on file descriptor 1; descriptor 2 empty; wait status 0 | Inherited descriptor, fire-and-forget, with no reply channel and no acknowledgement (Section 5.1.4) |
