#### 6.5.1.5 Scope and Verification Environment

Three constraints on the evidence in this section should be stated so its claims can be weighted correctly, and they follow the convention Section 6.4.1.5 establishes.

| Constraint | Consequence for this section |
|---|---|
| **No JDK is installed** in the environment used to verify the repository — `java`, `javac` and `javadoc` are absent from `PATH`, and `/usr/bin/time` is likewise absent | No run, timing measurement, exit-status capture or `javadoc` warning count could be produced first-hand. Every runtime figure quoted here — the 17-byte payload, the empty error stream, exit status 0, the single implicit-constructor warning and the 49-of-49 check record — is attributed to `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` as **recorded** evidence on OpenJDK 25.0.3 |
| Git and standard POSIX text tooling are present | All repository-state findings are **first-hand**: the 109 artifact probes, the telemetry-data search, the 64-marker source census, the strict service-level census, the history check across every branch, the tracked inventory and index modes, and the reflog and ref/tag counts |
| No service-level figure, threshold or capacity target exists in any tracked file | This section defines none. Where the prompt calls for SLA requirements, thresholds or capacity figures, what is documented is the **contract** the repository actually publishes and the **absence** of any target, never an invented number (Sections 6.5.3.4, 6.5.3.6 and 6.5.3.5) |

The one untracked file in the working tree, `tech_spec.md`, is an authoring artifact of the documentation process. It is not tracked, is not a system file, and is excluded from every census and figure above.


### 6.5.2 Monitoring Infrastructure

No monitoring infrastructure exists in this repository, and no component capable of hosting one is present. This sub-section addresses each infrastructure concern the specification calls for, records what plays the corresponding role in an invoke-and-exit console application, and states what is verifiably absent.

#### 6.5.2.1 Metrics Collection

**Genuinely absent.** The program emits no metric. There is no counter, gauge, histogram, summary or timer; no `MeterRegistry`, `CollectorRegistry` or exporter; no JMX or `ManagementFactory` access; no JFR event; and no timing call of any kind — the 64-marker census in Section 6.5.1 found no `System.nanoTime`, `System.currentTimeMillis`, `Instant.now` or `Duration.` reference anywhere in `Hello.java`. With no listener there is also nothing to scrape: `Project Guide.md` Appendix B records that the program "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call," so no pull-based collector could reach it and no push-based client exists to send.

A collection pipeline would need five elements. None exists, and the absence is structural at each step.

| Pipeline element | Capability it would require | Observed state |
|---|---|---|
| Instrumentation | A metric instrument created and updated in application code | Absent. One API call exists in the whole program, `System.out.println` at line 17, and it emits the product rather than a measurement |
| Exposition | An endpoint, agent or push client able to surface samples | Absent. No port is bound, no agent jar is present (`opentelemetry-javaagent.jar`, `newrelic.jar`, `dd-java-agent.jar` and `jmx_exporter.yml` all probed absent), and JMX remote is unconfigured |
| Collection | A scraper, collector or forwarder with a target list | Absent. `prometheus.yml`, `otel-collector-config.yaml`, `statsd.conf`, `telegraf.conf` and `collectd.conf` are all absent, and no configuration file of any format exists in which a target could be declared |
| Storage | A time-series database or metric store | Absent. Section 6.2 records that no runtime path reaches durable media; the recursive telemetry-data search returns zero `*.prom`, `*.tsdb`, `*.jfr` or `*.hprof` files |
| Retention and aggregation | A downsampling, roll-up or retention rule | Absent. No sample is ever produced, so there is nothing to retain |

What the project has instead is a set of **counted quantities recorded by hand**. They are structural measurements of the artifact rather than runtime metrics: each has a single recorded value rather than a series, no timestamp beyond the document that carries it, and no collection mechanism at all. They are reproduced here as recorded, because no figure in this section is re-derived without the toolchain that produced it.

| Recorded quantity | Value as recorded | Source of record |
|---|---|---|
| Verification checks executed / passed / failed | 49 / 49 / 0 — 37 acceptance assertions plus 12 direct toolchain checks | `Project Guide.md` §3, on OpenJDK 25.0.3 |
| Compiler diagnostics, including under `-Xlint:all -Werror` | 0 | `Project Guide.md` §3, §9.4 |
| `javadoc` warnings | Exactly 1, for the implicit default constructor at `Hello.java:6` | `Project Guide.md` §9.6 |
| Documentation coverage | 2 of 3 documentable members; the third cannot carry a doc comment | `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Standard-output payload size | 16 ASCII characters plus one platform line separator — 17 bytes observed on an LF host | `Project Guide.md` §4; `README.md` lines 57–63 |
| Standard-error volume | 0 bytes on every run | `README.md` line 63 |
| Process exit status | 0, by normal return rather than `System.exit` | `README.md` line 63; `Project Guide.md` §9.7 |
| Compiled artifact size and instruction count | 420 bytes; `main` is four bytecode instructions | Section 5.4.5 |
| Cross-release compilation checks | Release targets 11, 17 and 21 exercised, 7 checks, all passed | `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Source footprint | 1 file, 20 lines, 1,073 bytes, 5 executable lines, 1 statement | Measured first-hand in the checkout |

#### 6.5.2.2 Log Aggregation

**Genuinely absent, and the distinction that makes it absent is deliberate.** `System.out.println` at line 17 emits the deliverable payload, not a diagnostic record; Section 5.4.2 states the position as "the program's single write is its product, not its log," and the line comment at line 16 fixes single-sink behaviour as a design property. There is no logging framework — the seventeen logging and shipping artifacts probed in Section 6.5.6.2 are all absent and the source declares zero imports — so there is no log level, formatter, appender, correlation identifier or structured record to aggregate, and nothing is written to storage from which an aggregator could read.

| Aggregation concern | Position at `HEAD` |
|---|---|
| Log producer | None. No `Logger`, `java.util.logging`, SLF4J, Log4j or Logback reference; `System.err` occurs zero times, so even the conventional diagnostic stream is deliberately silent |
| Log destination | The operator's terminal, and only for the duration of the run. Whether the bytes reach a terminal, a pipe or a redirect is decided outside the system boundary — the descriptor is inherited, never opened |
| Collection agent | None. `fluentd.conf`, `fluent-bit.conf`, `filebeat.yml`, `vector.toml`, `promtail.yaml`, `logstash.conf`, `rsyslog.conf` and `syslog-ng.conf` all probed absent |
| Index, search and storage tier | None. No log store, no `kibana.yml`, and zero `*.log` files anywhere in the checkout |
| Rotation, retention and shipping policy | None, and nothing to apply one to |
| Structured or correlated logging | None. No request identifier, correlation identifier or trace context exists, because there is no request and no hop to correlate (Section 5.4.2) |
| Toolchain diagnostics | The only error-stream traffic in the system originates outside the program: `javac` diagnostics (zero at `HEAD`), `java` launch failures, and the single expected `javadoc` warning. They are transient terminal output, not collected anywhere |
| Durable event record | **Inherited from Git.** 14 commit objects carry author identity and ISO-8601 timestamps in an append-only, content-addressed store that every clone replicates. `core.logallrefupdates` is `true` and `.git/logs/HEAD` records ref movements, but the reflog is untracked — `git ls-files .git/logs/HEAD` returns zero entries — so it is conveyed by no clone |
| Durable record of any observation | `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3 and §4, written by hand. Section 5.4.2 records the consequence: "auditability is documentary, not automatic" |

#### 6.5.2.3 Distributed Tracing

**Genuinely absent, and not applicable in principle.** Tracing correlates work as it crosses process, service or thread boundaries; this system has no boundary to cross. Section 5.4.2 states it exactly — "One process, one frame, one write — there is no span boundary anywhere in the system."

| Tracing element | Requirement it would need | Observed state |
|---|---|---|
| Tracer and span creation | An SDK and a span around a unit of work | Absent. No `OpenTelemetry`, `Tracer`, `Span`, `SpanBuilder` or `jdk.jfr` reference; the six tracing artifacts probed are absent |
| Trace and span identifiers | An identifier generated per operation | Absent. No `TraceId`, `SpanId` or `Baggage` reference, and no identifier of any kind is generated — the program allocates nothing itself |
| Context propagation | A carrier (header, envelope, thread-local) crossing a boundary | Absent. There is no network call, no message, no thread creation and no second frame; Section 6.1.2.2 records in-process invocation as the only mechanism in the system |
| Sampling policy | A rate or head/tail decision | Absent, and vacuous: a single deterministic execution has nothing to sample |
| Trace backend and UI | A collector and a query surface | Absent. `jaeger.yaml`, `zipkin.yml` and `tracing.yaml` probed absent; no service exists to receive spans |
| Causal record that does exist | — | The Git commit graph, which is a causal record of *changes* rather than of executions: 14 commits, append-only, content-addressed (Section 6.4.3.5) |

#### 6.5.2.4 Alert Management

**Absent and expected.** No alert rule, threshold expression, evaluator, receiver, silence, inhibition rule or paging integration exists: `alertmanager.yml`, `alerts.yml`, `alert.rules`, `rules.yml`, `pagerduty.yml`, `opsgenie.yml`, `slack.yml`, `statuspage.yml`, `uptime.yml` and `healthchecks.yml` are all absent, and there is no configuration file of any format in which a rule could be written. More fundamentally, Section 4.3.2.6 records the absence of a notification channel of any kind — there is nothing on which an alert could be raised even if a rule existed, a limitation Section 5.4.1 states as "there is no notification channel of any kind on which a failure could be raised."

| Alert-management element | Requirement it would need | Observed state |
|---|---|---|
| Rule definition | A file expressing a condition over a signal | Absent. No rule file, and no signal series to express a condition over |
| Evaluation engine | A process evaluating rules on a schedule | Absent. Nothing runs unattended: no CI descriptor, cron entry, systemd timer or active Git hook (ADR-002) |
| Notification channel | An email, chat, webhook or pager route | Absent (Section 4.3.2.6). The operator's terminal is the only signal channel in the system |
| Receiver and routing tree | A mapping from condition to recipient | Absent. Section 6.5.4.1 documents what replaces it: a single implicit route from the terminal to the person who typed the command |
| Deduplication, grouping, silencing | State carried between evaluations | Absent. Nothing persists between runs, so nothing can be deduplicated or silenced |
| Conditions that *are* defined | An expected result per documented command | **Selected.** `Project Guide.md` Appendix A pairs every command with its expected result, and §9.6 pairs every verification step with its expected value. Any deviation from a published expectation is the system's entire alert vocabulary — it is evaluated by a human, at the moment of the run, and nowhere else |

#### 6.5.2.5 Dashboard Design

**Genuinely absent.** There is no dashboard, panel, time-series visualisation, status page or metric UI, and no artifact capable of defining one: `grafana.ini`, `grafana-dashboard.json`, `dashboard.json`, `dashboards/` and `kibana.yml` are all absent. There is also nothing to plot — no series exists, because no sample is ever collected (Section 6.5.2.1) — and no UI in which to render it: `Project Guide.md` §4 records the program as "a console application with no user interface, no hosted page, no bound port and no external integration."

What functions as the project's review surface is static, text-based and read on demand rather than refreshed. Three published views make up the whole of it, and their arrangement is documented as a layout in Section 6.5.5.1.

| Review view | What it presents | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Command and expectation view | Nine commands, each paired with the exact result an operator should see — compile, launch, coverage, strict static check, change inspection, clean-tree check | `Project Guide.md` Appendix A |
| Verification procedure view | The ordered checks with their expected values — `javadoc` warning count, baseline parity via `cmp`, comment census `added=15 /**=2 */=2 //=2`, byte-format census `lf=20 cr=20 crlf=20`, guide-structure counts | `Project Guide.md` §9.6 |
| Fault and resolution view | Seven symptom / cause / resolution rows covering every fault an operator can encounter | `Project Guide.md` §9.8 |
| Result-of-record view | The check tally (49/49/0) by area, the runtime-validation checklist, and the risk register with severities and statuses | `Project Guide.md` §3, §4, §6 |

The one rendering dependency worth recording is that these views are Markdown: `Project Guide.md` §3 lists the rendered appearance of the documentation among the things never exercised, so the review surface itself is asserted against its source text rather than against a rendered page.

#### 6.5.2.6 Monitoring Architecture

The architecture below is the complete monitoring picture for this system. Every signal in it is transient, every comparison is made by a human against a published oracle, and the only durable record is the Git object store and the hand-written evidence in `Project Guide.md`.

**Figure 6.5.2-A — Monitoring architecture: the observable surface, the expectation set it is compared against, and the monitoring infrastructure verified absent**

Two properties of this architecture are worth stating plainly. First, **the collection tier and the evaluation tier are the same human**: there is no agent between the signal and the judgement, which is why every check in Section 6.5.1.3 is a comparison against a published expectation rather than a query over stored data. Second, **the signal is gone the moment the run ends** — Section 6.4.3.5 records that nothing captures that an execution occurred — so the architecture has no retrospective capability at all, and the evidence in `Project Guide.md` §3 is the one thing that survives a run.


### 6.5.3 Observability Patterns

Observability in this system is achieved by **comparison rather than instrumentation**: the program's entire contract is expressible in three values, so an operator establishes correctness by comparing those values against published oracles instead of querying collected telemetry. Section 5.4.1 records the same position and supplies the observables table this sub-section develops into per-pattern detail.

#### 6.5.3.1 Health Checks

**No health-check endpoint, liveness probe, readiness probe, startup probe or heartbeat exists**, and none can: there is no listener to answer a probe and no resident process to probe. The sixty-four-marker census found no `health`, `healthz`, `readiness`, `liveness` or `heartbeat` reference in `Hello.java`; `Dockerfile`, Compose, Kubernetes, `healthcheck.sh` and `healthchecks.yml` are all absent; and `Project Guide.md` §9.5 states "There is no service to start — the program writes one line and exits."

What functions as the health check is **running the program and comparing the three process observables**, plus three supporting checks on the build, the documentation and the checkout. Each is a documented command with a published expected result; each is run by a human on demand.

| Health check | Command | Expected signal — anything else is a failure |
|---|---|---|
| Program health (primary) | `java Hello; echo "exit=$?"` | `Hello from Java!` plus one platform line separator on standard output, an empty standard error, and `exit=0` (`Project Guide.md` §9.7) |
| Output-contract conformance | Capture standard output and compare against `README.md` lines 59–61 | Byte-identical to the fenced oracle; 17 bytes on an LF host (`Project Guide.md` §4) |
| Launch-path equivalence | `java Hello.java` compared with `java -cp "$B" Hello` | Byte-identical standard output from both paths; the source launch leaves no class file (`README.md` line 46) |
| Build health | `javac -Xlint:all -Werror -d "$B" Hello.java` | Exit 0, no diagnostics, empty error stream (`Project Guide.md` Appendix A) |
| Documentation health | `javadoc -d "$B/jd" -quiet Hello.java` | Exit 0 with exactly one warning, for the implicit default constructor at `Hello.java:6` |
| Checkout health | `git status --short` and `git ls-files` | No output from the first; the five tracked paths from the second |
| Regression health against a baseline | Compile revision `0726b1d`, run both builds, `cmp` both captured streams | "behaviour identical" — standard output, standard error and exit status all match the pre-comment build (`Project Guide.md` §9.6) |

Two properties distinguish this from a conventional health model. The check is **binary and total** rather than graded: Section 6.1.4.5 records that the architecture admits no degraded mode, so either the full contract is met or the workflow never reached the program. And the check is **synchronous with intent** — it runs only when a human runs it, so there is no interval, no timeout, no flap detection and no historical availability series.

#### 6.5.3.2 Performance Metrics

**No performance metric is collected, and no timing measurement of any kind is recorded in any tracked file.** Section 5.4.5 states the position for the specification as a whole; the strict census in Section 6.5.1.1 confirms zero occurrences of latency, throughput, percentile, response-time or millisecond vocabulary in `Hello.java`, `README.md` and `LICENSE`.

What exists is a set of **structural baselines** — size and quality quantities, not performance targets. They are reported as recorded, with the measurement source named, and no figure is asserted that the repository does not carry.

| Performance-adjacent quantity | Definition | Recorded value |
|---|---|---|
| Work per invocation | Bytecode instructions executed in `main` | 4 — `getstatic`, `ldc`, `invokevirtual`, `return` (Section 5.4.5) |
| Output volume per invocation | Bytes written to file descriptor 1 | 16 ASCII characters plus one platform separator — 17 bytes on an LF host, 18 on a CRLF host |
| Error-stream volume per invocation | Bytes written to file descriptor 2 | 0 on every run |
| Deployable artifact size | Size of the compiled class | 420 bytes |
| Compilation input size | Size of the single compilation unit | 1,073 bytes, 20 lines, 5 executable lines |
| Dependency-resolution cost | Artifacts fetched at build time | 0 — no manifest exists and nothing is downloaded (`README.md` line 18) |
| Allocation performed by the program | Objects allocated in application code | 0 — one compile-time string constant, no loop, no branch |
| Start-up latency, wall-clock runtime, CPU and memory | — | **Not measured anywhere.** Section 5.4.5 records that runtime cost is dominated by JVM start-up rather than by anything the program does, "a characteristic the repository notes nowhere and measures nowhere" |
| Launch-path cost difference | Compile-then-run versus single-file source launch | **Not quantified.** Compile-then-run pays compilation once; the source launch recompiles in memory per run. Outputs are byte-identical, which is why the choice is operational rather than performance-driven |

#### 6.5.3.3 Business Metrics

**The program transacts no business, so it emits no business metric.** There is no user, no order, no session, no conversion and no revenue event: the program reads no input, serves no request and stores nothing. No business event is counted, emitted or aggregated anywhere in the repository.

The project does, however, record **delivery and documentation-quality measures** — the closest thing it has to a business-outcome view, all of them hand-counted in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` and all of them point-in-time.

| Delivery measure | Recorded value | Where recorded |
|---|---|---|
| Overall completion | 84.2% complete — 32.0 of 38.0 hours, 6.0 remaining | `Project Guide.md` §1.2 |
| Functionalities documented | 4 of 4 commented, one comment per written functionality | `Project Guide.md` §8 (line 241) |
| Guide sections delivered | 8 of 8 present, in the required order | `Project Guide.md` §8 |
| Changes highlighted in the summary | 2 of 2 | `Project Guide.md` §8 |
| Observable behaviours documented | 3 of 3 — standard output, standard error, exit status | `Project Guide.md` §8 |
| Documentable-member coverage | 2 of 3; the implicit constructor cannot carry a doc comment | `Project Guide.md` §3, §8 |
| Verification outcome | 49 checks executed, 49 passed, 0 failed | `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Open items outstanding | 11 unresolved items, with a two-hour critical path | `Project Guide.md` §1.4, §8 |

None of these is emitted by software, none is collected on a schedule, and none has a series behind it. They are counted once, written into prose, and go stale the moment the repository changes — which is the same limitation Section 5.4.2 records for every observation in this system.

#### 6.5.3.4 SLA Monitoring

**The repository defines no service-level agreement, no service-level objective, no error budget and no availability target, and none is asserted here.** Section 5.4.5 records the position explicitly: "no latency target, no throughput figure, no availability objective, no capacity plan, no error budget and no timing measurement of any kind" appears in any tracked file. The strict census in Section 6.5.1.1 independently confirms zero hits for `SLA`, `SLO`, `service level`, `availability`, `uptime`, `MTTR`, `MTBF`, `RTO` and `RPO` across `Hello.java`, `README.md` and `LICENSE`. There is consequently nothing to monitor an SLA against, no compliance percentage to compute and no burn rate to track.

What the repository does publish is a **conformance contract** and, in the licence, an explicit **disclaimer of any service commitment**. Both are documented here because they are what an operator or a downstream consumer can actually rely on.

| Published commitment | What it obliges | Where published |
|---|---|---|
| Standard-output content | The literal `Hello from Java!` followed by exactly one platform line separator, byte-identical across both launch paths | `README.md` lines 57–63, with the fenced oracle at lines 59–61 |
| Standard-error content | Empty on every run | `README.md` line 63 |
| Termination behaviour | Exit status 0, produced by normal return from `main` with no `System.exit` — "a deliberate property of the program rather than an omission" | `README.md` line 63; `Hello.java` line 18 |
| Argument insensitivity | Output identical whether or not arguments are supplied; the array is never dereferenced | `README.md` lines 46–53; `Hello.java` lines 11–13 |
| Toolchain floor | Compile-then-run carries no stated version floor and was exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21; the single-file source launch requires JDK 11 or later | `README.md` lines 18–20; `Project Guide.md` §3, §9.1 |
| Warranty and liability position | **No warranty of any kind and limited liability** — GPL v3 §§15–17, which Section 5.4.5 records as the project's entire warranty position, with no separate warranty, support or service-level statement anywhere | `LICENSE` lines 589, 600, 612 |

Two consequences follow for SLA monitoring. Compliance is **binary per invocation** rather than aggregated over a window: a run either meets the published contract in all four observable respects or it does not, and Section 6.1.4.5 records that no intermediate state exists. And compliance is **unmeasured over time**: with no notification channel, no recorded execution history and nothing re-running any check (ADR-002), the only SLA-like evidence in existence is the point-in-time record of 49 of 49 checks passing on OpenJDK 25.0.3 in `Project Guide.md` §3.

| Service-level dimension | Position at `HEAD` |
|---|---|
| Availability target and measurement window | None defined. There is no resident service to be available, and no uptime series exists |
| Latency or response-time objective | None defined, and no timing measurement has ever been taken |
| Error budget and burn-rate policy | None defined. Section 6.1.4.5 records the binary outcome model that makes a partial-failure budget meaningless |
| Recovery objectives (RTO, RPO) | None defined. Section 5.4.6 records that no recovery-time or recovery-point objective exists anywhere in the repository, and that nothing the program does needs recovering |
| Support commitment or response time | None. No `SUPPORT.md`, `SECURITY.md` or contact address exists in any tracked file, so no disclosure or response path is published (Section 6.4.5.3) |
| Conformance criterion actually in force | The four-part output contract above, evaluated by an operator per run against `README.md` lines 57–63 |

#### 6.5.3.5 Capacity Tracking

**No capacity plan, quota, limit or growth projection exists**, and no resource-limiting flag is set anywhere: Section 6.1.3.3 records that a grep across the tracked files finds no `-Xmx`, `-Xms`, `-XX:`, `JAVA_OPTS`, `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, `_JAVA_OPTIONS`, `ulimit`, cgroup, `nice` or `taskset` usage, so the JVM runs with host defaults on every invocation. Concurrency is an operator choice rather than an elastic property — each launch is an independent process that shares nothing, so Section 6.1.3.1 records horizontal capacity as unbounded in principle and entirely manual in practice, with the ceiling set by host capacity that the repository never measures.

What can be tracked is **artifact and repository footprint**, measured first-hand in the checkout at `HEAD`.

| Capacity dimension | Measured value at `HEAD` | Measurement basis |
|---|---|---|
| Tracked file count | 5 files, all index mode `100644` | `git ls-files -s` |
| Tracked byte total | 925,008 bytes — of which 1,073 are source and 884,733 are the two Markdown records under `blitzy/documentation/` | `wc -c` over the tracked set |
| Object store footprint | 37 objects in 1 pack, 302 KiB pack size, 0 loose objects, 0 garbage | `git count-objects -v` |
| History size | 14 commits, 8 refs at 3 distinct commits, 0 tags | `git rev-list --all --count`, `git show-ref`, `git tag` |
| Per-run disk footprint | One 420-byte class file in a per-run `mktemp -d` directory, removed afterwards; zero bytes persisted by the program | Section 5.4.5; `README.md` line 30 |
| Per-run process footprint | One JVM process, one written file descriptor, zero threads created by the program | `Hello.java` lines 15–19 |
| Concurrency ceiling | **Not defined by the system**; bounded only by host capacity, since invocations share nothing | Section 5.2.7 |
| Growth trend | **Not tracked.** No size history, budget or projection exists; the one growth signal available is that the two documentation records are roughly 824 times the size of the source they describe | Measured here |

For an operator, capacity planning reduces to two host-level questions the repository leaves open — how many JVM start-ups per unit time the host absorbs, and how much terminal or pipeline throughput the accumulated standard output needs. Section 6.1.3.5 records that neither has an answer in the tracked files, and none is invented here.

#### 6.5.3.6 Alert Threshold Matrix

Every threshold in this system is **exact rather than statistical**: the expected value is a literal, and any deviation from it is the alert. There is no warning band, no percentile, no duration-for clause and no evaluation interval, because there is no series to evaluate over and no evaluator to run (Section 6.5.2.4). The matrix below is therefore a conformance matrix that a human applies at the moment of a run, and the fault identifiers are those catalogued in Section 4.3.2.2.

| Signal | Pass threshold | Deviation means | Fault |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard-output content | Byte-identical to `README.md` lines 59–61 — `Hello from Java!` plus one separator | The output contract is broken; the program no longer matches its published oracle | None catalogued — no such deviation has been observed |
| Standard-error volume | Exactly 0 bytes | A toolchain diagnostic was raised before or instead of program entry | E-1, E-2, E-7 |
| Process exit status | Exactly 0, by normal return | The workflow did not complete; the program was never entered or the JVM failed | E-1, E-7 |
| `javac` diagnostics under `-Xlint:all -Werror` | Exactly 0, empty error stream | The source no longer compiles cleanly; the project's only static gate has failed | E-2 |
| `javadoc` warning count | Exactly 1, for the implicit default constructor at `Hello.java:6` | 0 or ≥2 means comment coverage changed; 1 is expected and requires no action | E-6 (accepted by design) |
| `git status --short` output | Zero lines | An untracked or modified file is present — most commonly `Hello.class` after an in-place compile, since no ignore rule exists | E-3 |
| `Hello.java` line-ending census | `lf=20 cr=20 crlf=20` | An editor normalised the file to LF; all 20 lines were rewritten and the blob digest changed | E-5 |
| `README.md` byte format | `cr=0` with a trailing newline | The guide's LF-only, newline-terminated format was altered | E-5 (same class) |
| Comment-census tally | `added=15 /**=2 */=2 //=2` against baseline `0726b1d` | With the wrong baseline the comparison is empty and four checks fail on a correct tree — re-run with the pre-comment revision | E-4 |
| Behaviour-parity comparison | `cmp` reports both streams identical to the `0726b1d` build | A change altered executable behaviour, not just comments | None catalogued |
| Guide-structure counts | 8 sections in order; summary 55 words against a 70-word limit; exactly 2 relative links | The guide's required structure has drifted | None catalogued |
| Acceptance suite V1–V9 | 49 of 49 checks pass | Any failure is the deliverable's own regression signal; the suite lives outside the checkout and is never committed | Per failing check |
| Cross-release compilation | Exit 0 at release targets 11, 17 and 21 | The documented version-floor claim no longer holds | E-7 |

Three characteristics of this matrix should be read alongside it. The thresholds are **published rather than configured** — they live in `README.md` and `Project Guide.md` prose, not in a rules file, because no rules file exists. They are **evaluated only on demand**, so a violation introduced by a commit stays undetected until someone re-runs the checks, which is the Medium-severity Open risk `Project Guide.md` §6 records for the absent gate. And one row is an **expected non-zero value**: the single `javadoc` warning is the system's only permanently "firing" condition, documented as requiring no action because documenting an implicit constructor would require declaring one.


### 6.5.4 Incident Response

Incident response in this system is entirely human and entirely synchronous with the run that produced the fault. Section 5.4.3 records the governing pattern — "documented manual recovery, in the human layer" — and notes that with no CI gate, no scheduler and no loop anywhere in the system there is no automated retry and no automated escalation. What the repository provides instead is a complete, published fault catalogue with a resolution for every entry.

#### 6.5.4.1 Alert Routing

**There is exactly one route, and it is implicit: signal → terminal → the person who typed the command.** No routing tree, receiver, severity mapping, notification channel, acknowledgement step or on-call rota exists — Section 4.3.2.6 records the absence of a notification channel of any kind, and the eighteen alerting and paging artifacts probed in Section 6.5.6.2 are all absent, as are `SUPPORT.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `CODEOWNERS` and any `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE`. No tracked file contains a contact address, so there is no destination to route to even outside the repository.

| Routing concern | Position at `HEAD` |
|---|---|
| Channel | The operator's terminal, for the duration of the run. Section 5.4.3 names it "the only signal channel that exists" |
| Recipient | Whoever invoked the command. There is no second recipient and no hand-off |
| Severity classification | None declared. Every deviation is equally actionable because every threshold is exact (Section 6.5.3.6) |
| Acknowledgement and ownership | None mechanised. `Project Guide.md` §1.4 assigns owners in prose — "Maintainer", "Owner decision", "Accepted" — per item, not per incident |
| Detection window | The moment of the run only. If nobody is watching, the signal is lost: Section 6.4.3.5 records that nothing records that a run occurred — no log file, no exit-status record, no metric and no trace |
| Suppression and deduplication | Not applicable. Nothing persists between runs, and the single expected `javadoc` warning is documented as requiring no action rather than suppressed by a rule |

**Figure 6.5.4-A — Alert flow: how a deviation is detected, classified, routed and resolved, and the automated alert path verified absent**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Trigger(["A deviation occurs during a documented<br/>workflow — W-1 through W-4"])
    Observed{"Is a human reading the terminal<br/>at the moment of the run?"}
    Missed["Undetected. No log, metric, trace or exit-status<br/>record exists, so the signal is lost with the session"]
    Classify{"Which observable carried<br/>the deviation?"}

    subgraph SignalClass["Signal classification — exact thresholds, evaluated by eye"]
        S1["Standard error non-empty, or exit status<br/>non-zero: a toolchain fault — E-1, E-2, E-7"]
        S2["javadoc warning count not exactly 1:<br/>comment coverage changed — E-6"]
        S3["git status --short prints a line:<br/>untracked build output — E-3"]
        S4["Census mismatch: wrong baseline — E-4,<br/>or line endings normalised — E-5"]
        S5["Standard output differs from the oracle at<br/>README.md lines 59-61: contract breach"]
    end

    subgraph Routing["Routing — one implicit route to the person who typed the command"]
        RB["Runbook lookup: Project Guide section 9.8,<br/>seven symptom, cause and resolution rows"]
        RE["Apply the documented resolution and re-run the<br/>deterministic command; the payload is a<br/>compile-time constant, so a re-run is idempotent"]

        RB --> RE

    end

    end

    subgraph AbsentRouting["Verified absent — there is no automated alert path"]

        NR1 --- NR2
        NR2 --- NR3
        NR3 --- NR4
    end

    Trigger --> Observed
    Observed -->|"no"| Missed
    Observed -->|"yes — the only detection mechanism"| Classify
    Classify -->|"stderr or exit status"| S1
    Classify -->|"javadoc output"| S2
    Classify -->|"working tree"| S3
    Classify -->|"verification census"| S4
    Classify -->|"stdout content"| S5
    S1 --> RB
    S2 --> Accepted(["Accepted by design: coverage stands at<br/>2 of 3 documentable members; no action"])
    S3 --> RB
    S4 --> RB
    S5 --> RB
    RB -->|"no row matches, or the fix is a policy decision"| ES1
    VF --> Closed(["Resolved: correct stdout, empty stderr,<br/>status 0, clean working tree"])
    ES2 --> Carried(["Carried in Project Guide section 6 risk register<br/>with severity, probability and status"])
```

#### 6.5.4.2 Escalation Procedures

**No escalation procedure is mechanised, and the escalation target is named only in prose.** There is no severity ladder, no time-based escalation, no rota and no paging tier; Section 5.4.3 records the human-layer path as "escalate to the repository owner as a recorded open item," and Section 6.1.4.1 notes there is no process manager, supervisor or watchdog to restart anything on an operator's behalf.

The repository's own escalation model is a three-level one, expressed through ownership assignments and statuses rather than through routing configuration.

| Level | Who acts | Trigger and recorded outcome |
|---|---|---|
| L1 — Operator, in session | The person who ran the command | Any deviation with a matching row in `Project Guide.md` §9.8. Apply the documented resolution and re-run; Section 5.4.3 records why the re-run is safe — deterministic command, compile-time-constant payload, zero dependency resolution, and a fresh `mktemp -d` directory per attempt |
| L2 — Maintainer | The maintainer, out of session | Items requiring a procedure change rather than a re-run. `Project Guide.md` §1.4 assigns the verification-invocation baseline item to "Maintainer" with a 1.0 h ETA, and §1.6 ranks it `[High]` |
| L3 — Repository owner | The owner, as a decision rather than a fix | Items recorded as "Owner decision" — the four repository-hygiene exclusions (2.0 h), the absent automated gate (Deferred) and the four out-of-scope infrastructure items (Deferred). These are carried in the §6 risk register with severity, probability and status rather than resolved in session |

Three properties of this model should be recorded honestly. There is **no notification step at any level** — escalation means writing the item into a document, not sending a message. There is **no external reporting path**: no vulnerability-disclosure route, support address or issue template exists (Section 6.4.5.3 carries the absent disclosure path as a residual risk). And **no access or availability obstacle has been encountered**: `Project Guide.md` §1.5 records "No access issues identified," with the repository, its branch and the JDK toolchain reachable throughout and no credential, network egress or secret used by anything in the project.

#### 6.5.4.3 Runbooks

**A runbook does exist, and it is the one incident-response artifact the repository genuinely carries** — the seven-row troubleshooting table at `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.8, complemented by the verification procedures in §9.6 and the command-and-expected-result reference in Appendix A. No file named `RUNBOOK.md`, `OPERATIONS.md` or `INCIDENT.md` exists; the runbook lives inside the project guide. Each row maps to a catalogued fault in Section 4.3.2.2, with the recovery procedures elaborated in Section 4.3.2.7.

| Fault | Symptom the operator sees | Documented resolution |
|---|---|---|
| E-1 | `Could not find or load main class Hello` | No compiled class on the classpath, or the wrong directory. Compile first, or launch with `java -cp <build dir> Hello`; the class is in the default package, so the bare name is correct |
| E-2 | `error: class Hello is public, should be declared in a file named Hello.java` | The source was exported under another name — common when writing a baseline revision to a scratch file. Export into a directory as `Hello.java`, as the verification steps do |
| E-3 | `javac Hello.java` leaves `Hello.class` in `git status` | There is no ignore rule in this repository. Delete it, or compile to a directory outside the checkout with `-d` |
| E-4 | Verification reports `block census wrong: /**=0 */=0 //=0` | The census was given the current commit as its baseline, where the comments are already committed. Re-run with the pre-comment revision `0726b1d` |
| E-5 | Verification reports mixed line endings or `final terminator not CRLF` | An editor normalised `Hello.java` to LF on save. Restore the file and re-apply the edit in byte mode, re-emitting CRLF on every line including added ones |
| E-6 | `javadoc` reports one warning | Expected: the implicit default constructor can carry no doc comment. No action; documenting it would require declaring a constructor, which is out of scope |
| E-7 | The direct source launch fails on an older JDK | Single-file source launch needs JDK 11 or later. Use the compile-then-run path, which has no such floor |

Two supporting procedures complete the runbook and are worth naming because they are what an operator actually runs after applying a resolution. The **parity procedure** in §9.6 rebuilds revision `0726b1d`, runs both builds and `cmp`s both captured streams, printing "behaviour identical" when the program is unchanged. The **cleanup procedure** removes every scratch directory and confirms with `rm -rf "$B" "$O" "$S" && git status --short`, expecting no output. `Project Guide.md` §9.6 also records a standing constraint on the runbook itself: the full acceptance suite V1–V9 must be saved outside the checkout and never committed, "since build, test and CI files are out of scope for this repository."

#### 6.5.4.4 Post-Mortem Processes

**No post-mortem process, template, incident log or blameless-review practice exists in the repository**, and no incident has ever been recorded: `POSTMORTEM.md`, `INCIDENT.md`, `incident.md` and every related artifact probed in Section 6.5.6.2 are absent, and Section 6.4.3.5 records that no run leaves evidence of itself, so there is no execution history a review could reconstruct.

What the project performs instead is a **retrospective review of the change, written at delivery time rather than after a failure**. Four artifacts make it up, all in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md`, and together they are the closest thing the repository has to a post-incident record.

| Retrospective artifact | What it records | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| Verification record | 49 checks executed, 49 passed, 0 failed across nine acceptance groups plus 12 toolchain checks, with a per-area breakdown of what each area proves | `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Explicit "Not Covered" statement | What was *not* verified and why — no unit or integration tests exist, the guide's rendered appearance was never checked, the JDK 11 floor was not exercised on a JDK 11 runtime, comment and prose wording is not machine-checkable, and the comment census fails vacuously under its default baseline | `Project Guide.md` §3 |
| Compliance and divergence review | A twelve-row compliance matrix plus a divergence analysis explaining the citation budget, the required pre-comment baseline, the safe alternate build path, the unavoidable `javadoc` warning and the deferred policy decisions, each with a remedy | `Project Guide.md` §5.1, §5.2 |
| Risk register | Eight forward-looking risks, each with category, severity, probability, mitigation and status — including the Medium/Medium "no build descriptor, test suite or CI workflow" entry and the "Open — accepted by design" CRLF entry | `Project Guide.md` §6 |

The register's framing is itself the honest statement of this system's post-mortem posture: it records **forward-looking risk to the documentation and to future edits** rather than analysis of past failures, because no past failure exists to analyse. `Project Guide.md` §6 also disposes of whole risk categories in one line — the program "reads no input, dereferences no argument, opens no resource, binds no port, makes no network call and has no dependency manifest" — which is why the register contains no availability, data-loss or security-incident entry.

#### 6.5.4.5 Improvement Tracking

**Improvement tracking exists as prose and as commit messages, not as a tracker.** No issue tracker, project board, `CHANGELOG.md` or `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE` is present in the repository. What the project uses is a numbered open-item register carried in the documentation, referenced from commit messages, and re-stated with priorities and estimates.

| Improvement item | Priority and estimate | Status at `HEAD` |
|---|---|---|
| Run the comment-census verification with the pre-comment revision as its baseline | `[High]`, 1.0 h, owner "Maintainer" | Open — the item that makes a correct tree score 33 of 37 under the default baseline |
| Push the branch and merge the two-file change | `[High]`, 0.5 h | Open — `main` sits at `0726b1d`, 11 commits behind `jr_java1` (Section 5.4.6) |
| Decide citation coverage — two references, or every section with the budget and its check amended | `[Medium]`, 1.0 h | Open — owner decision |
| Confirm the `JDK 11 or later` floor on a JDK 11 runtime, or soften the claim | `[Medium]`, 1.0 h | Open — recorded as Partial in the runtime-validation checklist |
| Take the deferred hygiene decisions: licence notice, ignore rule, line-ending policy, version pin | `[Low]`, 2.0 h | Open — owner decision, four items |
| Adopt an automated gate that re-runs the documentation checks | ETA "Deferred" | Open — the Medium/Medium risk that `Project Guide.md` §8 calls "the one recommendation that outlives this change" |
| `javadoc` implicit-constructor warning | No ETA | **Accepted** — coverage stands at 2 of 3 documentable members, with no functional impact |

The mechanics of the tracking are worth recording because they are unusual: **11 items remain open**, of which the delivered change closed 2, and closure is expressed in the history rather than in a tool — commit `ce8e85c` carries the message line "Closes OI-9 and OI-12." Progress is reconciled arithmetically in `Project Guide.md` §2.3 against a 38.0-hour total with 32.0 hours completed and 6.0 remaining, and §1.2 states the resulting figure of 84.2% complete.

Two limitations follow, and both are the same limitation in different clothing. Because nothing re-runs the checks, **an improvement's effect is only ever verified by hand**, so the 49-of-49 record ages the moment the source changes; and because the register lives only in `Project Guide.md`, **the tracker and the evidence share a single point of failure** — Section 5.4.6 records that this prose is the one asset in the system with no mechanical recovery path.


### 6.5.5 Review Surface and Conditions for Re-Evaluation

#### 6.5.5.1 Dashboard Layout of the Review Surface

No dashboard software exists (Section 6.5.2.5), so the layout below documents the **static review surface** an operator actually reads: four panels of published text, arranged in the order the repository's own procedures use them. Every tile names the exact expected value, because in this system the expectation *is* the dashboard — there is no current-value rendering to compare against, only a command whose output the reader compares by eye.

Three properties of this layout follow from the absence of a dashboard tier. It is **pull-only**: nothing refreshes, so every tile is as current as the last time someone ran its command. It carries **no history**: no tile has a previous value, so a trend cannot be read anywhere in the system. And it is **asserted against source text rather than a rendered page** — `Project Guide.md` §3 lists the guide's rendered appearance among the things never exercised, so the review surface itself is verified as Markdown, not as a view.

#### 6.5.5.2 Changes That Would Make a Monitoring Architecture Applicable

The determination in Section 6.5.1 is a statement about the repository at commit `2a78292` on branch `jr_java1`, not a permanent property. Each change below would satisfy one of the failed preconditions M1–M7 and would oblige this section to be rewritten as a substantive monitoring architecture rather than amended.

| Repository change | Precondition it would satisfy | Sub-sections that would need content |
|---|---|---|
| A server loop, listener, scheduler or daemon entry point — any process that outlives one write | M1 — a steady state to observe | 6.5.2.1 metrics collection; 6.5.3.1 health checks; 6.5.3.5 capacity tracking |
| A first logging framework, or any write to `System.err` | M2 and M3 — a log producer and a destination | 6.5.2.2 log aggregation in full; 6.5.3.6 would gain its first non-exact threshold |
| A second compilation unit or any remote call — socket, HTTP, gRPC, broker | M2 — a boundary across which work can be correlated | 6.5.2.3 distributed tracing; 6.5.2.6 the architecture figure would gain its first collection tier |
| A bound port or an HTTP endpoint of any kind | M1 and M3 — something a probe or scraper could reach | 6.5.3.1 probe design; 6.5.2.1 exposition and scrape configuration |
| A notification channel — webhook, email, chat or pager configuration | M4 — a channel on which an alert can be raised | 6.5.2.4 alert management; 6.5.4.1 alert routing; 6.5.4.2 escalation would gain a real ladder |
| A declared SLA, SLO, threshold or error budget in any tracked file | M5 — a target to compare an observation against | 6.5.3.4 SLA monitoring; 6.5.3.6 would become a genuine threshold matrix with bands |
| Any configuration file — `*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.json`, `*.properties`, `*.toml` | M6 — a place to express monitoring configuration | 6.5.2.1, 6.5.2.4 and 6.5.2.5, each of which is currently vacuous for want of a descriptor |
| A CI descriptor, cron entry, systemd timer or active Git hook | M7 — an automated executor | 6.5.1.3 basic practices; 6.5.3.6 evaluation intervals; 6.5.4.5 improvement tracking; the ADR-002 position would be superseded |
| A container, Compose or Kubernetes manifest | M1, M6 and M7 — a placement model with probe and restart semantics | 6.5.3.1 liveness and readiness probes; 6.5.2.6 monitoring architecture |
| A persisted artifact — a file written by the program, a datastore or a cache | M3 — storage whose growth and health must be tracked | 6.5.3.5 capacity tracking; 6.5.2.2 retention |
| Any committed timing measurement or benchmark | M5 — a performance baseline to regress against | 6.5.3.2 performance metrics, which currently records baselines but no target |

Three further changes would **not** make a monitoring architecture applicable, but would each close a limitation this section records:

- **A committed automated gate** would make the 49 checks re-runnable and turn the point-in-time record in `Project Guide.md` §3 into a repeatable signal. It is the Medium-severity Open risk in `Project Guide.md` §6 and the `[Deferred]` item in §1.4.
- **A `.gitignore`** would remove the standing false-positive source in the hygiene tile: fault E-3 exists only because an in-place compile leaves an untracked class file that no ignore rule covers.
- **A `SUPPORT.md` or `SECURITY.md` with a contact address** would give escalation a destination outside the operator's own session; Section 6.4.5.3 carries the absent disclosure path as a residual risk with no compensating control.

## 6.6 Testing Strategy

### 6.6.1 Testing Approach

#### 6.6.1.1 Applicability Determination

**Detailed Testing Strategy is not applicable for this system.**

At commit `2a78292` on branch `jr_java1` the repository tracks five files, of which exactly one is executable. `Hello.java` is 20 lines and 1,073 bytes; its only member is `main(String[] args)` at line 15; and a census of non-comment, non-blank lines returns exactly five — lines 6, 15, 17, 19 and 20, of which the single behavioural statement is `System.out.println("Hello from Java!")` at line 17. There is one class, one method, one statement, no field, no constructor, no `import`, no branch and no loop. A program of that shape has no unit to isolate from another unit, no collaborator to substitute, no return value to assert on and no second component to integrate with.

The repository states the position itself. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §3 opens with "The repository carries no committed test suite, and adding one is outside this change's scope, so there is no unit- or integration-test coverage figure to report," and its "Not Covered" list is more emphatic still: "No unit or integration tests exist. The repository has never had a test file and this change adds none." Appendix F closes the tooling question for the project as a whole — "No linter, formatter, documentation generator, build tool or test framework is configured in the repository, and none is introduced by this change." §9.6 adds the standing constraint that makes the absence deliberate rather than accidental: the verification suite must be saved outside the checkout and run there, "never commit it, since build, test and CI files are out of scope for this repository."

What exists instead, and what this section documents as the approach in force, is a **nine-group acceptance and toolchain check suite (V1–V9) executed by an operator from a scratch directory outside the checkout**, whose recorded outcome is **49 checks executed, 49 passed, 0 failed** on OpenJDK 25.0.3 — 37 acceptance assertions plus 12 direct toolchain checks (`Project Guide.md` §3).

Declaring non-applicability does not discharge the areas this section must address. Sections 6.6.1.2 through 6.6.3 take each in turn — unit, integration and end-to-end testing, mocking, coverage, naming, test data, CI integration, triggers, parallelism, reporting, failure and flake handling, quality gates, performance thresholds and security testing — and label each as exactly one of:

- **Genuinely absent** — no corresponding surface exists, so the practice cannot be applied and its absence is structural rather than an omission.
- **Selected** — the repository itself chose a mechanism in place of the conventional one and states the reason.
- **Inherited** — the capability is in force but supplied by the JDK, Git, the host shell or the hosting platform rather than implemented in the repository.
- **Absent and expected** — a practice a maintained project would reasonably carry, and it is missing; each is carried as a recorded risk.

##### 6.6.1.1.1 Preconditions Tested

Seven preconditions must hold before a comprehensive testing strategy has anything to describe. All seven fail, and each was tested against the checkout.

| # | Precondition | Verified result |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | More than one unit of behaviour to isolate | **Fails.** One compilation unit, one class, one method, one statement. The executable-line census returns lines 6, 15, 17, 19 and 20, and there is no branch or loop, so the whole program is a single straight-line path |
| T2 | A seam or collaborator that could be substituted | **Fails.** A 68-marker in-source census returns **zero hits**, including zero `interface`, `abstract`, `implements` and `extends` occurrences, zero fields and zero explicit constructors. `Hello.java` declares no `import` at all, so the only collaborator is `java.lang.System`, reached statically. Nothing in the program can be injected, overridden or stubbed |
| T3 | A return value, thrown exception or mutated state to assert on | **Fails.** `main` returns `void`, declares no `throws`, contains no `assert`, allocates nothing and keeps no state. The only observables are process-level — standard-output bytes, standard-error emptiness and exit status — all three of which `README.md` lines 57–63 publish as a contract |
| T4 | A second component, service or datastore to integrate with | **Fails.** A 16-marker input/egress census over `Hello.java` (`args[`, `Runtime`, `exec`, `ProcessBuilder`, `Socket`, `URL`, `http`, `File`, `Files`, `Reader`, `Writer`, `System.getenv`, `System.getProperty`, `Class.forName`, `reflect`, `serial`) returns **zero hits**. `Project Guide.md` Appendix B records that the program "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call; there is no service, database, broker or cache in this project" |
| T5 | A UI, client or hosted surface to drive end to end | **Fails.** `Project Guide.md` §4, line 130, records "a console application with no user interface, no hosted page, no bound port and no external integration." The only view-like artifact in the project is the Markdown documentation, and §3 lists its rendered appearance among the things never exercised |
| T6 | A manifest in which a test framework could be declared, or a build task that could run one | **Fails.** §9.3 is categorical: "None. There is no `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `Makefile`, `package.json` or lock file of any kind, and nothing is downloaded at build time." With no manifest there is no `test` scope, no test task and no way to resolve a test dependency |
| T7 | An automated executor able to run a suite unattended | **Fails.** Nineteen CI-executor probes are absent, and all **14 entries in `.git/hooks` end in `.sample`** — the non-sample count is zero — so no commit-, push- or schedule-driven executor exists locally or remotely. ADR-002 records the decision; `Project Guide.md` §6 carries "No build descriptor, test suite or CI workflow, so nothing re-runs the documentation checks" as an Open operational risk at Medium severity and Medium probability |
