### 7.1.2 The Console Surface in Place of a User Interface

What a user interface would have provided is supplied instead by a process contract: an operator types one documented command in a shell and observes one line on standard output. `README.md` documents that contract in full, and it is the only interaction the system defines.

| Surface element | Contract | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Invocation | `java Hello` after `javac Hello.java`, or the direct source launch `java Hello.java` on JDK 11 or later; both from the repository root | `README.md` lines 36–38, 42–44 |
| Standard output | The literal `Hello from Java!` followed by one platform line separator — 17 bytes where the separator is a single newline | `README.md` lines 57–61; `Project Guide.md` line 133 |
| Standard error | Always empty; no diagnostic, prompt or progress text is ever written | `README.md` line 63; `Hello.java` line 16 |
| Exit status | 0, reached by normal return from `main` with no `System.exit` call | `README.md` line 63; `Hello.java` line 18 |
| Argument handling | `String[] args` is accepted only to satisfy the entry-point signature and is never read, so output is identical whether or not arguments are passed | `README.md` lines 48–51 |
| Launch-path equivalence | Both documented launch paths produce byte-identical standard output | `README.md` line 46 |

The complete rendered experience is one line of text:

```text
Hello from Java!
```

`blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` line 139 records that this fenced block in the guide "compares byte-identical to real standard output," and line 136 records that runs "with no arguments, many arguments, and hostile arguments including shell and injection payloads all produce identical output." There is therefore no state to present, no navigation, no mode, no error display and no user-triggered variation in what is shown.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Operator(["Operator or learner<br/>at a terminal"])
    Shell["POSIX shell in the<br/>repository root"]
    JVM["JVM process - class Hello,<br/>main at Hello.java line 15"]
    Stmt["Single statement at line 17<br/>System.out.println"]
    Stdout["Standard output - the literal<br/>plus one platform separator"]
    Stderr["Standard error<br/>deliberately left empty"]
    Exit(["Exit status 0 - normal return,<br/>no System.exit"])
    Term(["Terminal display -<br/>the whole user experience"])

    Operator -->|"types a documented command"| Shell
    Shell -->|"java Hello or java Hello.java"| JVM
    JVM --> Stmt
    Stmt --> Stdout
    JVM -->|"never written"| Stderr
    JVM --> Exit
    Stdout --> Term
```

*Diagram 7.1.2-A — The only human-facing boundary in the system: a shell invocation in, one line of standard output back. No presentation layer, client, view or renderer participates.*

### 7.1.3 Disposition of the Topics This Section Would Otherwise Cover

Each subject a User Interface Design section normally specifies is recorded below with the reason it does not apply, so that the absence is explicit rather than an omission.

| Topic | Applicability | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core UI technologies | **Not applicable.** No UI technology of any kind is present — no GUI toolkit, no web framework, no templating engine, no styling system, no terminal-UI library | Section 3.2.1 records a verified null framework result; the census in Section 7.1.1 found zero toolkit and zero front-end tokens |
| UI use cases | **Not applicable.** The system's four documented workflows W-1 to W-4 in Section 1.3.1.1 are all shell operations — compile, launch, launch from source, verify the output contract. None involves a UI, and no actor interacts with the program after launch | `README.md` lines 27, 30, 37, 43, 57–63 |
| UI / backend interaction boundaries | **Not applicable.** There is no client and no backend to separate. The system is one single-threaded JVM process with no port, no listener, no network call and no API, so there is no request, response, session, transport, contract version or error-propagation boundary to define | `Project Guide.md` Appendix B and §9.1; Section 1.3.1.2 network-surface row |
| UI schemas | **Not applicable.** There is no form, field, validation rule, payload or view model. The whole data domain of the system is a single compile-time string constant and the host-supplied line separator | `Hello.java` line 17; Section 1.3.1.2 data-domains paragraph |
| Screens required | **Not applicable — no screen exists in the repository.** There is no screen, page, view, dialog, panel or wizard to enumerate, and the semantic searches for screens, views and templates returned no files at all | Section 7.1.1 file-extension, directory and semantic-search rows |
| User interactions | **Not applicable.** The only interaction is the invocation itself. After launch nothing is read: `args` is never dereferenced, standard input is never read, and no keystroke, click, gesture, focus change or shortcut is handled | `Hello.java` lines 11–15; `README.md` lines 48–51 |
| Visual design considerations | **Not applicable.** No layout, typography, colour, spacing, theme, icon set, responsive rule or accessibility affordance is expressible: the program emits plain ASCII with no escape sequence, and its appearance is entirely determined by the operator's terminal | Section 7.1.1 terminal-styling and asset rows |
| Accessibility and internationalisation | **Not applicable.** There is no rendered control to label and no locale handling; the greeting is a hard-coded ASCII literal with no resource bundle, and Section 1.3.2.1 excludes internationalisation and localisation outright | `Hello.java` line 17; Section 1.3.2.1 |
| UI state management and routing | **Not applicable.** The program keeps no state within or between runs and has a single code path with no branch, loop or navigation | `README.md` line 12; `Hello.java` lines 15–19 |

### 7.1.4 Documentation Rendering Is Not an Application Interface

One presentation concern is recorded in the repository and must not be mistaken for a user interface. The three Markdown documents — `README.md` and the two files under `blitzy/documentation/` — are displayed by whatever renderer the hosting platform provides. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` Appendix D records the dialect as "GitHub Flavored Markdown over CommonMark" and states that "no generator or renderer is part of the project," and Section 3.2.5 records that convention as one of only two external standards the project relies on.

Consequently the renderer is outside the system boundary, contributes no tracked artifact, and defines no screen the project owns. The repository tracks the review of that rendered appearance as documentation work, not UI work: `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` line 123 records that emphasis, the two tables, the four fenced blocks and both relative links "were asserted against the Markdown source, never against a rendered page," and Section 1.3.2.2 carries "Review the rendered guide on the hosting platform" as a deferred Medium item of 0.5 hours. Line 143 of the same guide explains why nothing was checked in a browser: there is no UI and no hosted page. The only navigational affordance anywhere in the project is the pair of relative Markdown links in `README.md` — `[Hello.java](Hello.java)` at line 71 and `[LICENSE](LICENSE)` at line 77 — which resolve as file paths on disk.

The same distinction applies to the `javadoc` HTML that the project's comment-coverage check can generate from `Hello.java`: Appendix F of the guide records that the tool is run for validation and that its HTML output is never committed, so no generated page is part of the delivered system.

### 7.1.5 Conditions That Would Require This Section to Be Written

This determination is a property of the current tree, not a permanent one. Any of the changes below would introduce a presentation surface and would require this section to be replaced with a full design.

| Trigger | First artifact that would appear | Sub-sections that would become required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A desktop GUI is added | An `import javax.swing.*`, `java.awt.*` or `javafx.*` statement in a source file, plus an `.fxml` layout or window construction code | Core UI technologies, screens, user interactions, visual design |
| A web or mobile front end is added | A `package.json`, a bundler configuration, an `index.html` or a `static/`, `templates/` or `public/` directory | All topics in Section 7.1.3, including UI schemas and the UI/backend boundary |
| The program becomes network-served | A bound port and a listener, invalidating the Appendix B "no port, no listener" record and the network-surface row of Section 1.3.1.2 | UI/backend interaction boundaries, transport and error contracts |
| An interactive console mode is added | A `System.in`, `Scanner`, `BufferedReader` or `Console` read, ending the "reads no input" property of `README.md` line 12 | UI use cases, user interactions, prompt and input-validation schemas |
| A command-line presentation layer is added | Any executable read of `args`, or a CLI-parsing dependency, producing flags, sub-commands and `--help` output | UI use cases, user interactions, textual output schemas |
| Terminal styling is introduced | ANSI escape sequences or a terminal-UI library, ending the plain-ASCII, escape-free output established in Section 7.1.1 | Visual design considerations |

Until one of these appears in the tracked tree, the correct content of this section is the single statement with which it opens: no user interface is required.

# 8. Infrastructure

## 8.1 Infrastructure Applicability Assessment

**Detailed Infrastructure Architecture is not applicable for this system.**

At commit `2a78292` on branch `jr_java1` the repository tracks five files totalling 925,008 bytes, of which exactly one is executable: `Hello.java`, 20 lines and 1,073 bytes, whose entire behaviour is the single statement at line 17 — `System.out.println("Hello from Java!")`. There is no artifact to place, no host to provision, no endpoint to expose and no state to protect. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` §9.5 states the operational consequence in one sentence — "There is no service to start — the program writes one line and exits" — and Appendix B disposes of the entire network and service tier: "Not applicable. The program binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call; there is no service, database, broker or cache in this project."

The determination is not a summary of absent features; it is the conclusion of seven preconditions tested against the checkout, each of which must hold before an infrastructure architecture has anything to describe. All seven fail. Section 1.3.2.4 records the same verdict from the scope side, listing "Deploying it as a service" as an unsupported use case because "no listener, no port, no packaging, and no deployment descriptor exist," and Section 3.6 opens with the matching technology-stack verdict: "no build system, no containerisation, no CI/CD and no deployment mechanism."

What remains, and what the rest of this section documents, is the **minimal build and distribution surface** the prompt's non-applicability branch calls for: a JDK on an operator's `PATH`, a POSIX shell, a per-run temporary build directory, and a Git remote from which the source is cloned. Sections 8.3 through 8.8 then take each infrastructure concern the specification calls for in turn — deployment environment, cloud services, containerisation, orchestration, CI/CD and infrastructure monitoring — and record for each whether it is **genuinely absent** (no corresponding surface exists, so the concern cannot be applied), **inherited** (in force but supplied by the host, the JDK or the hosting platform rather than by anything in the repository), **selected** (the repository chose a mechanism and states the reason), or **absent and expected** (a control a maintained project would reasonably carry, missing, and carried as a recorded risk). This is the same four-way classification Section 6.5.1 applies to monitoring, used here so that the two non-applicability determinations read consistently.

### 8.1.1 Preconditions Tested

| # | Precondition for an infrastructure architecture | Verified result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I1 | A deployable artifact — package, image, archive or binary | **Fails.** No packaging step exists and nothing is published. A recursive search for `*.jar`, `*.war`, `*.ear`, `*.zip`, `*.tar`, `*.tgz`, `*.class`, `*.so`, `*.exe`, `*.deb`, `*.rpm`, `*.apk`, `*.img` and `*.iso` outside `.git` returns **zero files**; the only build output is a 420-byte class file created in a per-run `mktemp -d` directory and deleted afterwards |
| I2 | A runtime host that must be provisioned, sized or configured | **Fails.** The JDK is host-supplied and never vendored (Section 3.7.1), and Section 3.6.6 records the runtime environment as "any host with a JDK on `PATH` and a POSIX shell." Section 1.3.1.2 places the JDK and the host operating system **outside** the system boundary |
| I3 | A network surface to expose, route, balance or firewall | **Fails.** `Project Guide.md` Appendix B records that the program "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call." The only network path in the whole project belongs to Git, not to the program (Section 8.3.1.4) |
| I4 | State that must be persisted, backed up or replicated | **Fails.** Section 6.2 records that no runtime path reaches durable media, and Section 6.5.3.5 records zero bytes persisted by the program per run. The only durable state in the system is the Git object store — 37 objects in one 302.84 KiB pack |
| I5 | An environment-specific configuration surface | **Fails.** A recursive census finds **zero** configuration files of any format in the checkout (`*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.tf`, `*.sh`, `*.properties`, `*.xml`, `*.json`, `*.toml`, `*.ini`, `*.cfg` — confirmed first-hand). `Project Guide.md` §9.2 opens "Nothing to configure. No environment variable or secret is read by any tracked file," and Section 3.6.6 records that "no environment-specific configuration exists to differentiate dev, test and production" |
| I6 | An automated executor able to provision, build or deploy | **Fails.** No CI descriptor, `Makefile`, wrapper script, cron entry or systemd unit exists, and all **14** entries in `.git/hooks` are `*.sample` — zero active hooks. ADR-002 records the position; the only automation-adjacent facility is the hosting platform's pull-request merge (Section 3.6.5) |
| I7 | A declared target environment, region or tenancy model | **Fails.** No infrastructure descriptor of any kind exists (Section 8.1.2), and Section 1.3.1.2 states the position directly: "Not applicable in any deployment sense — there is no hosted service, no region, no tenancy model" |

### 8.1.3 What Constitutes "Infrastructure" For This System

Three elements, and only three, play an infrastructure role. Naming them precisely is what makes the rest of this section documentable: every requirement, cost, risk and maintenance procedure below attaches to one of them.

| Element | Role it plays | Ownership |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Operator workstation** — a host with a JDK on `PATH` and a POSIX shell with GNU `grep`, `diff`, `awk` and coreutils | The complete build and runtime environment. It compiles the single unit, launches the JVM, and is where the output contract is observed | Outside the system boundary (Section 1.3.1.2); supplied by the operator, never provisioned by the repository |
| **Git remote on GitHub** — `github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java.git` over HTTPS | The sole distribution channel and the only durable store: it conveys five text files and the 14-commit history, and hosts the pull-request merge that promotes a branch | Inherited from the hosting platform; the repository holds no configuration for it beyond the remote URL |
| **Per-run `mktemp -d` build directory** | The ephemeral output location for `Hello.class`, created fresh per build and removed afterwards. Section 3.6.1 records `mktemp -d` as the tool that "generates the per-run build and scratch directories, keeping class output out of the checkout" | Selected by the repository as a documented practice in `README.md` line 30; created and destroyed by the operator, never persisted |

## 8.2 Minimal Build and Distribution Requirements

This is the whole of the system's infrastructure requirement: a toolchain the operator already has, a temporary directory, and a clone. Nothing below is provisioned, templated or automated — each requirement is satisfied by a command an operator types, and every expected result is published in the repository so that satisfaction can be confirmed rather than assumed.

### 8.2.1 Build Requirements

| Requirement | Specified value | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Toolchain | **A JDK, and nothing else.** `README.md` line 18: "A JDK is all that is required" | `README.md` line 18; Section 1.3.1.1 |
| Version floor — compile-then-run | **None stated.** Documented as working on "considerably older releases"; exercised at release targets **11, 17 and 21** | `README.md` line 20; `Project Guide.md` §9.1 |
| Version floor — single-file source launch | **JDK 11 or later**, and the claim is **not yet confirmed on a JDK 11 runtime** — corroborated only by compiling at targets 11, 17 and 21 and by `java --source 11` on a JDK 25 toolchain | `README.md` line 20; `Project Guide.md` §3, §9.1 |
| Toolchain version recorded | OpenJDK **25.0.3** for `java`, `javac` and `javadoc`; language level "None declared" — no `--release` or `--source` setting exists anywhere | `Project Guide.md` Appendix D |
| Shell and utilities | A POSIX shell; GNU `grep`, `diff`, `awk` and coreutils only if the structural verification commands are to be run | `Project Guide.md` §9.1 |
| Dependency resolution | **None.** "There is no `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `Makefile`, `package.json` or lock file of any kind, and nothing is downloaded at build time" | `Project Guide.md` §9.3 |
| Network access at build time | **None required.** Zero artifacts fetched; the source imports nothing outside `java.lang` | `Project Guide.md` §9.1; Section 6.5.3.2 |
| Configuration | **None.** No environment variable or secret is read by any tracked file; `JAVA_HOME` is not required | `Project Guide.md` §9.2, Appendix E |
| Build output location | A per-run `mktemp -d` directory, outside the checkout — the recommended path, because no `.gitignore` exists | `README.md` line 30 |

Two build paths are documented, and the difference between them is a repository-hygiene decision rather than a performance one.

```bash
javac Hello.java                                        # Path A — in place
B="$(mktemp -d)"; javac -Xlint:all -d "$B" Hello.java   # Path B — recommended
```

`Project Guide.md` §9.4 records the expected result for both as "exit status 0 and no output at all," adds that "`-Xlint:all` is clean, and so is `-Werror`," and supplies the Path A cleanup `rm -f Hello.class && git status --short`. Path B exists for a stated security reason rather than convenience: `README.md` line 30 explains that `mktemp -d` "returns a uniquely named one readable only by its owner, whereas a fixed, predictable destination can be pre-created, replaced or redirected through a symbolic link by another local process before the compiler writes into it." Section 3.7.5 records that reintroducing a fixed compiler-output path would forfeit that mitigation.

### 8.2.2 Runtime Requirements

| Requirement | Specified value | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runtime host | Any host with a JDK on `PATH` and a POSIX shell. No environment-specific configuration differentiates dev, test and production | Section 3.6.6 |
| Launch forms | `java -cp "$B" Hello` (pairs with Path B), `java Hello` (pairs with Path A, bare name because the class is in the default package), `java Hello.java` (source launch, JDK 11+, leaves no class file) | `Project Guide.md` §9.5; `README.md` lines 37, 43 |
| Process model | One JVM process, one thread of control, one written file descriptor, zero threads created by the program | Section 6.5.3.5; `Hello.java` lines 15–19 |
| JVM tuning | **None.** No `-Xmx`, `-Xms`, `-XX:`, `JAVA_OPTS`, `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, `_JAVA_OPTIONS`, `ulimit`, cgroup, `nice` or `taskset` usage exists in any tracked file; the JVM runs with host defaults on every invocation | Section 6.1.3.3 |
| Output contract | `Hello from Java!` plus exactly one platform line separator on standard output; standard error empty; exit status 0 by normal return with no `System.exit` | `README.md` lines 57–63; `Hello.java` lines 16–18 |
| Ports, listeners, network | **None.** "The program binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call" | `Project Guide.md` Appendix B |
| Persistence | **None.** No state is kept within or between runs; zero bytes are persisted by the program | `README.md` line 12; Section 6.2 |
| Concurrency ceiling | **Not defined by the system.** Invocations share nothing, so horizontal capacity is unbounded in principle and entirely manual in practice, bounded only by host capacity the repository never measures | Sections 6.1.3.1, 5.2.7 |

### 8.2.3 Distribution Requirements

Distribution is **source-only, over Git, addressed by commit SHA**. Nothing is packaged, published, versioned or installed, and the consequence is that "distribution" and "clone" are the same operation.

| Dimension | Position at `HEAD` | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Channel | Git clone over HTTPS from `github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java.git`, conveying five text files totalling **925,008 bytes** | `git remote -v`; `git ls-files`; Section 3.6.6 |
| Packaging | **None.** No jar, war or archive is produced or committed; **zero** binary blobs are tracked, all five index entries are mode `100644` | Recursive archive search; `git ls-files -s` |
| Published coordinates | **None declared anywhere**, so the program is never consumed as a dependency. The class sits in the default package, which code in a named package cannot import | Sections 1.3.2.3, 1.3.2.4, 3.3.2 |
| Release line and versioning | **None.** `git tag` returns **zero tags across 14 commits**; requirement versions are anchored to commit SHAs instead | `git tag`; Section 2.6.3 |
| Integrity of the conveyed tree | Content-addressed: 37 objects in 1 pack, 302.84 KiB, 0 loose objects, 0 garbage; each file identified by its blob digest | `git count-objects -vH`; Section 6.4.3.5 |
| Byte-format obligation | `Hello.java` must arrive CRLF on all 20 lines and `README.md` LF-only. No `.gitattributes` exists and `core.autocrlf`/`core.eol` are unset, so preservation depends on editor discipline | Direct measurement; Sections 3.6.1, 3.7.5 |
| Licence obligation | `LICENSE` must remain verbatim GPL v3 (674 lines, 35,149 bytes) and a modified covered work must carry a dated modification notice — present at `README.md` line 5 | Sections 3.7.2, 1.3.1.1 |
| Outstanding delivery state | **Not yet on the default branch.** `git rev-list --left-right --count main...HEAD` reports `0 11`: `main` is an ancestor of `jr_java1` and 11 commits behind it | Direct measurement; Section 3.6.6.2 |

Because the distributed tree is the source tree, the GPL v3 Corresponding Source obligation is discharged by the act of distribution itself — there is no object code to accompany, and Section 8.1.2 confirms that no compiled artifact has ever been tracked.

### 8.2.4 Resource Sizing Guidelines

Every figure below is either measured first-hand in the checkout or attributed to the repository's recorded evidence. No headroom multiplier, growth projection or capacity target is asserted, because Section 6.5.3.5 records that none exists in any tracked file.

| Resource | Sizing guideline | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compute (build) | One `javac` invocation over **one** compilation unit of 1,073 bytes with zero dependency resolution. No dedicated build host is required; any developer workstation suffices | `git ls-files`; `Project Guide.md` §9.3 |
| Compute (run) | One JVM process executing **four** bytecode instructions in `main` — `getstatic`, `ldc`, `invokevirtual`, `return`. Cost is dominated by JVM start-up rather than by the program, which the repository notes nowhere and measures nowhere | Sections 5.4.5, 6.5.3.2 |
| Memory | JVM host defaults; **no heap or metaspace setting exists anywhere**, and the program allocates zero objects in application code | Section 6.1.3.3 |
| Storage — source tree | 925,008 tracked bytes: 1,073 bytes of source, 39,202 bytes of licence and guide, and 884,733 bytes in the two `blitzy/documentation/` records | `wc -c` over the tracked set |
| Storage — object store | 302.84 KiB pack (37 objects, 0 loose, 0 garbage); `.git` occupies 496 KiB and the working tree excluding `.git` occupies 1.8 MiB, the excess being the untracked authoring copy | `git count-objects -vH`; `du -sh` |
| Storage — per build | **420 bytes**, one class file, in a `mktemp -d` directory that is removed afterwards. Zero bytes are persisted by the program itself | Sections 5.4.5, 6.5.3.5 |
| Network — build | **Zero bytes.** Nothing is downloaded at build time | `Project Guide.md` §9.3 |
| Network — distribution | One clone of the 302.84 KiB pack over HTTPS; no subsequent traffic, since the program makes no network call | `git count-objects -vH`; Appendix B |
| Network — runtime output | 17 bytes to standard output per invocation on an LF host (16 ASCII characters plus one separator), 18 on a CRLF host; 0 bytes to standard error | Sections 6.5.2.1, 6.5.3.2 |
| Concurrency | Independent processes sharing nothing; the ceiling is host capacity, which the repository does not measure or constrain | Sections 6.1.3.1, 5.2.7 |

### 8.2.5 Cost Structure and Estimates

**No cost figure of any kind appears in any tracked file.** What can be documented is the cost *structure* — where a cost could arise, what the measured consumption is, and which external pricing terms would apply — with the repository's own contribution to each line being zero provisioned resource.

| Cost element | Consumption attributable to this system | Cost position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compute — build and run | One `javac` call and one short-lived JVM process per invocation, on a workstation the operator already owns | **No incremental cost.** No dedicated, reserved or on-demand compute is provisioned; Section 8.4 records that no cloud runtime exists |
| Toolchain licensing | A JDK, host-supplied and never vendored; the recorded build is OpenJDK 25.0.3 | **Not recorded and not constrained.** No licence key, subscription or credential is read by anything in the project, and Section 3.7.3 records that the repository neither records nor enforces which JDK build an operator uses — so any support or subscription cost is a property of that choice, outside this system |
| Source hosting | One repository holding 925,008 tracked bytes and a 302.84 KiB pack on GitHub | Governed by the account's plan. <cite index="1-3">GitHub Free for personal accounts covers unlimited collaborators on unlimited public repositories with a full feature set, and unlimited private repositories with a limited feature set</cite>, so at this footprint the hosting line is plan-determined rather than usage-determined. The repository's visibility and plan are not recorded in the checkout, so no specific figure is asserted |
| CI/CD execution | **Zero minutes.** No pipeline exists (Section 8.7), so no runner time is consumed | If the deferred automated gate were adopted, <cite index="2-5,2-7,2-8">GitHub Actions usage is free for standard GitHub-hosted runners in public repositories and for self-hosted runners, while for private repositories each account receives a quota of free minutes and storage depending on plan, with any usage beyond the included amounts billed to the account</cite>. A gate for this project would be one `javac` and one `javadoc` invocation over a single 1,073-byte file |
| Artifact storage and registries | **Zero.** Nothing is published; no coordinates are declared and no registry is used | No cost line exists (Section 1.3.2.3) |
| Data services and egress | **Zero.** No database, broker or cache, and no network call at runtime | No cost line exists (Appendix B) |
| Monitoring and observability tooling | **Zero.** Section 8.8 records that no monitoring infrastructure exists or ever has | No cost line exists |
| Human effort — the only material cost | 6.0 hours of recorded remaining work against a 38.0-hour total, 32.0 hours completed (84.2% complete), across 11 open items | `Project Guide.md` §1.2, §1.4; Section 1.3.2.2 |

The honest summary is that this system's infrastructure cost is **the operator's existing workstation plus whatever plan the source host already runs under**, and the only quantity the repository itself measures in hours is the outstanding documentation work.

### 8.2.6 Maintenance Procedures

Maintenance here means re-establishing the published expectations by hand, because Section 8.7 records that nothing re-runs them. Each procedure below is documented in the repository, with an expected result that makes success checkable.

| Trigger | Procedure | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Any edit to `Hello.java` | Re-run the static gate: `javac -Xlint:all -Werror -d "$B" Hello.java` | Exit 0, no diagnostics, empty error stream — this is the project's entire static-analysis surface, as no linter is configured | 
| Any edit to a doc comment | `javadoc -d "$B/jd" -quiet Hello.java` | Exit 0 with **exactly one** warning, for the implicit default constructor at `Hello.java:6`; 0 or ≥2 warnings means coverage changed |
| Any behavioural review | Rebuild baseline revision `0726b1d`, run both builds and `cmp` the captured streams | `behaviour identical` — standard output, standard error and exit status all match the pre-comment build |
| After a Path A build | `rm -f Hello.class && git status --short` | No output. The class file is untracked because no ignore rule exists, and `README.md` line 30 instructs "Do not commit the class file either way" |
| After any verification run | `rm -rf "$B" "$O" "$S" && git status --short` | No output. The acceptance suite must be saved outside the checkout and never committed, "since build, test and CI files are out of scope for this repository" |
| Before a release or hand-off | `git status --short` expecting nothing, `git ls-files` expecting the five tracked paths, and the byte-format census `Hello.java lf=20 cr=20 crlf=20`, `README.md cr=0` | The checkout matches the distributed tree; the CRLF/LF split is intact in the absence of a `.gitattributes` policy |
| Toolchain upgrade on the host | Re-exercise the compile-then-run path and, where the version floor matters, the source launch | Section 3.7.3 records the risk being managed: the toolchain is unpinned, so "a future JDK could change documentation-tool defaults or single-file launch behaviour" |


## 8.3 Deployment Environment

There is no deployment environment in the conventional sense: nothing is placed anywhere, and the program's execution environment is created and destroyed by the operator within a single shell command. This sub-section documents that environment precisely — what it consists of, what it requires, what obligations attach to it, and how it is managed — because those are the questions the specification asks of a deployment environment, and each has a verifiable answer here even though the answer is minimal.

### 8.3.1 Target Environment Assessment

#### 8.3.1.1 Environment Type

**Operator-local, ephemeral, and per-invocation.** The environment is neither on-premises, cloud, hybrid nor multi-cloud, because none of those categories applies to a process that exists for the duration of one write. Section 3.6.6 records the runtime environment as "any host with a JDK on `PATH` and a POSIX shell," and adds that "no environment-specific configuration exists to differentiate dev, test and production."

| Candidate classification | Applicability | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On-premises deployment | **No.** Nothing is installed on a server; no machine is dedicated to or provisioned for this system | Section 8.1.1 precondition I2 |
| Cloud (IaaS/PaaS/FaaS) | **No.** No cloud provider, account, region, credential, SDK import or PaaS descriptor exists in any tracked file | Section 8.4; Section 3.7.4 |
| Hybrid or multi-cloud | **No.** Vacuous — there is no first environment for a second to be paired with | Section 8.1.1 precondition I7 |
| Container or orchestrated workload | **No.** `Project Guide.md` §9.1 lists the container among the non-prerequisites; no manifest of any kind exists | Sections 8.5, 8.6 |
| **Operator workstation, ephemeral** | **Yes — this is the environment.** A JDK on `PATH`, a POSIX shell, and a `mktemp -d` directory that exists only for the duration of the build | `Project Guide.md` §9.1, §9.5; `README.md` line 30 |
| **Hosted source remote (SaaS), non-runtime** | **Yes, for distribution only.** The GitHub remote stores and conveys the repository; it executes nothing, because no workflow exists | `git remote -v`; Section 3.7.4 |

The distinction in the last two rows is the one that matters for the rest of this section: the system has a **hosted dependency** but no **hosted runtime**. Section 8.4.2 develops that distinction and explains why it does not make this a cloud-deployed system.

#### 8.3.1.2 Geographic Distribution Requirements

**None.** Section 1.3.1.2 records the position in full: "Not applicable in any deployment sense — there is no hosted service, no region, no tenancy model." There is no region selection, no replication topology, no latency-driven placement, no data-residency constraint and no edge or CDN tier, because there is no served request and no stored datum to place.

Exactly one aspect of behaviour is host-dependent, and it is documented as a property rather than a variable to be managed: the line separator. `README.md` line 63 records that the separator "is the one the host defines, so the exact byte count varies between platforms; the literal and its single trailing separator do not" — which is why the published output oracle is expressed as the literal plus one separator rather than as a fixed byte count. Section 1.3.1.2 further records that no locale handling, resource bundle or character-set configuration exists and that the greeting is a hard-coded ASCII literal, so no locale or encoding differs between hosts.

The one geographic consideration that does exist belongs to the hosting platform rather than to this system: where the Git remote is served from, and under which account terms, is determined by GitHub and is not recorded anywhere in the checkout.

#### 8.3.1.3 Resource Requirements

The measured footprint is documented in full in Section 8.2.4. Summarised against the four resource dimensions the specification asks for:

| Dimension | Requirement | Measured or recorded value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compute | One `javac` invocation and one short-lived JVM process; no dedicated, reserved or scaled compute | `main` executes **4** bytecode instructions; cost dominated by JVM start-up, which the repository measures nowhere |
| Memory | JVM host defaults; no heap, metaspace, cgroup or `ulimit` setting exists anywhere in the tracked tree | Zero objects allocated in application code |
| Storage | 925,008 tracked bytes and a 302.84 KiB object-store pack for the source; 420 bytes of ephemeral build output per run | `.git` 496 KiB; working tree excluding `.git` 1.8 MiB |
| Network | Zero bytes at build time (nothing is downloaded); one HTTPS clone for distribution; 17 bytes of standard output per run on an LF host | No runtime network call of any kind |

No headroom, burst, quota or growth figure is stated, because Section 6.5.3.5 records that no capacity plan, quota, limit or growth projection exists in any tracked file. For an operator, the two open capacity questions are host-level and unanswered in the repository: how many JVM start-ups per unit time the host absorbs, and how much terminal or pipeline throughput accumulated standard output needs.

#### 8.3.1.4 Network Architecture

The program has **no network surface at all** — `Project Guide.md` Appendix B: "binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call." Consequently there is no load balancer, ingress, service mesh, subnet, security group, firewall rule, DNS record or TLS termination point to document, and none exists in the checkout.

Exactly one network path exists in the whole project, and it belongs to Git rather than to the application: the operator's `git` client reaching the GitHub remote over HTTPS. Section 3.7.1 records it as the "GitHub origin remote over HTTPS," and `git remote -v` confirms an HTTPS URL carrying a short-lived `x-access-token` credential supplied by the hosting platform's app installation rather than by anything in the repository — `Project Guide.md` §1.5 records that "no credential, key, network egress, environment variable or secret is used by anything in this project."

#### 8.3.1.5 Compliance and Regulatory Requirements

**No compliance or regulatory framework is named, claimed or implemented anywhere in the repository.** A first-hand case-insensitive census over `Hello.java`, `README.md` and `LICENSE` for GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, PCI, ISO 27001, FedRAMP, CCPA, "data residency", "personal data", PII, "export control", encryption, TLS, "audit log", retention and sovereignty returns **zero hits**.

That result is structural rather than an omission, and the reasons are individually verifiable:

| Regulatory concern | Position | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Personal or regulated data | **None processed.** The system has exactly one data element — the compile-time constant `Hello from Java!` — and one derived value, the host line separator. No schema, record, serialisation or data at rest exists | Section 1.3.1.2 |
| Data residency and cross-border transfer | **Not applicable.** No hosted service, region or tenancy model, and no stored datum to locate | Section 1.3.1.2 |
| Credential and secret handling | **None.** "No credential, key, network egress, environment variable or secret is used by anything in this project" | `Project Guide.md` §1.5, Appendix E |
| Audit and traceability obligations | **Documentary, not automatic.** The Git commit graph — 14 commits with author identity and timestamps in an append-only, content-addressed store — is the only durable record; Section 6.4.5.2 carries control row SC-22 recording that no run leaves evidence of itself | Section 6.4.3.5 |
| Licence compliance — **the one real obligation** | GPL v3 governs the covered work. `LICENSE` holds the verbatim text (674 lines, 35,149 bytes) with the Disclaimer of Warranty at line 589, the Limitation of Liability at line 600 and their interpretation clause at line 612; a modified covered work must carry a dated modification notice, present at `README.md` line 5 | `LICENSE`; Sections 3.7.2, 6.5.3.4 |
| Vulnerability disclosure | **Absent and expected.** No `SECURITY.md`, `SUPPORT.md`, `CODEOWNERS` or contact address exists in any tracked file; Section 6.4.5.3 carries the missing disclosure path as a residual risk with no compensating control | Section 6.4.5.3 |
| Supply-chain attestation | **Nothing to attest.** Zero dependencies, zero downloads at build time, and no published artifact to sign. The unpinned toolchain means runtime CVE exposure is a property of the operator's chosen JDK build, neither recorded nor constrained by the repository | `Project Guide.md` §9.3; Section 3.7.3 |

### 8.3.2 Environment Management

#### 8.3.2.1 Infrastructure as Code Approach

**No infrastructure-as-code exists, and there is no infrastructure for it to describe.** Section 8.1.2 records that `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, `terraform.tfvars`, `.terraform`, `pulumi.yaml`, `cdk.json`, `template.yaml`, `cloudformation.yaml`, `ansible.cfg`, `playbook.yml`, `Vagrantfile` and the Nix descriptors are all absent and have never been tracked. Section 3.7.4 records the same result for Terraform specifically, with the reason stated in four words: "There is no infrastructure to describe."

What plays the role IaC would play — a reproducible, reviewable definition of how the environment is brought up — is **documented commands under version control**. The practice is real, and it is worth naming precisely because it is the mechanism on which every claim in this section depends:

| IaC concern | What stands in for it | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declarative environment definition | A prerequisites list: a JDK, `git`, a POSIX shell with GNU text tools, and explicitly "no package manager step, no virtual environment, no container, no database, no broker and no bound port" | `Project Guide.md` §9.1 |
| Provisioning steps | Two build paths and three launch forms, each a literal command with its expected exit status and output | `README.md` lines 27–44; `Project Guide.md` §9.4, §9.5, Appendix A |
| Idempotence | Guaranteed by construction: the payload is a compile-time constant, dependency resolution is zero, and each build writes into a fresh `mktemp -d` directory, so a re-run is idempotent | Section 6.5.4.2; `README.md` line 30 |
| Review and change control | Git: 14 commits, pull-request review, and citation by stable symbol so that each documented claim can be checked at its origin | `git log`; Section 3.7.2 |
| Drift detection | `git status --short` expecting no output, plus the byte-format census `Hello.java lf=20 cr=20 crlf=20` and `README.md cr=0` | `Project Guide.md` §9.2, §9.6 |
| Version pinning — **the recorded gap** | **None.** The toolchain is unpinned by choice: Section 3.7.3 records the position as "portability over reproducibility — versions are recorded, never enforced," so a build is reproducible in *behaviour* but not in *toolchain* | `README.md` line 18; ADR-007 |

#### 8.3.2.2 Configuration Management Strategy

**There is nothing to configure, and no mechanism with which to configure it.** A recursive census of the checkout finds **zero** files in every configuration format (`*.yml`, `*.yaml`, `*.json`, `*.toml`, `*.ini`, `*.cfg`, `*.properties`, `*.xml`, `*.sh`, `*.tf`), confirmed first-hand, and `Project Guide.md` §9.2 opens with "Nothing to configure. No environment variable or secret is read by any tracked file."

| Configuration concern | Position at `HEAD` |
| --- | --- |
| Application configuration | **None.** No property, flag, profile or feature switch exists; the one behavioural value in the program is a hard-coded literal at `Hello.java` line 17 |
| Environment variables | **None consumed.** `JAVA_HOME` is explicitly not required and "not used by anything in this project"; the `PATH` binaries are sufficient (Appendix E) |
| Secret management | **None, and none needed.** No credential, key or token is read by any tracked file (§1.5) |
| Per-environment overrides | **None, and none possible.** Section 3.6.6 records that nothing differentiates dev, test and production |
| Toolchain configuration | **Recorded, not enforced.** OpenJDK 25.0.3 is recorded in `Project Guide.md` Appendix D; no `--release`, `--source`, `.java-version`, `.sdkmanrc` or `.tool-versions` constrains it |
| Repository-level configuration — **the recorded gap** | **Absent by decision.** No `.gitignore`, no `.gitattributes`, no `.editorconfig`; `core.autocrlf` and `core.eol` are unset, so `Hello.java`'s CRLF bytes and `README.md`'s LF bytes are preserved by editor discipline alone. Section 3.6.1 carries this as a Medium-severity technical risk, "Open — accepted by design" |

What the project does have is **branch promotion under review**, and that is the only promotion mechanism in the system.
