#### 8.3.2.4 Backup and Disaster Recovery

**Backup is inherited entirely from Git's distributed replication, and no recovery objective is defined anywhere.** Sections 5.4.6 and 6.5.3.4 record that no RTO, RPO, availability target or continuity plan exists in any tracked file, and none is asserted here.

| Recovery concern | Position at `HEAD` | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What must be recovered | The five tracked files and their history. Nothing else exists: no runtime state, no database, no configuration and no artifact | Sections 6.2, 8.2.3 |
| Backup mechanism | **Inherited — full replication per clone.** Every clone carries all 37 objects and all 14 commits, content-addressed so that corruption is detectable; `git fsck` is recorded clean in Section 6.4.3.5 | `git count-objects -vH` |
| Off-host copy | The GitHub remote, holding 8 refs at 3 distinct commits. The delivery branch exists both locally and as `origin/jr_java1`, plus `origin/blitzy-6d6c8680-…`, so more than one remote ref reaches the current work | `git show-ref`; `git branch -a` |
| Recovery procedure — source | Re-clone from the remote, then confirm with `git status --short` (no output) and `git ls-files` (five paths) | `Project Guide.md` §9.2 |
| Recovery procedure — build output | **Not needed.** The 420-byte class file is regenerated deterministically by one `javac` call with zero dependency resolution; nothing is restored, only rebuilt | Sections 8.2.1, 8.2.4 |
| Recovery point | The last pushed commit. Local-only commits are the exposure, which is precisely the outstanding `0 11` divergence between `main` and `jr_java1` | Direct measurement |
| Not conveyed by any clone | The reflog: `core.logallrefupdates` is `true` and `.git/logs/HEAD` exists locally, but it is untracked, so ref-movement history is lost with the host | Section 6.5.2.2 |
| **The one asset with no mechanical recovery path** | The hand-written evidence in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` — the 49-of-49 check record, the risk register and the open-item register. Section 5.4.6 records that this prose cannot be regenerated by any tool, only re-derived by re-running the checks on a JDK-equipped host | Section 5.4.6 |
| Declared objectives | **None.** No RTO, RPO, backup schedule, retention policy or restore test exists; the GPL v3 warranty disclaimer at `LICENSE` line 589 and liability limitation at line 600 are the project's entire continuity position | Sections 5.4.6, 6.5.3.4 |


## 8.4 Cloud Services

**This system uses no cloud services, and no cloud provider selection, service inventory, high-availability design or cloud cost model applies to it.** The reason is the same one that makes Section 8.1's determination hold: there is nothing to run in a cloud. The program binds no port, starts no listener and makes no network call (`Project Guide.md` Appendix B); it has no artifact to upload, no state to store and no request to serve.

The absence is verified rather than assumed. Section 3.7.4 records the result of searching for a cloud footprint in the tracked tree: "No cloud SDK import, credential, region or endpoint in any tracked file; no IaC descriptor," with the reason recorded as "Nothing is deployed." Section 8.1.2 adds the full probe set — no `template.yaml`, `samconfig.toml`, `cloudformation.yaml`, `cdk.json`, `pulumi.yaml`, `main.tf`, `app.yaml`, `fly.toml`, `render.yaml`, `vercel.json`, `netlify.toml`, `heroku.yml`, `.elasticbeanstalk`, `.gcloudignore`, `.azure`, `firebase.json` or `serverless.yml` at any point in the 14-commit history of any branch. `Hello.java` declares **zero** imports, so no SDK could be referenced even in principle, and `Project Guide.md` §1.5 records that no external service, registry or credential is used by anything in the project.

### 8.4.1 Cloud Concerns and Why Each Is Vacuous

| Cloud concern the specification asks for | Position | Reason it does not apply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider selection and justification | **No provider selected.** No account, project, subscription or tenant is referenced anywhere | There is no workload to place. Section 1.3.2.4 records "Deploying it as a service" as unsupported |
| Core services with versions | **None.** No compute, storage, database, queue, identity or networking service is used | Section 1.3.2.3 records that no service registry, artifact repository, broker, cache, database, identity provider or secret store is integrated |
| High-availability design | **Vacuous.** There is no resident process to keep available, no replica to balance and no failover target | `Project Guide.md` §9.5: "There is no service to start." Section 6.1.4.5 records the binary outcome model that admits no degraded mode |
| Cost optimisation strategy | **No cloud cost line exists.** Section 8.2.5 documents the whole cost structure: an operator workstation and a source host, with zero provisioned resource | No metered resource is consumed by this system |
| Security and compliance considerations | Inherited from the host and the hosting platform only. No credential, key or secret is read by any tracked file, and no compliance framework is named anywhere | `Project Guide.md` §1.5; Section 8.3.1.5 |

### 8.4.2 The One Hosted Dependency, and Why It Is Not a Cloud Runtime

The project does depend on one hosted service — the Git remote at `github.com/rjhonsi/BlitzyRepo2_Java.git` — and honesty requires documenting it rather than claiming a zero-dependency posture. It is a **source-hosting and review dependency, not a runtime**.

| Property | Observed value | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it hosts | Five text files and a 14-commit history: 8 refs at 3 distinct commits, 0 tags, a 302.84 KiB pack | It stores and conveys the system; it never executes it |
| What it executes | **Nothing.** No `.github/` workflow exists, so no runner, job or build is triggered by any push or merge | Section 3.7.4: "The hosting platform *is* GitHub, but no workflow exists" |
| Interface used | `git` over HTTPS for clone, fetch and push, plus the platform's pull-request merge — `HEAD` = `2a78292`, "Merged via API" | The only network path in the project (Section 8.3.1.4) |
| Presentation coupling | The platform's GitHub Flavored Markdown renderer displays `README.md` and resolves its two relative links. `Project Guide.md` §3 records that the rendered appearance has never been reviewed | A Medium-priority 0.5-hour open item, not a runtime dependency |
| Availability exposure | If the remote were unavailable, an existing clone still builds and runs unchanged, because the build needs no network access at all | `Project Guide.md` §9.3; Section 8.2.1 |
| Lock-in exposure | Low and mechanical: the dependency is plain Git over HTTPS with no platform-specific descriptor, so relocating the remote is a URL change | No workflow YAML, action, environment or platform integration exists to port |
| Cost exposure | Plan-determined rather than usage-determined at this footprint; the repository records neither its visibility nor its plan | Section 8.2.5 |

The distinction matters for the specification's cloud question: a hosted **source** dependency does not make a system cloud-deployed, because nothing about the running program touches it. Section 8.2.2 records that the runtime requirement is a JDK and a POSIX shell, and Section 8.3.1.1 classifies the environment as operator-local and ephemeral for exactly this reason.

### 8.4.3 What Would Make Cloud Services Applicable

The determination above describes the repository at commit `2a78292`, not a permanent property. Each change below would introduce the first genuine cloud concern and would oblige this sub-section to be rewritten as a substantive cloud-services architecture.

- **A bound port, listener or HTTP endpoint of any kind** — the first thing that would need hosting, and the first thing a provider, region and availability design would have to be chosen for.
- **A published artifact with declared coordinates** — the first thing that would need a registry, and the point at which release promotion (Section 8.3.2.3) would gain an artifact rather than only a branch.
- **Any persisted datum** — the first thing that would need durable, backed-up, region-resident storage, which Section 6.2 records no runtime path currently reaches.
- **A first cloud SDK import or credential** — the first supply-chain and secret-management surface, both of which Sections 3.7.5 and 8.3.2.2 record as currently absent by construction.
- **A CI workflow using hosted runners** — the first metered consumption attributable to this system, and the point at which the conditional cost terms in Section 8.2.5 would become an actual bill.


## 8.5 Containerization

**This system is not containerised, and no container platform, base-image strategy, image-versioning scheme, build-optimisation technique or image-scanning requirement applies to it.** `Project Guide.md` §9.1 states the position among the prerequisites that do not apply: "No package manager step, no virtual environment, **no container**, no database, no broker and no bound port."

The absence is verified at three levels. **At `HEAD`:** `Dockerfile`, `Containerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `docker-compose.yaml`, `compose.yml` and `.dockerignore` are all absent, as is `.devcontainer` (Section 8.1.2). **Across history:** `git log --all --pretty=format: --name-only` confirms that only the five known paths have ever been tracked on any branch, so no container descriptor was ever added and later removed. **In the stack assessment:** Section 3.7.4 records Docker as absent with the verification performed, and Section 1.3.2.1 lists "Containerisation / orchestration / IaC" among the explicitly excluded capabilities.

### 8.5.1 Why Containerisation Adds Nothing Here

Containerisation solves problems this system does not have. Each row below pairs the usual motivation with the property of this repository that already satisfies it.

| Usual motivation for a container | Why it does not apply | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Freeze a dependency set so builds are reproducible | There is no dependency set. "There is no `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `Makefile`, `package.json` or lock file of any kind, and nothing is downloaded at build time," and `Hello.java` declares zero imports | `Project Guide.md` §9.3 |
| Package an application with its runtime for deployment | Nothing is packaged or deployed. Zero archives or class files are tracked, and no deployment descriptor exists | Section 8.1.2; Section 1.3.2.4 |
| Provide an isolated, disposable filesystem for the build | Already provided, more cheaply, by `mktemp -d`: a uniquely named directory readable only by its owner, created per run and removed afterwards | `README.md` line 30; Section 8.1.3 |
| Make the environment portable across hosts | Already portable by construction: a JDK alone builds and runs the program, and the compile-then-run path was exercised at release targets 11, 17 and 21 | `Hello.java` lines 2–4; `Project Guide.md` §9.1 |
| Isolate a long-running process and bound its resources | There is no long-running process. `main` is invoked once, executes one statement and returns; no port is bound and no resource limit is set anywhere | `Project Guide.md` §9.5; Section 6.1.3.3 |
| Pin the toolchain version in an image tag | Deliberately not done. Section 3.7.3 records the position as "portability over reproducibility — versions are recorded, never enforced"; adopting a pin is an open Owner decision, not a planned task | ADR-007; `Project Guide.md` §1.4 |

Adding a container image would also contradict a stated constraint rather than merely adding weight: `Hello.java`'s class Javadoc records that the program "imports nothing outside `java.lang`, so a JDK alone builds and runs it," and Section 3.7.4 notes that adopting any default-stack element "would contradict the stated constraint that a JDK alone builds and runs the program." Section 3.7.5 records the concrete consequence — a container descriptor is a build/CI artifact, and committing one invalidates requirements F-004-RQ-001 and F-005-RQ-001 and changes the tracked-file census that requirement F-005-RQ-001 fixes.

### 8.5.2 What Would Make Containerisation Applicable

- **A first third-party dependency or a second compilation unit**, which would create the dependency-resolution and build-ordering concerns Section 2.4.3 records the project as currently having none of — the point at which freezing an environment starts to pay.
- **A bound port or resident process**, which would need isolation, a restart policy and a health probe; Section 6.5.3.1 records that no liveness, readiness or startup probe can exist today because there is no listener to answer one.
- **A decision to pin the toolchain**, since an image tag is one way to enforce what Section 3.7.3 records as deliberately unenforced.
- **A CI pipeline**, which would need a reproducible build environment; Section 8.7 records that none exists and that build, test and CI files are out of scope by declaration.

Were any of these to land, the specification would need a container platform selection, a base-image and patching policy, an image-tagging scheme tied to the commit SHA (the repository's existing addressing scheme, since Section 2.6.3 records zero tags), a layer-caching strategy, and an image-scanning requirement in the CI gate. None of that can be specified today without inventing infrastructure the repository does not have.


## 8.6 Orchestration

**This system requires no orchestration, and no orchestration platform, cluster architecture, service-deployment strategy, auto-scaling configuration or resource-allocation policy applies to it.** Orchestration schedules, places, scales and heals long-lived workloads; this system's workload is one JVM process that executes four bytecode instructions and returns. `Project Guide.md` §9.5 records the operational fact that removes the entire concern: "There is no service to start — the program writes one line and exits."

The absence is verified: `k8s/`, `kubernetes/`, `helm/`, `Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, `deployment.yaml`, `skaffold.yaml`, `Tiltfile`, `nomad.hcl`, `task-definition.json`, `ecs-params.yml`, `Procfile`, `crontab`, `hello.service` and `systemd/` are all absent at `HEAD` and have never been tracked on any branch (Sections 8.1.2, 6.5.1.2). Section 1.3.2.1 lists orchestration among the explicitly excluded capabilities, and Section 3.7.4 records the same result for Terraform and Docker with the verification performed.

### 8.6.1 Orchestration Concerns and Their Observed Substitutes

| Orchestration concern | Position | What plays the role instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Platform selection | **None.** No orchestrator is referenced anywhere in the tracked tree | The operator's shell. Section 6.5.2.6 records that "the collection tier and the evaluation tier are the same human"; the same is true of scheduling |
| Cluster architecture | **Vacuous.** There is no node, pool, control plane or data plane; the unit of execution is one process on one host | A single workstation, outside the system boundary (Section 1.3.1.2) |
| Service deployment strategy | **None.** Nothing is deployed; Section 8.7.2 records that the only promotion in the system is branch-to-branch under human review | `git push` plus a pull-request merge |
| Scheduling and placement | **None.** No scheduler, cron entry, systemd timer or active Git hook exists — all 14 `.git/hooks` entries are `*.sample` | A human typing `java Hello`. Execution is synchronous with intent (Section 6.5.3.1) |
| Auto-scaling configuration | **Vacuous, and unbounded in principle.** Section 6.1.3.1 records horizontal capacity as unbounded in principle and entirely manual in practice, because each launch is an independent process that shares nothing | Launching the program more times; the ceiling is host capacity, which the repository never measures |
| Resource allocation policy | **None.** No `-Xmx`, `-Xms`, `-XX:`, `JAVA_OPTS`, `ulimit`, cgroup, `nice` or `taskset` setting exists in any tracked file; the JVM runs with host defaults on every invocation | Host defaults, unconstrained (Section 6.1.3.3) |
| Service discovery and networking | **Vacuous.** No port, listener, endpoint or URI exists to register or resolve | Not applicable (Sections 8.3.1.4, 6.3.1.2) |
| Self-healing and restart policy | **None.** Section 6.1.4.1 records that no process manager, supervisor or watchdog exists to restart anything on an operator's behalf | Re-running the command, which is safe because the payload is a compile-time constant and a re-run is idempotent (Section 6.5.4.2) |
| Rolling updates and versioned rollout | **None.** Zero tags across 14 commits and no artifact to roll out | Rollback is `git checkout` of an earlier commit (Section 8.7.2.3) |

### 8.6.2 What Would Make Orchestration Applicable

Orchestration becomes a genuine concern the moment the workload stops being an invoke-and-exit process. The triggers are the same ones Section 6.5.5.2 records for monitoring, because both concerns depend on the same missing precondition — a resident process:

- **A server loop, listener, scheduler or daemon entry point**, which would introduce placement, restart and probe semantics for the first time.
- **More than one cooperating process or a second compilation unit**, which would introduce ordering, dependency and discovery concerns Section 2.4.3 records as absent today.
- **A declared availability or capacity target**, which would give an autoscaler something to act on; Sections 5.4.5 and 6.5.3.5 record that no such target exists in any tracked file.
- **A container image**, since Section 8.5 records that none exists and orchestration of an uncontainerised single-file program has nothing to schedule.


## 8.7 CI/CD Pipeline

**No continuous-integration or continuous-delivery pipeline exists in this repository, and none has ever existed.** Section 8.1.2 records the probe set — `.github/`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.circleci/`, `Jenkinsfile`, `.travis.yml`, `azure-pipelines.yml`, `bitbucket-pipelines.yml`, `.drone.yml`, `.buildkite`, `woodpecker.yml`, `buildspec.yml`, `codeship-services.yml`, `cloudbuild.yaml` and `appveyor.yml`, all absent — and the full-history check confirms none was ever tracked on any of the eight refs. All 14 entries in `.git/hooks` are `*.sample`, so no local automation runs either. `README.md` line 18 records the same absence from the version-pinning angle: the repository carries no "CI descriptor … in which a version could be recorded."

The absence is a **declared scope boundary, not an oversight**. `Project Guide.md` §9.6 instructs that the acceptance suite be saved outside the checkout and run there, "never commit it, since build, test and CI files are out of scope for this repository," and §5 records that "No ignore rule and no build, test or CI descriptor was added." Adopting an automated gate is carried as an open **Owner decision** with ETA "Deferred" (`Project Guide.md` §1.4), and as the Medium-severity, Medium-probability risk that §8 calls "the one recommendation that outlives this change." ADR-002 is the recorded decision.

What follows therefore documents the **pipeline that is actually in force: a manual one**, with every stage, trigger, gate and expected result named, so that an operator can execute it and a reviewer can tell whether it was executed.

### 8.7.1 Build Pipeline

#### 8.7.1.1 Source Control Triggers

| Trigger point | Automated? | What actually happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local commit | **No** — no `pre-commit`, `commit-msg` or `pre-push` hook is active; all 14 hook files are `*.sample` | The operator is expected to have run the gates in Section 8.7.1.4 by hand beforehand |
| Push to `origin` | **No** — no server-side workflow is configured | The remote accepts the ref; nothing is built or validated |
| Pull request opened | **No** — no required status check exists, because no check exists to require | Human review is the only gate (Section 8.3.2.3) |
| Pull request merged | **No pipeline.** The merge itself is the only automation-adjacent facility: `HEAD` = `2a78292` "Merge pull request #1", recorded as "Merged via API" by `blitzy-qa[bot]` | Section 3.6.5 characterises it as "a human/bot workflow step, not a pipeline" |
| Tag or release created | **Never occurs.** `git tag` returns zero tags across 14 commits | No release trigger exists to wire a pipeline to |
| Scheduled build | **None.** No cron entry, systemd timer or scheduled workflow exists | Nothing re-runs on a schedule; the 49 recorded checks are a point-in-time observation |

#### 8.7.1.2 Build Environment Requirements

A JDK on `PATH` and a POSIX shell — the full requirement set is documented in Section 8.2.1. Three properties make the build environment unusually cheap to satisfy, and each is verifiable: **no network access is needed** (nothing is downloaded), **no configuration is read** (no environment variable or secret is consumed), and **no state carries between runs** (each build writes into a fresh `mktemp -d` directory). The recorded reference environment is a Linux host with OpenJDK 25.0.3, on which `Project Guide.md` §9 states every documented command was executed.

#### 8.7.1.3 Dependency Management

**There is nothing to manage.** `Project Guide.md` §9.3: "None. There is no `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `Makefile`, `package.json` or lock file of any kind, and nothing is downloaded at build time." `Hello.java` declares zero imports and relies only on `java.lang`, which the JVM supplies. The consequences for a pipeline are worth stating because they eliminate most of what a build pipeline normally does: no resolution step, no lock-file verification, no private registry credential, no cache to warm, no vulnerability feed to consult for direct dependencies, and zero supply-chain surface of the project's own. The residual exposure is the toolchain itself, which Section 3.7.3 records as unpinned by choice — runtime CVE exposure is a property of the operator's chosen JDK build.

#### 8.7.1.4 Quality Gates

Five gates exist. All are commands with published expected results; **none runs automatically**, and their only durable record is prose in `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md`.

| Gate | Command | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compilation | `javac Hello.java` | Exit 0, no diagnostics |
| Static analysis — the project's entire surface, "as no linter is configured" | `javac -Xlint:all -Werror -d "$B" Hello.java` | Exit 0, empty error stream |
| Documentation coverage | `javadoc -d "$B/jd" -quiet Hello.java` | Exit 0 with **exactly one** warning, for the implicit default constructor at `Hello.java:6`; coverage 2 of 3 documentable members |
| Behaviour parity against baseline `0726b1d` | Rebuild the baseline, run both builds, `cmp` both captured streams | `behaviour identical` — stdout, stderr and exit status all match |
| Repository hygiene | `git status --short`; `git ls-files` | No output from the first; the five tracked paths from the second |
| Acceptance suite V1–V9, run from a scratch directory outside the checkout | `bash "$S/verify.sh" "$PWD" …` | **49 checks executed, 49 passed, 0 failed** — 37 acceptance assertions plus 12 direct toolchain checks, recorded on OpenJDK 25.0.3 |
| Cross-release compilation | Compile at release targets 11, 17 and 21 | Exit 0 at each; 7 checks, all passed |

Two operational notes belong with this table. The `javadoc` gate has a **permanently expected non-zero result** — one warning is correct, and 0 or ≥2 signals that coverage changed. And the acceptance suite's comment-census check must be given the **pre-comment revision `0726b1d`** as its baseline; run against the current commit the comparison is empty and four checks fail on a tree that is correct, which `Project Guide.md` §8 names as "the single most likely thing to mislead the next person."

#### 8.7.1.5 Artifact Generation and Storage

| Concern | Position |
| --- | --- |
| Artifact produced | One `Hello.class` file, **420 bytes**, written into a per-run `mktemp -d` directory |
| Artifact retention | **None.** The directory is removed by `rm -rf "$B" …`, and `README.md` line 30 instructs "Do not commit the class file either way" |
| Artifact repository | **None.** No registry, no coordinates, and zero binary blobs tracked in the five-file index |
| Reproducibility | Behaviourally reproducible, not bit-reproducible by policy: any JDK produces the same program output, but no toolchain version is recorded in or enforced by the build |
| Provenance record | The Git commit graph only — content-addressed blobs and 14 commits with author identity and timestamps |

### 8.7.2 Deployment Pipeline

#### 8.7.2.1 Deployment Strategy

**No deployment strategy applies, because nothing is deployed.** Blue-green, canary and rolling strategies all presuppose a running instance to shift traffic between, and Section 8.1.1 records that this system has no artifact, no host and no network surface. Section 1.3.2.4 lists "Deploying it as a service" as unsupported.

The delivery model that does exist is **source promotion**: the working branch is merged into the default branch under human review, and consumers clone and build locally. Section 8.3.2.3 documents the mechanism and its current outstanding state — `main` is 11 commits behind `jr_java1`.

**Figure 8.7.2-A — Deployment workflow: the manual build-and-verify pipeline in force, the promotion step, and the automated pipeline verified absent**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start(["Operator clones or pulls the repository<br/>git clone over HTTPS, 302.84 KiB pack"])
    Prep["Create a per-run build directory<br/>B=\$(mktemp -d) — owner-readable, unique"]
    Build["Compile the single unit<br/>javac -Xlint:all -d \$B Hello.java"]
    BuildOK{"Exit 0 and<br/>no diagnostics?"}
    Doc["Documentation gate<br/>javadoc -d \$B/jd -quiet Hello.java"]
    DocOK{"Exactly one<br/>expected warning?"}
    Run["Launch: java -cp \$B Hello<br/>or java Hello.java on JDK 11+"]
    Verify{"Three observables match<br/>README.md lines 59-63?"}
    Parity["Behaviour parity against baseline 0726b1d<br/>cmp both captured streams"]
    Hygiene["Hygiene: rm -rf \$B<br/>then git status --short"]
    HygieneOK{"Working tree<br/>clean?"}
    Record["Record the outcome by hand in<br/>Project Guide sections 3 and 4"]
    Promote["Promote: commit, push,<br/>open a pull request, merge to main"]
    Done(["Delivered: correct stdout, empty stderr,<br/>exit status 0, clean tree"])
    Fix["Consult the runbook — Project Guide section 9.8,<br/>seven symptom, cause and resolution rows"]

    subgraph AbsentPipeline["Verified absent — every stage above is executed by a human"]
        NP1["No CI descriptor, workflow, runner<br/>or required status check"]
        NP2["No artifact registry, release tag<br/>or version number"]
        NP3["No deployment target, environment,<br/>approval record or rollout window"]
        NP4["No automated post-deployment probe,<br/>smoke test or alert on failure"]
        NP1 --- NP2
        NP2 --- NP3
        NP3 --- NP4
    end

    Start --> Prep
    Prep --> Build
    Build --> BuildOK
    BuildOK -->|"no"| Fix
    BuildOK -->|"yes"| Doc
    Doc --> DocOK
    DocOK -->|"no — 0 or 2+ warnings"| Fix
    DocOK -->|"yes"| Run
    Run --> Verify
    Verify -->|"no"| Fix
    Verify -->|"yes"| Parity
    Parity --> Hygiene
    Hygiene --> HygieneOK
    HygieneOK -->|"no — untracked Hello.class,<br/>no ignore rule exists"| Fix
    HygieneOK -->|"yes"| Record
    Record --> Promote
    Promote --> Done
    Fix -->|"apply the documented resolution<br/>and re-run; a re-run is idempotent"| Prep
    Start -.->|"no stage in this workflow is automated"| NP1
```

#### 8.7.2.2 Environment Promotion Workflow

Documented in full in Section 8.3.2.3 and depicted in Figure 8.3.2-A. In summary: `jr_java1` → pull request → human review → merge commit on `main`; no environment tier, no automated gate, no artifact and no tag participate. The outstanding promotion — `main` 11 commits behind — is recorded as a High-priority 0.5-hour item in `Project Guide.md` §1.6, and Section 2.6.4 notes that completing it closes requirement F-005-RQ-005.

#### 8.7.2.3 Rollback Procedures

Rollback is a Git operation on source, not a redeployment, and it is unusually safe here for three reasons the repository records: the build resolves nothing, the payload is a compile-time constant, and each build writes into a fresh directory.

| Failure | Rollback action | Verification after rollback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A bad commit on the working branch | `git revert` or reset to the prior commit; the history is append-only and content-addressed, so every prior state is recoverable | `git status --short` clean; re-run the Section 8.7.1.4 gates |
| A regression in program behaviour | Rebuild baseline revision `0726b1d` and `cmp` both captured streams, per `Project Guide.md` §9.6 | `behaviour identical` |
| A bad merge on `main` | Revert the merge commit; `HEAD` is itself a merge (`2a78292`), so the pattern is already exercised in this history | `git log`; re-run the gates from a clean clone |
| A stale or corrupted local checkout | Re-clone from the remote; every clone replicates all 37 objects | `git ls-files` returns the five tracked paths |
| Untracked build output left behind | `rm -f Hello.class` (Path A) or `rm -rf "$B"` (Path B) | `git status --short` prints nothing |
| A consumer already holding a bad revision | **No recall mechanism exists.** With no tags, no registry and no published artifact, the only addressing scheme is the commit SHA; Section 2.6.3 records that requirement versions are anchored to SHAs for exactly this reason | The consumer re-clones or checks out a known-good SHA |

#### 8.7.2.4 Post-Deployment Validation

There is no deployment to validate, so validation is **post-build and post-merge**, and it is the same three-value check that serves as the system's health check (Section 6.5.3.1):

```bash
java Hello; echo "exit=$?"     # expect: Hello from Java!  then  exit=0
```

Standard output must be byte-identical to the fenced oracle at `README.md` lines 59–61, standard error must be empty, and the exit status must be 0 by normal return. `Project Guide.md` §9.7 records exactly that transcript. Two limitations are recorded rather than mitigated: **no run leaves evidence of itself** (Section 6.4.5.2, control row SC-22), and **there is no channel on which a failure could be announced** (Section 6.5.4.1) — detection depends on a human reading the terminal at the moment of the run.

#### 8.7.2.5 Release Management

| Release concern | Position at `HEAD` |
| --- | --- |
| Release line | **None.** Zero tags across 14 commits; no version number appears in any tracked file |
| Version addressing | Commit SHA. Section 2.6.3 records SHA anchoring as the requirement-versioning rule, and Section 3.7.5 records that adopting tags would invalidate requirement F-005-RQ-003 |
| Change record | Commit messages and the documentation itself. There is no `CHANGELOG.md`; `README.md` lines 5–8 carry a dated summary of changes, which also discharges the GPL v3 modification-notice obligation |
| Release notes and readiness statement | `Project Guide.md` §1.6 records "Production readiness: **ready to merge**", with the risk of releasing described as close to zero "for a documentation change to a program whose behaviour is provably untouched" |
| Release gate | Human review on the pull request. No automated gate exists, and Section 1.3.2.4 lists "Expecting a committed gate to validate a change" as an unsupported use case |
| Sign-off evidence | The point-in-time record of 49 of 49 checks passing on OpenJDK 25.0.3 in `Project Guide.md` §3 — hand-written, and stale the moment the source changes |
| Commit signing | **Not in force.** Commit-signing infrastructure is one of the four items `Project Guide.md` §1.4 classes as "Non-documentation items outside this scope," marked Owner decision and Deferred |

### 8.7.3 Consequences of Having No Pipeline

| Consequence | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| The 49 recorded checks were run manually and are not repeatable automatically | `Project Guide.md` §1.4, §3 |
| Verification tooling must **not** be committed, by declared scope | `Project Guide.md` §9.6; Section 2.4.1 F-009 |
| The documentation checks will not re-run on future changes, so the guide's accuracy depends on future editors honouring its stable-symbol citations | `Project Guide.md` §1.4, §8 |
| Any change to `Hello.java` requires a manual `javac -Xlint:all -Werror` re-run | Section 2.4.5 F-004 |
| Adopting an automated gate is an open Owner decision with ETA "Deferred", carried as a Medium/Medium risk | `Project Guide.md` §1.4, §6 |
| A violation introduced by a commit stays undetected until someone re-runs the checks | Section 6.5.3.6 |

Section 6.5.5.2 records the three changes that would close these limitations without altering any applicability determination: a committed automated gate, a `.gitignore` (which would remove the standing untracked-class-file false positive, fault E-3), and a `SUPPORT.md` or `SECURITY.md` with a contact address.


## 8.8 Infrastructure Monitoring

**No infrastructure monitoring exists, and no component capable of hosting it is present.** Section 6.5 reaches the parallel determination for application monitoring — "Detailed Monitoring Architecture is not applicable for this system" — supported by 109 existence probes returning zero present files, a 64-marker in-source observability census returning exactly one hit (the payload `println` at line 17), and a recursive telemetry-data search returning zero `*.log`, `*.jfr`, `*.hprof`, `*.prom` or `*.tsdb` files.

This sub-section does not repeat that analysis. It addresses the narrower question the infrastructure section asks: **of the three elements that play an infrastructure role** — the operator workstation, the Git remote and the per-run `mktemp -d` directory (Section 8.1.3) — what is monitored, by what mechanism, and what is verifiably not. Each concern below is labelled **genuinely absent**, **inherited**, **selected** or **absent and expected**, using the classification Section 8.1 establishes.

### 8.8.1 Resource Monitoring

**Genuinely absent for the host; selected and manual for the repository.** No host metric is collected: no CPU, memory, disk or network sample is taken, no agent is installed, no scrape target exists and nothing is bound for a collector to reach (`Project Guide.md` Appendix B). The workstation lies outside the system boundary (Section 1.3.1.2), so its resources are the operator's concern and the repository neither measures nor constrains them — Section 6.1.3.3 records that no `-Xmx`, `-Xms`, `-XX:`, `JAVA_OPTS`, `ulimit` or cgroup setting exists anywhere.

What is monitored is the **footprint of the artifacts themselves**, by commands an operator runs on demand. These are structural measurements with a single recorded value each, not series:

| Resource observed | Command | Expected or measured value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tracked inventory | `git ls-files -s` | Five entries, all index mode `100644` |
| Tracked byte total | `wc -c` over the tracked set | 925,008 bytes — 1,073 of source, 884,733 in the two `blitzy/documentation/` records |
| Object-store footprint | `git count-objects -vH` | 37 objects in 1 pack, 302.84 KiB, 0 loose, 0 garbage |
| Object-store integrity | `git fsck` | No output — clean |
| History size | `git rev-list --all --count`; `git show-ref`; `git tag` | 14 commits, 8 refs, **0 tags** |
| Working-tree cleanliness | `git status --short` | No output; a line means untracked build output, since no ignore rule exists |
| Branch position | `git rev-list --left-right --count main...HEAD` | `0 11` — the outstanding promotion state |
| Per-run build output | Inspect the `mktemp -d` directory | One 420-byte class file, removed by `rm -rf "$B"` |

Three limitations follow, and all three are recorded rather than mitigated. Nothing collects these values on a schedule; **no run leaves evidence of itself** (Section 6.4.5.2, control row SC-22); and no threshold or trend exists to compare a value against, because Section 6.5.3.5 records that no capacity plan, quota or growth projection exists in any tracked file. The one growth signal available is descriptive rather than governed: the two documentation records are roughly 824 times the size of the source they describe.

### 8.8.2 Performance Metrics Collection

**Genuinely absent.** No timing measurement of any kind is recorded in any tracked file, and no instrument exists to take one — the observability census found no `System.nanoTime`, `System.currentTimeMillis`, `Instant.now` or `Duration.` reference in `Hello.java`. Section 5.4.5 records the position for the specification as a whole, and notes that runtime cost is dominated by JVM start-up rather than by anything the program does, "a characteristic the repository notes nowhere and measures nowhere."

What exists instead are **structural baselines** — properties of the artifact, not of a run, and each with a named source:

| Baseline | Recorded value | Source of record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work per invocation | 4 bytecode instructions in `main` | Section 5.4.5 |
| Deployable artifact size | 420 bytes | Section 5.4.5 |
| Compilation input | 1 file, 20 lines, 1,073 bytes, 5 executable lines, 1 statement | Measured first-hand |
| Standard-output volume | 16 ASCII characters plus one platform separator — 17 bytes on an LF host | `Project Guide.md` §4 |
| Standard-error volume | 0 bytes on every run | `README.md` line 63 |
| Dependency-resolution cost | 0 artifacts fetched, 0 bytes downloaded | `Project Guide.md` §9.3 |
| Build outcome | Exit 0 with no diagnostics, including under `-Xlint:all -Werror` | `Project Guide.md` §3, §9.4 |
| Start-up latency, wall-clock, CPU, memory | **Not measured anywhere** | Section 5.4.5 |

Section 1.3.2.4 records the corresponding unsupported use case: "Using the program as a performance, load, or soak benchmark," because "no measurement, instrumentation, or timing exists; no such target is recorded anywhere."

### 8.8.3 Cost Monitoring and Optimisation

**Genuinely absent, and there is no metered consumption to monitor.** No billing account, usage export, budget, tag-based allocation or spend alert is referenced anywhere in the repository, and Section 8.2.5 records why: the system provisions no compute, no storage service, no registry, no data service and no CI runner minutes. `Project Guide.md` §1.5 records that no external service, registry or credential is used by anything in the project.

| Cost-monitoring concern | Position |
| --- | --- |
| Usage telemetry | **None.** No metered resource is consumed by this system, so there is no meter to read |
| Budget and spend alerting | **None, and no notification channel exists on which an alert could be raised** (Section 6.5.4.1) |
| Cost allocation | **Not applicable.** No resource exists to tag, and no account boundary belongs to this system |
| Hosting spend | Plan-determined at this footprint, and the plan is not recorded in the checkout (Section 8.2.5) |
| Optimisation levers available | **Structurally exhausted.** Zero dependencies to cache, zero artifacts to retain, zero runners to right-size, and a 420-byte build output already deleted after each run |
| The one quantity the project does track | Human effort: 32.0 of 38.0 hours completed (84.2%), 6.0 remaining across 11 open items — counted by hand in `Project Guide.md` §1.2 and §1.4, with no series behind it |

The honest optimisation statement is that the only cost this system can incur is **avoidable work**, and the repository's own mechanism for containing it is the published command-and-expected-result reference in `Project Guide.md` Appendix A, which lets an operator confirm an outcome instead of investigating one.

### 8.8.4 Security Monitoring and Compliance Auditing

#### 8.8.4.1 Security Monitoring

**Absent and expected** for scanning and alerting; **selected** for the two compile-time controls the project does operate. No security tooling of any kind is configured: `.github/dependabot.yml`, `.github/codeql-config.yml`, `.snyk`, `trivy.yaml`, `.trivyignore`, `.semgrep.yml`, `sonar-project.properties`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `checkstyle.xml`, `spotbugs.xml`, `pmd.xml`, `SECURITY.md` and `CODEOWNERS` are all absent, verified first-hand at `HEAD`. Section 6.4.5.2 carries monitoring, alerting and incident detection as control row SC-23, "Absent and expected."

| Security-monitoring concern | Position at `HEAD` |
| --- | --- |
| Dependency and supply-chain scanning | **Not needed for dependencies, because there are none** — zero imports, no manifest, nothing downloaded at build time. No scanner is configured either way |
| Static application security testing | **Selected, minimally.** `javac -Xlint:all -Werror` is "the project's static-analysis surface, as no linter is configured" (`Project Guide.md` Appendix F); it is run by hand, never automatically |
| Secret scanning | **No secret exists to detect.** No credential, key, token or environment variable is read by any tracked file (`Project Guide.md` §1.5, Appendix E) |
| Filesystem hardening at build time | **Selected.** `mktemp -d` yields a uniquely named, owner-readable output directory per build, specifically to avoid the pre-creation and symlink-redirection exposure a fixed path carries (`README.md` line 30) |
| Runtime intrusion and network monitoring | **Vacuous.** No port, listener or network call exists to monitor (Appendix B) |
| Commit provenance | **Partially in force and not verifiable here.** `git log --pretty='%G?'` reports **no signature** for 10 of the 14 commits, and for the remaining 4 reports a signature that could not be verified in this environment. Commit-signing infrastructure is one of the four items `Project Guide.md` §1.4 classes as outside scope, marked Owner decision and Deferred |
| Vulnerability disclosure route | **Absent and expected.** No `SECURITY.md`, `SUPPORT.md` or contact address exists; Section 6.4.5.3 carries the missing disclosure path as a residual risk with no compensating control |
| Residual technology exposure | The **unpinned toolchain**: runtime CVE exposure is entirely a property of the operator's chosen JDK build, neither recorded nor constrained by the repository (Section 3.7.3, ADR-007) |

#### 8.8.4.2 Compliance Auditing

**Inherited from Git, and documentary rather than automatic.** No audit framework, evidence pipeline, control catalogue or attestation exists in the repository, and Section 8.3.1.5 records that no compliance regime is named anywhere — a case-insensitive census over `Hello.java`, `README.md` and `LICENSE` for GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, PCI, ISO 27001, FedRAMP, CCPA, data-residency, personal-data, PII, export-control, encryption, audit-log and retention terms returns zero hits.

| Audit concern | What actually serves as the record | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change history | The Git commit graph: 14 commits with author identity and ISO-8601 timestamps in an append-only, content-addressed store that every clone replicates, `git fsck` clean | Records *changes*, never *executions*; 10 of 14 commits are unsigned, so author identity is asserted rather than cryptographically proven |
| Review record | Pull-request review on the hosting platform; `HEAD` = `2a78292` "Merge pull request #1", "Merged via API" | Held by the platform, not by the repository; no approval artifact is tracked |
| Verification evidence | `Project Guide.md` §3 and §4: 49 checks executed, 49 passed, 0 failed on OpenJDK 25.0.3, with an explicit "Not Covered" list | Hand-written and point-in-time; stale the moment the source changes, because nothing re-runs it |
| Ref-movement history | `.git/logs/HEAD`, with `core.logallrefupdates` set to `true` | **Untracked** — conveyed by no clone, so it is a local artifact rather than a distributable audit record (Section 6.5.2.2) |
| Licence compliance | Verbatim GPL v3 in `LICENSE`, with the dated modification notice at `README.md` line 5 | Compliance is asserted in prose; no automated licence check exists |
| Execution audit trail | **None.** Section 6.4.5.2 control row SC-22 records that no run leaves evidence of itself — no log file, exit-status record, metric or trace | Detection of any failure depends on a human watching the terminal at the moment of the run |

### 8.8.5 Conditions That Would Make Infrastructure Monitoring Applicable

The determination above describes the repository at commit `2a78292` on branch `jr_java1`. Each change below would satisfy a precondition that currently fails and would oblige this sub-section — and, in most cases, Sections 8.3 through 8.7 — to be rewritten as substantive infrastructure documentation rather than amended.

| Repository change | Precondition it would satisfy | What would then need documenting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A resident process, server loop, listener or bound port | I1, I3 — a deployable, reachable workload | Host and process resource monitoring, health probes, availability targets, and the network architecture Section 8.3.1.4 currently records as absent |
| A container image, Compose file or Kubernetes manifest | I1, I6, I7 — a placement model with restart and probe semantics | Sections 8.5 and 8.6 in full, plus image scanning and a base-image patching policy |
| A CI descriptor, cron entry, systemd timer or active Git hook | I6 — an automated executor | Section 8.7 as a real pipeline: runner sizing, quality-gate enforcement, artifact retention, and the first metered cost line (Section 8.2.5) |
| A cloud account, IaC descriptor or PaaS manifest | I7 — a declared target environment | Section 8.4 in full: provider selection, service inventory, HA design, cost monitoring and region/residency compliance |
| Any persisted datum or published artifact | I1, I4 — state and artifacts to protect | Backup schedules, retention, restore testing, and the RTO/RPO objectives Section 5.4.6 records as currently undefined |
| A first configuration file of any format | I5 — a place to express environment-specific settings | Configuration management, promotion between environments, and secret handling |
| A declared SLA, SLO, threshold or capacity target | — | Alert thresholds with bands rather than the exact-value conformance matrix Section 6.5.3.6 documents today |
| A first third-party dependency | — | Supply-chain scanning, lock-file verification and a vulnerability feed, none of which is needed while `Hello.java` declares zero imports |

Three further changes would **not** alter any applicability determination but would each close a limitation recorded above: a **committed automated gate**, which would make the 49 checks repeatable and turn a point-in-time record into a signal; a **`.gitignore`**, which would remove the standing untracked-class-file false positive in the hygiene check (fault E-3); and a **`SECURITY.md` with a contact address**, which would give the disclosure and escalation path a destination outside the operator's own session.

### 9.1.2 Source Byte Anatomy of the Compilation Unit

Sections 4.3, 5.1 and 6.6 all rest on the claim that the documentation change added comments and altered no code. That claim is verifiable at byte level, and the arithmetic is recorded here because it is unusually clean.

| Portion of `Hello.java` | Lines | Bytes including CRLF |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Executable code — lines 6, 15, 17, 19, 20 | 5 | 127 |
| Comments — class Javadoc, `main` Javadoc, two line comments | 15 | 946 |
| **File total** | **20** | **1,073** |

**The five executable lines occupy exactly 127 bytes, which is the entire size of the original pre-comment file** introduced at `f1847fa` and recorded in Section 2.6.3. The code region is therefore byte-identical in both content and extent to the file as first committed, and every one of the 946 added bytes is comment. Expressed as proportions, 88.2 per cent of the file's bytes and 75 per cent of its lines are documentation — the measured form of the "comment-only, additions-only edit" that ADR-008 records and that requirement F-008-RQ-003 asserts through the `added=15` census.

The longest line in the file is 141 characters, inside the `main` Javadoc; no executable line exceeds 48 characters.

### 9.1.3 Compiled Artifact Anatomy and Target Equivalence

Sections 5.4.5 and 6.6.1.4.4 quote the compiled artifact as 420 bytes with four bytecode instructions in `main`. The structure behind those two figures is **recorded** in the archived specification, which inspected the class file with `javap -v -p` on a `javac` 21.0.12 toolchain against the pre-comment revision. It is reproduced here because it is the only description of the artifact anywhere in the project, and because it resolves an apparent arithmetic gap.

| Class-file property | Recorded value |
| --- | --- |
| Magic, minor/major version | `ca fe ba be`, 0 / 65 — the Java 21 class-file format, from the unpinned toolchain |
| Access flags, `this_class` / `super_class` | `0x0021` (`ACC_PUBLIC`, `ACC_SUPER`); `Hello` over `java/lang/Object` |
| Interfaces, fields | 0 and 0 |
| Methods, class attributes | 2 methods; one attribute, `SourceFile: "Hello.java"` |
| Constant pool | 28 entries: 17 `Utf8`, 4 `Class`, 3 `NameAndType`, 2 `Methodref`, 1 `String`, 1 `Fieldref` |
| Artifact size | 420 bytes |

**The instruction counts reconcile as follows.** The class contains seven bytecode instructions and three line-table entries; four of the seven are the `main` body that Section 5.4.5 names (`getstatic`, `ldc`, `invokevirtual`, `return`) and the remaining three are the implicit default constructor the compiler synthesises (`aload_0`, `invokespecial`, `return`). The same implicit constructor is the member that caps documentation coverage at 2 of 3 and produces the single standing `javadoc` warning recorded in Section 6.6.3.1 — so one synthetic member accounts for both the instruction gap and the coverage gap.

The four `Class` constant-pool entries — `java/lang/Object`, `java/lang/System`, `java/io/PrintStream` and `Hello` — are the complete external type surface of the compiled program, matching the API inventory in Section 3.2.2 and ADR-003. The single `String` entry holds `Hello from Java!` and is, as Section 3.5.5 puts it, the whole of the system's data at rest.

**Target equivalence (recorded).** The archived specification compiled the unit at four release levels and compared the artifacts byte by byte.

| `--release` target | Class-file major version | Recorded outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | 52 | Compiles, with obsolescence warnings for source and target |
| 11 | 55 | Compiles with no diagnostics |
| 17 | 61 | Compiles with no diagnostics |
| 21 | 65 | Compiles with no diagnostics; the default on that host |

Every one of the four artifacts is exactly 420 bytes and **any pair differs in exactly one byte** — offset 7, the low half of the major-version field, holding `0x34`, `0x37`, `0x3D` and `0x41`. The recorded compiler rejected `--release 7` at the bottom of the range and 22, 23 and 25 at the top, so the compatibility range of this source is set entirely by which compiler an operator happens to have — the consequence ADR-007 accepts. Note that the Project Guide's own cross-release run, reported in Section 6.6.1.3.1, exercised targets 11, 17 and 21 on OpenJDK 25.0.3; the release-8 result and the one-byte comparison come from the earlier 21.0.12 host and have not been re-observed.

One reproducibility consequence deserves stating plainly, because nothing else in this document states it: **a one-byte version difference produces an entirely different artifact digest**, so comparing class-file hashes across two build hosts proves nothing about source drift unless the target release is pinned — and no file in this repository pins one. The artifact digest the archive recorded (`0edbc17a3477…`, at target 21, with debug information) must therefore not be used as an expected value for the current source: the comment insertion moved every code line, which changes the `LineNumberTable` values even though it leaves the size and structure untouched. The Project Guide's parity check accounts for exactly this by suppressing debug information, at which point the two revisions' class files compare identical (Section 6.6.1.4.1).

### 9.1.4 Output-Contract Sensitivities

Sections 4, 5 and 6 quote the emitted payload as 17 bytes on an LF host and 18 on a CRLF host. The archived specification measured the full sensitivity of that figure, and two of its four conditions appear nowhere else in this document.

| JVM property | Value on the recording host | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `file.encoding`, `native.encoding` | `UTF-8` | Platform encoding; irrelevant to the payload, which is pure ASCII |
| `stdout.encoding`, `stderr.encoding` | `UTF-8` | Determines how `PrintStream` converts the string to bytes |
| `line.separator` | `\n` | Determines the terminator `println` appends |

| Condition | Recorded stdout bytes | Consequence for a byte-count oracle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default: LF separator, UTF-8 sink | 17 | The baseline every other section quotes |
| `-Dline.separator` set to CRLF | 18 | A Windows-default host emits 18 bytes with no source change |
| `stdout.encoding` `ISO-8859-1` or `US-ASCII` | 17 | Any single-byte encoding leaves the payload unchanged |
| `stdout.encoding` `UTF-16` | 36 | A byte-oriented comparison fails although the characters are identical |

The practical reading is that the payload's **characters** are invariant while its **byte count** depends on two host settings, only one of which — the line separator — this document discusses elsewhere. This is why `README.md` line 63 expresses the contract as the literal plus its single trailing separator rather than as a byte count, and it is the reason the corresponding open item is recorded as closed in Section 9.3.

### 9.1.5 Runtime Footprint and One-Off Timing Measurements

Sections 5.4.5, 6.5.3.2 and 6.6.1.4.4 state, correctly, that the repository declares **no** performance requirement, service-level objective, latency budget or capacity plan, and that no timing could be taken in the environment used to produce this specification. For completeness this appendix records that one-off measurements nevertheless exist, in the archived committed specification, taken on its own `21.0.12` host against the pre-comment revision. They are reproduced with that provenance and carry no normative force: they are not targets, not thresholds, not re-verified here, and they describe a different toolchain and a different revision of the source.

| Recorded quantity | Value | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wall clock, pre-compiled run | ≈ 29 ms (30, 29, 29 and 29, 29, 32 ms across two batches) | Dominated by JVM start-up, not by application work |
| Wall clock, single-file source launch | ≈ 341–344 ms | Compilation is repeated in memory on every invocation |
| Wall clock and memory, compile | 342 ms at 82 MB peak RSS | The compiler, not the program, sets the machine requirement |
| Peak resident memory, run | ≈ 39 MB against a 536,870,912-byte (512 MB) initial heap reservation | The gap between reservation and residency bounds invocation density |
| Cold end-to-end gate suite | 779 ms for compile, static gate and run | Two compilations plus one harness run |
| Platform class loads per run | 479 with class-data sharing disabled, of which exactly **one** (`Hello`) comes from the application classpath | All 13 network-named loads come from `jrt:/java.base` |

| Runtime packaging option | Recorded size | Modules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full JDK installation on the recording host | 286 MB | 69 |
| `jlink` image containing only `java.base` | 57 MB | 1 |
| The program itself | 420 bytes | — |

`jdeps` reported `java.base` as the compiled class's only module requirement, and the minimal `jlink` image executed the program and produced the same 17-byte payload. The forward-looking implication is the one Section 8.5 reaches from the containerisation side: a self-contained distribution of this program is bounded below by roughly 57 MB of runtime, some 142,000 times the artifact it exists to run, and no module-selection work would be required to build it.

One instrumentation figure is worth recording because it quantifies an absence this document asserts qualitatively. Enabling JDK Flight Recorder on a run produced a 199–206 KB recording holding 2,390 events but **zero** `jdk.ExecutionSample` events and only four `jdk.ObjectAllocationSample` events, while raising peak memory to 109,180 kB and runtime to 340 ms — roughly eleven times the cost of the work being observed. It also writes a start-up banner to standard output, making the payload 238 bytes instead of 17 unless `-Xlog:disable` is supplied. That is the measured reason why, as Section 5.4.1 concludes, there is nothing here worth instrumenting: a 29-millisecond process produces no execution sample, and the observer costs an order of magnitude more than the observed.

### 9.1.6 Repository Internals at `HEAD`

Section 6.2 documents the Git object store as the system's only durable structure, its ten blobs and its index and pack files. The object-level and configuration figures below were measured here and complete that picture.

The remote URL is deliberately omitted from that table: the clone's own URL embeds a working credential, which Section 6.4 classifies without reproducing and which this appendix likewise never reproduces. The three unset keys are load-bearing rather than incidental — with `core.autocrlf` and `core.eol` unset and no `.gitattributes` in the tree, nothing normalises line endings, which is why `Hello.java` round-trips its CRLF bytes (requirement F-005-RQ-004), and with `commit.gpgsign` unset, signing is a per-author choice rather than a repository policy.

**The eight refs resolve to three distinct commits**, which is the measured form of the delivery gap Section 4.4.4 records: `refs/heads/jr_java1` and `refs/remotes/origin/jr_java1` at `2a78292`; `refs/remotes/origin/blitzy-6d6c8680-f3ef-4055-9d11-0fc35e375843` at `b4a1188`; and `refs/heads/main`, `refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`, `refs/remotes/origin/main`, `refs/remotes/origin/jr_java2` and `refs/remotes/origin/jr_java3` all still at `0726b1d`. Four of the eight refs therefore point at the version-1.0 baseline.

Four observations follow, none of them recorded elsewhere in this document:

- **The original program and licence were authored in a 118-second window.** The first three commits are 47 and 71 seconds apart; the whole 14-commit history spans 532,021 seconds — 6 days and 3 hours — of which 437,146 seconds is the single gap between the last content commit and the pull-request merge.
- **The tracked tree has been frozen since `297792f`.** Commits `297792f`, `2c27dcf`, `cff1dd1`, `9f7e12c`, `b4a1188` and the merge `2a78292` all point at the same tree, `a837de2a`, and `git diff --stat 297792f b4a1188` is empty. Five of the fourteen commits — including the merge that is `HEAD` — introduce no content change whatever, which is why requirement-set version 2.0 can be anchored at `2a78292` while every byte it describes was written at `297792f`.
- **The growth curve is almost entirely documentation.** From 35,317 bytes at the version-1.0 baseline the tree grew to 925,008 bytes; 884,733 of the 889,691 added bytes are the two files under `blitzy/documentation/`, added in two consecutive commits seven seconds apart. The source itself grew by 946 bytes and the guide by 4,012.
- **One commit shrank the tree.** `14ed6db` removed 33 bytes (a duplicate source citation) and `ce8e85c` a further 620, because tightening the Javadoc removed more bytes from `Hello.java` than the safer build guidance added to `README.md`. Both are refinements inside the comment-only change, not reversals of it.

The signature histogram — 4 commits reporting `E` and 10 reporting `N` — is documented in Section 6.4.3.5. The additional detail measurable here is its distribution: every `rjhonsi` commit and the bot merge carry a signature that cannot be verified without the signer's key, while all ten `Blitzy Agent` commits carry none, and `commit.gpgsign` is unset, so nothing in the repository requested otherwise.

| "Three commits, all carrying a `gpgsig` header"; five refs all at `0726b1d` | archived spec §9.1.6 | 14 commits with a 4-`E` / 10-`N` signature histogram; 8 refs at 3 distinct commits |
| Nine objects in a 15.84 KiB pack; `.git/index` 289 bytes; `HEAD` tree `dfdbb032` with 3 entries | archived spec §9.1.6 | 37 objects in a 302.84 KiB pack; index 574 bytes; `HEAD` tree `a837de2a` with 4 entries |

Two structural warnings belong with the ledger. **The archived specification's identifier namespaces are incompatible with this document's**: it numbers workflows `WF-01`…`WF-05`, failure modes `ERR-01`…`ERR-10`, decisions `ADR-01`…`ADR-07`, security controls with a reused `C-` prefix, and test cases `TC-01`…`TC-21`, none of which appear in this specification (Section 9.2 gives the current registry). A cross-reference read out of the archived document will not resolve against this one. **And its open-item register is partly superseded**: Section 9.3 reconciles it item by item.

The one thing the archived specification remains authoritative for is the body of runtime evidence reproduced in Sections 9.1.3 through 9.1.5, because it was gathered with a JDK on a host that had one, and no later document re-measured it.

### 9.1.12 Verification Environment for This Appendix

| Element | Observed value |
| --- | --- |
| Host | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel Linux 6.12.85+ |
| Git client | `git` 2.43.0; object format SHA-1 |
| JDK toolchain | **Absent.** `java`, `javac`, `javadoc`, `javap`, `jdeps`, `jlink` and `jfr` are all unresolvable on `PATH`; `JAVA_HOME` is empty |
| Other absent tools | `file` and `/usr/bin/time` are not installed, so no artifact typing or timing could be performed |
| Process defaults | `umask` 0022; `mktemp -d` produced a directory with mode 2700 while `/tmp` itself is mode 2777 |

The last row is a first-hand confirmation of the threat model behind ADR-009: a freshly generated destination is owner-only, whereas the world-writable directory it sits in is precisely the condition that makes a fixed, predictable compiler-output path pre-creatable or symlink-redirectable by another local process, exactly as `README.md` line 30 states.

Everything in this appendix labelled *measured here* was produced with `git`, `sha256sum`, `md5sum`, `wc`, `stat`, `awk`, `grep`, `sed` and `python3` against the checkout; nothing was executed that required a JDK. The single untracked file in the working tree, `tech_spec.md`, is an authoring artifact of the documentation process — byte-identical to the committed archive, as its shared MD5 in Section 9.1.1 shows — and it is excluded from every census and figure above.


## 9.2 Identifier Registry and Traceability Index

This specification assigns stable identifiers in nineteen namespaces across eight sections. No single section lists them all, and two prefixes are used twice with overlapping number ranges, so this registry is the resolution point for any identifier a reader meets out of context.

| `C-n` *(capability)* | C-1 … C-9 | 1.3.1.1 | Must-have capabilities: single compilable source, launchable entry point, fixed greeting, clean termination, argument insensitivity, launch-path equivalence, operator guide, licence terms, self-explaining source |
| `W-n` | W-1 … W-4 | 1.3.1.1, expanded in 4.1 | Operator workflows: compile in place then run; compile outside the checkout then run; single-file source launch; verify the output contract |
| `M-n` | M-1 … M-3 | 4.1, 4.3 | Maintenance flows: source edit with parity verification; verification and coverage measurement; commit, merge and delivery |
| `F-nnn` | F-001 … F-009 | 2.1 | Features, from the JVM entry-point contract to the project-status record |
| `F-nnn-RQ-nnn` | 45 requirements | 2.2 | Functional requirements, always compound and always scoped to the parent feature |
| `A-n` | A-1 … A-7 | 2.6.1 | Assumptions each requirement depends on, with the basis on which each was established |
| `K-n` | K-1 … K-7 | 2.6.2 | Constraints on the requirement set, including the absent gate (K-3) and the stale layout claim (K-6) |

Requirement-set versions are not a prefixed namespace but are identified in the same way: version 1.0 is anchored at commit `0726b1d` and version 2.0 at `2a78292`, because no tag exists to name either (Section 2.6.3, constraint K-4).

### 9.2.3 Disambiguation and Resolution Rules

Six rules resolve every ambiguity in the registry. They are stated because two of them cannot be resolved from the identifier alone.

- **The `C-` prefix is used twice, and its ranges overlap.** Section 1.3.1.1 numbers capabilities C-1 … C-9 and Section 5.1.2 numbers components C-1 … C-10, so `C-3` means the fixed-greeting capability in a requirements context and the standard-output write path in an architectural one. **Resolution depends on the citing section**, not on the number: Sections 1, 2 and 4.4.2 use the capability sense; Sections 5 and 6 use the component sense.
- **The `D-` prefix is used twice, and its ranges overlap.** Section 4 labels workflow decision points D-n; Section 6.4.4.1 labels data classifications D-1 … D-6. A `D-n` reference inside a workflow or flowchart discussion is a decision point; one inside the data-protection discussion is a data class.
- **Hyphenation separates two `P-`/`M-` families.** Persistence and flow identifiers are hyphenated (`M-1` is a maintenance flow); applicability preconditions are not (`M1` is a monitoring precondition, `P1` an architectural one). The precondition families are also section-local: `P1 … P5` in Sections 6.1 and 6.2 test different propositions from `P1 … P6` in Section 6.4.
- **Requirement identifiers are always compound.** A requirement is written with its feature prefix — `F-006-RQ-005` — so the bare form `RQ-005` never appears, and requirement numbers restart inside each feature.
- **Two namespaces are inherited rather than assigned here.** `V1 … V9` are the repository's own acceptance groups, defined in `Project Guide.md` §3; `OI-n` were first assigned by the archived specification and are re-anchored, renumbered where necessary and reconciled to `HEAD` in Section 9.3.
- **The archived specification's namespaces do not resolve against this document.** It used `WF-nn` for workflows, `ERR-nn` for failure modes, `ADR-nn` with two digits, `TC-nn` for test cases, `MUT-n` for injected defects, `QG-n` for quality gates, `TENV-n` for test environments, `IF-n` for interfaces, `DP-n` for decision points, `R-n` for residual risks, `ENV-n` and `STG-n` for absent environments and pipeline stages, and a reused `C-` prefix for security controls. None of those forms appears in this specification; Section 9.1.11 records the wider incompatibility.

### 9.2.5 Evidence and Status Vocabularies

Three closed vocabularies carry as much meaning in this document as the identifiers do, and each has a defining sub-section.

| Vocabulary | Values | Defined in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verification method | *static* — established directly against the tree; *recorded* — executed by the project's own validation run and reported in `Project Guide.md`; *open* — not satisfied or not verified at `HEAD` | 2.2.1, applied in 2.5.1 |
| Decision provenance | *Stated* — the repository names the choice and its reason; *Recorded* — the position is stated without argument; *Reconstructed* — evident only from what the artifacts do and do not contain | 5.3.1 |
| Applicability status | *Genuinely absent* — no corresponding surface exists; *Selected* — the repository chose a mechanism in place of the conventional one; *Inherited* — in force but supplied by the JDK, Git, the shell or the hosting platform; *Absent and expected* — a practice a maintained project would carry, and it is missing | 6.4.1, 6.5.1, 6.6.1.1 |

Only four decisions in the entire document carry the *Stated* label, which is why Section 5.3.1 enumerates them individually: the default package as the reason for bare-name launch, single-sink output, termination by normal return, and the freshly generated compiler-output directory.


## 9.3 Open Items and Known Gaps Register

Earlier sections each record the gaps they meet in their own scope — an unsatisfied requirement in Section 2.5, a residual risk in Section 6.4.5.3, an absent gate in Sections 3.6.3 and 6.6.2.1, a continuity item in Section 5.4.6. Nowhere are they collected. This register consolidates them under stable identifiers.

The `OI-n` identifiers were first assigned by the archived committed specification, which closed its register at twelve items. They are retained here rather than renumbered, because two of them were explicitly closed by a commit that cites them: `dabe2c9` "Replace README placeholder with project guide" ends its message with "Closes OI-9 and OI-12." One item is new. The arithmetic reconciles exactly to the count the repository itself publishes: `Project Guide.md` §1.4 states "No defect is open in the delivered code. **11 items remain open** — 10 of the 12 the specification tracks, this work having closed 2, plus 1 verification-invocation item."

### 9.3.1 Register

| ID | Open item | Status at `HEAD` | Where tracked in this document |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OI-1 | A rejected or discarded write to standard output still yields exit status 0 with an empty error stream, so a run can deliver nothing and report success | **Open.** Structural: the source queries no stream error state, and Section 5.3.3 records that the program "cannot detect delivery failure and does not try" | 5.3.3, 6.1.4.5; `Project Guide.md` §1.4 verification-oracle item, Owner decision, Deferred |
| OI-2 | `Hello.java` carries no per-file copyright or licence header, and no holder or year is recorded anywhere in the tree | **Open.** Cannot be closed until a rights holder and year exist to name | F-006-RQ-005; ADR-010; 2.4.4; hygiene group, Low, part of 2.0 h |
| OI-3 | No Java version, distribution or checksum is pinned; the compiler alone sets the compatibility range | **Open — accepted.** The trade ADR-007 makes; runtime CVE exposure is left to the operator's JDK | ADR-007; 3.7.3; 5.3.6 residual risk |
| OI-4 | Line endings are unmanaged: `Hello.java` is CRLF on all 20 lines, the other text files LF, with no `.gitattributes` and `core.autocrlf`/`core.eol` unset | **Open — accepted by design.** Normalising would rewrite all five code lines and change the file's digest | F-005-RQ-004, F-008-RQ-005; fault E-5; 9.1.6 |

| OI-6 | No automated correctness gate exists on any commit; verification is manual and nothing re-runs it | **Open — Deferred, owner decision.** All 14 `.git/hooks` entries are samples and no CI descriptor has ever been tracked | ADR-002; K-3; 3.6.3, 6.6.2.1 |
| OI-7 | `javadoc` emits "no comment" warnings for the documentable members | **Restated and largely closed.** Three warnings at the version-1.0 baseline; **exactly one** at `HEAD`, for the implicit default constructor, which can carry no doc comment. Recorded as Accepted with no action; coverage 2 of 3 | F-008-RQ-004; 6.6.3.1; 9.1.3 |

Feature F-007 was raised from Low to High | 2.6.3; F-007-RQ-001 … RQ-005 |

| OI-12 | A fixed 17-byte output oracle is host-conditioned: a CRLF separator yields 18 bytes, and a UTF-16 standard-output encoding 36, with no change to the source | **Closed** by `dabe2c9`: `README.md` line 63 now states the contract as the literal plus its single trailing separator and says explicitly that "the exact byte count varies between platforms" | 9.1.4; F-002-RQ-002; F-007-RQ-002 |
| OI-13 | The comment-census check compares the working source against the current commit, so under its default baseline it reports failures against a correct tree | **Open — new at this generation.** A correct tree scores 33 of 37; supplying the pre-comment revision `0726b1d` restores 37 of 37. The remedy is the invocation, since the suite is provisioned outside the repository | Fault E-4; 6.6.2.6; Maintainer, 1.0 h, High |

One item is deliberately excluded from the register and is recorded here so that its exclusion is not mistaken for an oversight: the working credential held in the clone's own `.git/config`. Section 6.4 classifies it without reproducing it, this appendix does not reproduce it either, and it is a property of the local clone rather than of the tracked tree — no clone conveys it.
